index.title: Go Proverb Database
index.content:
Welcome to the Go Proverb Database.
This is an interactive collection of classic Go sayings. Each entry starts with a proverb, then expands with diagrams and practical explanations.

“Some saying…”

Over time, each proverb page will include:

Interactive board diagrams
Move-by-move examples
Clear commentary on when the proverb applies (and when it does not)

If you are learning or teaching Go, this site is meant to be a practical reference you can return to often.

proverbs/Shapes/4th_line_lower_attatchme.title: 4th Line Lower Attachment
proverbs/Shapes/4th_line_lower_attatchme.content:
4th Line Lower Attachment
Meaning
The 4th line lower attachment is a contact play where you attach directly underneath an opponent’s high stone on the fourth line, placing your stone on the third line.
Because the fourth line stone emphasizes outward influence and center power, slipping directly underneath it challenges its base and establishes immediate local leverage. It forces the opponent to choose between defending their outward posture or descending to fight for territory.
Why it is useful

Rapid foundation: Carves out an instant base and eye potential on the third line.
Sabaki accelerator: Generates forcing moves that let an invading or reducing group stabilize with ease.
Limits enemy moyo: Restricts the downward expansion of the opponent’s fourth-line framework.

Limits

Strengthens the opponent’s outside: If the opponent hanes on top and builds outside thickness, make sure your surrounding stones are not endangered.
Avoid when behind in thickness: If the opponent’s fourth-line stone is backed by massive nearby strength, the attachment can be trapped.

Example
White holds the fourth line at jp. Black attaches directly underneath at A (jq) on the third line, probing White’s response and seeking quick stability.

proverbs/Shapes/answer_atari.title: Answer Atari
proverbs/Shapes/answer_atari.content:
Answer atari
What it means
A stone or group in atari has only one liberty. If the opponent can take it on the next move, first look for a way to save it by extending, connecting, or capturing the attacking stones.
Answering atari is the safe default because ignoring it usually loses stones. Before replying automatically, however, compare the value of the threatened stones with every forcing move available elsewhere.
When to answer
Answer the atari when the stones are important and the reply gives them a useful future. A good answer may:

connect the group to friendly stones;
capture the stones giving atari;
increase its liberties enough to escape; or
preserve cutting points, territory, or influence.

When not to answer
Do not save stones merely because they can be saved. Consider ignoring the atari when the stones are already expendable, when the escape would only create a weak group, or when you can play a larger forcing move such as an atari, capture, or ko threat of your own.
Before answering, ask: What happens if these stones are captured? If the loss is small and taking sente is worth more, sacrificing them may be the stronger choice.

proverbs/Shapes/armpithit.title: Armpit Hit
proverbs/Shapes/armpithit.content:
Armpit Hit
Meaning
The armpit hit is a contact move played directly underneath an opponent’s high stone (typically on the fourth line) on the third line, placed along the side of the stone. It contacts the stone just beneath its extended reach—analogous to hitting someone under the armpit.
It is a sharp, provocative technique used to flatten an opponent’s outward framework and establish a rapid, light foothold.
Why it is useful

Flattens enemy influence: Prevents the fourth-line stone from developing smooth outward influence.
Initiates sabaki: Forces the opponent to respond locally, creating leverage to settle your stones cleanly.
Probes intentions: Tests whether the opponent prioritizes territory on the side or influence toward the center.

Limits

Strengthens the opponent: Contact moves inherently give the contacted stone extra thickness if mishandled.
Read the push and cut: Be prepared for the opponent to hane on top or push down aggressively.

Example
White has a high stone at jp. Black strikes with the armpit hit at A (iq) or B (kq), contacting the stone from underneath to disrupt White’s framework.

proverbs/Shapes/arrowhead.title: Arrowhead
proverbs/Shapes/arrowhead.content:
Arrowhead
Meaning
The arrowhead (or spearhead shape) is an aggressive, triangular formation of stones pointing directly into the opponent’s sphere of influence or through a narrow corridor between enemy stones.
By consolidating local strength into a forward-pointing vertex, the arrowhead threatens to split opposing forces on either side while maintaining mutual support between the spearheading stones.
Why it is useful

Splitting power: Forces the opponent to defend two separate flanks at once.
Directional momentum: Creates a sharp forward thrust toward the center or into an enemy moyo.
Tactical stability: The stones reinforce each other diagonally and orthogonally, making them resilient under pressure.

Limits

Avoid overconcentration: Ensure the shape does not collapse into an empty triangle or become heavy if the opponent surrounds it.
Check cutting aji: Verify that the wings of the arrowhead cannot be isolated with counter-hane or crosscuts.

Example
Black plays at A (ee), completing the sharp arrowhead shape to pierce White’s formation and seize the tactical initiative in the center.

proverbs/Shapes/bamboo_joint.title: Bamboo Joint
proverbs/Shapes/bamboo_joint.content:
bamboo_joint
Example

Meaning
A bamboo joint is a strong, flexible connection made from two parallel pairs of
stones with a one-point gap between the pairs. In the example, playing at A
completes the shape; the two marked points are the gaps inside the joint.
The gaps are miai: if the opponent enters at either point, playing
at the other keeps the stones connected. This makes a direct cut ineffective
without requiring a solid connection in advance.
Why it is useful

Reliable connection: the opponent cannot normally separate the two pairs
with a single move.
Efficient shape: it connects while leaving more liberties and outward
development than a tightly packed formation.
Flexible response: either internal gap can serve as the connecting point,
so the shape is resilient under pressure.

Look for a bamboo joint when nearby stones need to cooperate in a fight, but a
solid connection would be slow or overconcentrated. Its strength often lets you
play elsewhere in sente instead of adding another defensive move.
Limits
The bamboo joint is strong, not automatic. Before relying on it, read whether
the opponent has an atari, shortage of liberties, snapback, or nearby cutting
stone that changes the local sequence. It can also be inefficient to complete
the shape when the groups are already safe or when a larger move is available.

proverbs/Shapes/bend.title: Bend
proverbs/Shapes/bend.content:
Bend (Magari)
Meaning
The bend (magari) is a powerful turn played at the head of a line of stones. Instead of continuing straight in the same direction, your stone turns at a right angle, pressing against the opponent’s advance or wrapping around their flank.
A well-timed bend is one of the most vital shape moves in Go: it often represents the border where two opposing lines of force collide, dictating which player seizes the outside and which is pressed down.
Why it is useful

Dominates the boundary: Reverses the direction of the local fight and blocks the enemy’s natural development.
Generates thickness: Creates a sturdy, forward-facing structure with abundant liberties and eye potential.
Maintains sente: An unanswered bend often allows a devastating follow-up hane or clamp.

Limits

Do not bend into bad shape: Ensure your bend does not give the opponent an easy double-atari or counter-cut.
Evaluate tempo: In the early game, make sure bending locally is more urgent than taking an open corner or large side point.

Example
In the diagram, Black bends at A (ed), rounding the corner against White’s two stones to block White’s expansion and establish control over the flank.

proverbs/Shapes/big_bend.title: Big Bend
proverbs/Shapes/big_bend.content:
Big Bend (Grand Turn)
Meaning
The big bend is a sweeping, large-scale turn played at the intersection of two major spheres of influence. When stones meet across open territory, bending around the corner of the opposing formation seals off expansive center potential while depriving the opponent of their natural growth direction.
It is often described as a move worth thirty points because of its dual impact: growing your own framework while flattening the opponent’s.
Why it is useful

Mutual influence pivot: Swings the entire balance of board influence in a single move.
Thick center presence: Gives your stones commanding presence looking into both the center and adjacent sides.
Prevents being capped: Turning first ensures your group is not capped or sealed into the lower lines.

Limits

Watch the cutting points: A wide turn can leave a diagonal gap if played too loosely; verify your supporting stones.
Ensure timing: Play the big bend when the boundary between opposing frameworks is contested, not after the area is already settled.

Example
Black plays the big bend at A (fd), dramatically expanding Black’s framework while pressing down White’s stone (ff) and dominating the center.

proverbs/Shapes/big_bulge.title: Big Bulge
proverbs/Shapes/big_bulge.content:
Big Bulge (Fukurami)
Meaning
The big bulge (fukurami) is an expanding shape move where a stone bows outward from a contact fight rather than retreating or connecting flatly. It pushes outward into the open space, challenging the opponent’s surrounding net and demanding an immediate response.
By “swelling” outward, the bulge simultaneously generates internal eye space and creates threats to cut or press against the opponent’s weaker stones.
Why it is useful

Instant eye potential: Opens up room for living eyes inside contested, tight quarters.
Relieves pressure: Breaks out of heavy enemy containment, forcing the opponent to reinforce their own perimeter.
Flexible sabaki tool: An indispensable technique when settling weak groups in the middle game.

Limits

Check liberties: Bulging can place your stone into close contact with enemy strength; ensure you have enough liberties to survive counter-ataris.
Do not create an empty triangle: Make sure the outward bulge does not deform into an inefficient, clustered shape.

Example
Black plays at A (ff), bulging powerfully into the open space between White’s stones to secure breathing room and establish eye shape.

proverbs/Shapes/butting_play.title: Butting Play
proverbs/Shapes/butting_play.content:
Butting Play (Tsukiatari)
Meaning
A butting play (tsukiatari) is a direct head-on collision where a stone is played straight into the head of an opposing stone along the same grid line. Unlike a grazing attachment or shoulder hit, the butting play hits head-to-head.
It is typically played to block an opponent’s advance decisively, reinforce a vital cutting point, or force an immediate defensive connection in sente.
Why it is useful

Direct stoppage: Instantly arrests an opponent’s forward push into your territory or eye space.
Forcing tempo: Threatens to cut through or push further, compelling the opponent to answer right away.
Reinforces local structure: Firms up your surrounding shape prior to launching an attack.

Limits

Can strengthen the opponent: Because it is a direct contact move, the opponent’s natural response will usually add a stone and gain liberties. Use it with a specific tactical aim.
Avoid clumsy collisions: Do not butt into enemy stones if doing so leaves your stone with only two liberties.

Example
Black butts directly at A (ee), slamming into White’s stone (fe) to block White’s march and seize immediate tactical control.

proverbs/Shapes/cap.title: Cap
proverbs/Shapes/cap.content:
Cap
What is a cap?
A cap is a move played in front of an opposing stone or group, usually one or two lines away. Rather than making direct contact, it uses nearby stones and outward influence to limit the opponent’s development.
The cap asks the running group an immediate question: can it escape, make shape, or counterattack before it is surrounded? A well-timed cap often keeps sente because the opponent must respond locally.
When to play it
A cap is most effective when:

your stones already support the capping move from both sides;
the opposing group is unsettled and has few useful directions to run;
driving the group toward your strength will create profit elsewhere; or
the cap also expands your framework or protects a weak point.

Do not expect every cap to capture. Its usual purpose is to restrict and attack for profit. While the opponent struggles to make shape, you may strengthen your outside position, build territory, or gain forcing moves.
What to read first
Before capping, check the opponent’s likely replies:

A jump underneath: Can the group slip past the cap or connect to friendly stones?
A contact move: If the opponent attaches, can you keep your stones connected without becoming heavy?
A counter-cut: Does the cap leave a cutting point that turns the attack against you?
A sacrifice: Can the opponent give up a few stones and take profit somewhere larger?

Keep enough distance to preserve flexibility. If the cap is too close, an attachment may make the opponent stronger. If it is too far away, the group may escape without difficulty.
Common mistake
Do not cap merely because a group is running. Capping from weak or unsupported stones can create two weak groups of your own. Strengthen your position first, then use the cap to guide the opponent toward your strongest area.
Example
The marked point A is the cap. It occupies the space in front of the white stone and restricts its route toward the center. The highlighted surrounding points show the area the cap is intended to influence; the exact follow-up depends on how White tries to escape.

proverbs/Shapes/clamp.title: Clamp
proverbs/Shapes/clamp.content:
Clamp (Hasami-tsuke)
Meaning
The clamp (hasami-tsuke) is a sharp contact tesuji where a stone is attached directly to the outside of an enemy stone that already faces another friendly stone. It traps the opponent in a tight pincer-like grip between two stones.
The clamp exerts extreme tactical pressure: it threatens to connect underneath to undercut territory, or cut on top to separate enemy stones and reduce their liberties.
Why it is useful

Under-the-stones connection: Threatens to slide underneath the opponent’s stone to steal base territory and connect home.
Forces heavy shape: Compels the opponent into awkward, heavy responses that lose tempo.
Severe endgame reduction: A staple endgame technique to shave points off an opponent’s border in sente.

Limits

Requires local support: If your clamping stone lacks nearby allies, the opponent can simply push and cut, capturing the clamp in atari.
Read variations on both sides: Always check whether the opponent will descend, connect over, or atari underneath before committing.

Example
Black plays the clamp at A (fe), attaching directly to White’s stone (ee) to squeeze its liberties and threaten a connection underneath.

proverbs/Shapes/connect_bamboo.title: Connect Bamboo
proverbs/Shapes/connect_bamboo.content:
Connect Bamboo
Meaning
Connecting into a bamboo joint is a fundamental technique for uniting two pairs of stones with absolute stability. When the opponent pushes or attempts to cut into the one-point gap, answering at the remaining open point immediately restores the mutual connection (miai).
Unlike a rigid clump of stones, a completed bamboo joint provides high structural integrity while leaving plenty of liberties and open pathways toward the outside.
Why it is useful

Unbreakable connection: Once the bamboo joint is reinforced, the opponent cannot cut through the formation with normal tactical moves.
Liberty efficiency: The shape maintains outward liberties on both sides, avoiding the cramped weakness of an empty triangle.
Tempo control: Because the connection is rock solid, you can often turn your attention elsewhere in sente without needing further defensive reinforcement.

Limits

Avoid redundant plays: If the opponent has not peeped or threatened the gap, adding a stone to connect the bamboo joint preemptively is often slow (gote) when larger whole-board moves are available.
Shortage of liberties: Be alert to nearby ataris or damezumari (shortage of liberties) that might prevent you from responding cleanly to a cut.

Example
In the diagram, White has pushed into the gap at cc. Black plays at A (cb) to complete the connection, securing the bamboo joint and leaving White with no cut.

proverbs/Shapes/connect_cut.title: Connect Cut
proverbs/Shapes/connect_cut.content:
Connect Across a Cut
Meaning
Connect your stones across a cutting point before your opponent can separate them. A timely connection keeps the stones working as one group, while an unanswered cut can leave two weak groups that must each find liberties, shape, and life.
When to apply it
Look for this move when two friendly groups touch only diagonally or share a single vulnerable cutting point. Connecting is especially urgent when either resulting group would be difficult to defend on its own.
Do not connect automatically. If both groups are already safe, the cut does not work tactically, or you can profitably sacrifice one side, playing elsewhere may be larger.
Practical check
Before choosing another move, ask:

Where would the opponent cut?
Can both halves survive and remain useful after that cut?
Does connecting now also improve shape or threaten an attack?

If the cut would create two burdensome groups, connect first.

proverbs/Shapes/corner_extension.title: Corner Extension
proverbs/Shapes/corner_extension.content:
Corner Extension (Shimari Development)
Meaning
A corner extension is a strategic extension from a settled corner enclosure (shimari) along the adjacent side. In Go opening theory, corner enclosures are formidable, but their full potential is only realized when paired with an extension along the side.
Extending along the side both converts the corner framework into vast, secure territory and stakes a claim toward the center.
Why it is useful

Magnifies corner value: Transforms a corner base into 20–30 points of side and corner territory.
Ideal spacing: Establishes harmonious coordinate spacing with existing stones along the third or fourth line.
Denies enemy counter-extensions: Prevents the opponent from approaching your enclosure and squeezing your position.

Limits

Avoid overextension: Extending too far (e.g. past the midpoint into enemy influence) invites easy invasions.
Balance third and fourth lines: Use the third line for secure cash territory and the fourth line for center influence.

Example
Black holds a corner enclosure at cp-eq. Black can extend along the side to A (ci), B (cj), C (di), or D (dj) to establish harmonious territorial balance.

proverbs/Shapes/crawl.title: Crawl
proverbs/Shapes/crawl.content:
Crawl (Hai)
Meaning
Crawling (hai) refers to extending repeatedly along the edge of the board (typically the second line) while directly touching an opposing wall of stones above it.
While crawling can secure minimal territory or keep a besieged group alive, it hands the opponent massive outward influence and thickness on the higher lines with every push. The classic proverb warns: “The second line is the line of defeat.”
Why it is useful

Emergency survival: Essential when a corner or side group has no other way to secure life or connect to living allies.
Liberty generation: Keeps your stones from being captured when running in a capturing race (semeai).

Limits

Avoid excessive crawling: Every move you crawl gives the opponent a free wall of immense power in the center.
Turn or jump when possible: Always look for the earliest opportunity to hane, turn, or tenuki once your group is safe.

Example
In the diagram, Black crawls at A (de), extending along the side in contact with White’s stone (ef) to preserve liberties and maintain survival.

proverbs/Shapes/crosscut.title: Crosscut
proverbs/Shapes/crosscut.content:
Crosscut (Cross-cut)
Meaning
A crosscut occurs when four stones touch each other in an interlocking 2x2 grid of alternating colors. It creates an explosive, highly tactical confrontation where all four stones have only two liberties each.
The universal Go proverb for this shape is: “Crosscut then extend!” Extending from a crosscut increases your stone’s liberties, clarifies your tactical objectives, and forces the opponent to choose which side to defend.
Why it is useful

Supreme sabaki tool: Creates instant confusion inside enemy spheres of influence, allowing weak groups to settle or sacrifice lightly.
Splits enemy forces: Severely tests the opponent’s reading and cuts their stones into two struggling factions.
Simplifies through extension: An extension immediately breaks the symmetry and takes the upper hand in liberties.

Limits

Read before cutting: Never crosscut blindly; the resulting fight will quickly lead to captures, ladders, or nets.
Don’t atari blindly: Beginning players often play atari immediately after a crosscut, which frequently helps the opponent make good shape. Extend first!

Example
Black plays the crosscut at A (fe), locking horns diagonally with White’s stones (ee, ff) and immediately challenging the local connection.

proverbs/Shapes/double_hane.title: Double Hane
proverbs/Shapes/double_hane.content:
Double hane
Meaning
A double hane is the forceful shape made by bending around an opposing
stone twice in succession. The second hane presses from the other side of the
contact, challenging the opponent’s connection and often creating a cut.
It is more aggressive than simply extending after the first hane. That extra
pressure can produce good shape, take the initiative, or separate opposing
stones—but it also leaves cutting points of its own.
When to consider it
Look for the double hane when:

the opponent’s stones are short of liberties or cannot connect cleanly;
nearby friendly stones support the fight;
a cut would divide the opponent into two weak groups; or
the sequence gives useful forcing moves and keeps sente.

Before playing it, read the opponent’s cut, atari, and counter-atari. Check any
ladder or capturing race that follows; without enough support, the double hane
can make your own stones heavy or leave them split.
Example
The move at A completes the double hane. It bends around the end of the
white stones a second time and puts immediate pressure on their connection.

Practical reminder
Treat the proverb as a prompt to read, not a command to play automatically.
When the cut works, the double hane is a powerful tesuji. When
the cut favors the opponent, a simple extension or connection is usually the
sounder choice.

proverbs/Shapes/double_keima_extension.title: Double Keima Extension
proverbs/Shapes/double_keima_extension.content:
Double Keima Extension (Ryo-Keima)
Meaning
A double keima extension (ryo-keima) uses two coordinated knight’s moves extending from a base or anchor stone. Instead of advancing in a straight line, the stones step diagonally like a pair of wings.
This configuration allows swift territorial coverage and rapid adaptation to enemy threats coming from multiple directions.
Why it is useful

Speedy coverage: Encloses territory and projects influence faster than solid jumps.
Flexible options: Provides multiple branching paths to connect or counter-attack when approached.
Natural eye shape: Creates multiple overlapping pockets that easily form two eyes.

Limits

Diagonal cut vulnerability: Knight’s moves contain internal gaps; ensure you can defend the waist of the keima if the opponent cuts.
Not for dense fighting: Best deployed in open board situations during the opening.

Example
Black coordinates stones at ee and dg, extending rapidly with another knight’s move to A (gd) to form a swift double-keima framework.

proverbs/Shapes/empty_triangle.title: Empty Triangle
proverbs/Shapes/empty_triangle.content:
Empty Triangle (Aki-sankaku)
Meaning
The empty triangle (aki-sankaku) is a formation where three friendly stones form an “L” or triangular corner around an empty intersection. It is universally condemned as the quintessential example of bad shape in Go.
Unlike a full triangle that has captured or surrounded an opposing stone, the empty triangle commits three stones to cover an empty point, resulting in severe overconcentration, reduced liberties, and clunky movement.
Why it is useful (to avoid)

Liberty deficiency: An empty triangle has only 7 liberties instead of the 8 liberties provided by three stones in a straight line or bend.
Wasted efficiency: Three stones do the work of two, falling behind in the race for development.
Vulnerable to attack: Heavy shapes make easy targets for enemy peeps, caps, and squeezing tactics.

Limits

Tactical exceptions: In rare tactical emergencies, making an empty triangle may be the only legal way to connect, save cutting stones, or win a tight capturing race. Play it only when forced by pure calculation.

Example
Black stones at de and ee risk forming an empty triangle if Black plays at the marked intersection dd without capturing an enemy stone.

proverbs/Shapes/extend_from_attatchment.title: Extend From Attachment
proverbs/Shapes/extend_from_attatchment.content:
Extend From Attachment (Nobi)
Meaning
The proverb “Against contact, extend” (tsuke ni wa nobi) is one of the most fundamental shape rules in Go. When an opponent attaches directly to your stone, your default and most solid answer is to extend straight forward (nobi).
Extending directly increases your stone’s liberties from three to at least five, solidifies your local structure, and denies the opponent easy crosscuts or double ataris.
Why it is useful

Liberty assurance: Immediately removes any risk of being overwhelmed by contact tactics.
Maintains good shape: Produces thick, clean formations without leaving tactical weaknesses behind.
Strategic patience: Often keeps sente or sets up a powerful counter-attack once the opponent’s contact stones are overextended.

Limits

Evaluate hane: When you have overwhelming local superiority, playing hane instead of extending can apply stronger pressure.
Do not extend into danger: Make sure the direction of your extension heads toward open board space or friendly strength.

Example
White attaches at ef. Black responds calmly by extending at A (de), solidifying the shape and securing extra liberties.

proverbs/Shapes/extend_weak_group.title: Extend Weak Group
proverbs/Shapes/extend_weak_group.content:
Extend from a weak group
Meaning
A weak group needs room to develop. Extending from it adds liberties, creates space for eye shape, and gives the stones a route toward safety. Playing elsewhere too soon may let the opponent confine or attack the group while building strength.
Choosing the extension
Extend far enough to make efficient shape, but close enough that the new stone still supports the group. The right distance depends on the opponent’s nearby stones:

extend farther when the surrounding area is open;
play closer when opposing stones can cut or invade; and
head toward friendly strength or open space rather than toward a strong enemy position.

When to play elsewhere
Do not extend automatically. A group may already be stable, may be light enough to sacrifice, or may have a more urgent tactical move such as a capture or connection. A large move elsewhere can also be better if an attack on the group would not be severe.
Before extending, ask: Does this move make the group safer while remaining useful on a larger scale? The best extension both settles the weak stones and contributes to territory, influence, or an attack.

proverbs/Shapes/eye_remove1.title: Remove Eye (Vital Point)
proverbs/Shapes/eye_remove1.content:
Remove Eye (Vital Point Strike)
Meaning
In life and death (tsumego), a group must form two independent eyes to live. When an opponent’s enclosed area is on the verge of making two eyes, striking the vital eye point (me-no-kyusho) preemptively destroys their second eye and condemns the entire group to death.
The proverb “The enemy’s vital point is your vital point” applies directly: the intersection the defender needs to make two eyes is the exact spot the attacker must occupy.
Why it is useful

Decisive capture: Converts an apparently living group into dead stones without allowing seki.
Forces shortage of liberties: Crowds the defender’s interior, making internal defense impossible.
Maintains initiative: Leaves the opponent with zero eye potential, preventing counter-attacks.

Limits

Read outside liberties first: Ensure your attacking stone cannot be captured in a way that gives the defender extra eyes.
Check for seki: Verify whether the sequence results in a kill or a shared living seki.

Example
White’s corner formation is struggling to live. Black strikes the vital eye-destroying point at A (ab), denying White a second eye and securing the kill.

proverbs/Shapes/eye_stealing.title: Eye Stealing Tesuji
proverbs/Shapes/eye_stealing.content:
Eye-Stealing Tesuji (Me-Tsubushi)
Meaning
The eye-stealing tesuji (me-tsubushi) is an aggressive placement that attacks the opponent’s eye-generating shape from within. Rather than surrounding from the outside, the stone penetrates directly into the eye space to prevent it from dividing into two true eyes.
Depriving a group of its eyes forces it to flee into the center as a heavy, eyeless dragon, creating endless attacking opportunities for profit across the whole board.
Why it is useful

Denies local life: Prevents the defender from settling comfortably on the side or corner.
Forces heavy running: Transforms a settled formation into a burdensome weak group.
Builds outside profit: As you chase the eyeless group across the board, you naturally build territory and influence along its escape path.

Limits

Do not die inside: Ensure your eye-stealing stone is not easily swallowed without accomplishing its purpose.
Balance with surrounding: Sometimes sealing the group from the outside is more profitable than an immediate eye-stealing invasion.

Example
White attempts to make eye shape at cb-db. Black plays the eye-stealing strike at A (dd), crushing White’s eye potential and keeping the group under heavy attack.

proverbs/Shapes/footsweep.title: Footsweep
proverbs/Shapes/footsweep.content:
Footsweep (Low Slide / Suberi)
Meaning
The footsweep (a low knight’s move slide or suberi) is a glide down to the second line beneath the opponent’s stones. It strikes directly at the “feet” of the opponent’s group, scooping out the foundation needed for eye space.
By sweeping underneath, you simultaneously settle your own stones with an easy base while leaving the opponent’s stones floating without ground.
Why it is useful

Two-way swing: Establishes a comfortable territorial base for yourself while destroying the enemy’s.
Stabilizes invading stones: The standard follow-up after an approach move to achieve quick sabaki.
Reduces liberties: Puts low-line pressure on the enemy’s corner or side stones.

Limits

Watch the clamp: Be alert to an opponent’s clamping tesuji or attachment that can cut off the sliding stone.
Not for the first line: Keep the sweep on the second or third line; dropping too low without purpose loses tempo.

Example
Black plays the footsweep slide at A (hr), sliding underneath White’s stone (iq) to undercut White’s side base and secure Black’s group.

proverbs/Shapes/hane_at_headof2.title: Hane at the Head of Two Stones
proverbs/Shapes/hane_at_headof2.content:
Hane at the Head of Two Stones
Meaning
The proverb “Hane at the head of two stones without hesitation” (nicho no atama hane-yo) highlights one of the most critical tactical imperatives in Go. When two adjacent enemy stones march in a line, bending around the front stone with a hane exerts tremendous structural pressure.
Bending at the head immediately restricts the opponent’s forward development, reduces their liberties, and tilts the entire local balance of power in your favor.
Why it is useful

Stops momentum: Blocks the opponent’s march dead in its tracks.
Takes the outside: Secures outside thickness and leaves the opponent crawling on lower lines.
Creates cutting points: Forces the opponent into defensive concessions while creating tactical targets for follow-up attacks.

Limits

Mind the cut: A hane naturally leaves a cutting point behind your head stone. Read the counter-cut and ensure you have sufficient liberties or ladder support.
Double hane follow-up: Be prepared to follow up with a double hane or connection depending on the opponent’s answer.

Example
White pushes with two stones (ee, ef). Black strikes decisively at the head of the two stones at A (ed), bending around White to seize the initiative.

proverbs/Shapes/hane_from_attatchment.title: Hane From Attachment
proverbs/Shapes/hane_from_attatchment.content:
Hane From Attachment
Meaning
While extending (nobi) is the solid answer to an attachment, haning against an attachment is the dynamic, aggressive counter. Instead of passively stepping back, your stone bends around the contacting stone, pinning it and contesting the line of development.
Haning is favored when you want to wrap around the opponent, block their escape path, or force them into an immediate tactical struggle on your terms.
Why it is useful

Seizes tempo: Puts immediate pressure on the opponent’s stone and demands a defensive response.
Blocks expansion: Prevents the opponent from extending cleanly along their desired axis.
Shapes the boundary: Dictates where the wall or territory will form.

Limits

Leaves a cutting point: Haning inherently creates a cut behind your stone. Never play hane if the opponent’s cut leads to a fatal double atari or capturing race.
Requires backup: Ensure you have enough supporting stones to handle the ensuing crosscut or counter-hane.

Example
White attaches at ef. Black plays an aggressive hane at A (df), wrapping around White’s stone and taking control of the local fight.

proverbs/Shapes/hem_play.title: Hem Play
proverbs/Shapes/hem_play.content:
Hem Play (Susoharai)
Meaning
The hem play (susoharai, or sweeping the hem) is an undercut played along the second line beneath an opponent’s high corner or side position (such as a 4-4 stone or high enclosure).
Like sweeping beneath a hanging garment, the hem play slips under the opponent’s territorial perimeter, scooping out secure eye space and drastically reducing their anticipated territory in sente.
Why it is useful

Severe reduction: Destroys the opponent’s corner or side points from underneath.
Carves out eye space: Threatens to connect underneath or live locally, forcing a submissive response.
Huge endgame value: Often worth 10 to 15 points in the late middle game or early endgame.

Limits

Timing is critical: Playing the hem too early in the fuseki can be premature if whole-board development points are larger.
Check surrounding blockers: Ensure the opponent cannot cap or cut off your sliding stone from above.

Example
In the diagram, Black plays at bd beneath White’s high stone at dd, sweeping the hem along the edge to deflate White’s corner territory.

proverbs/Shapes/high_table1.title: High Table
proverbs/Shapes/high_table1.content:
High Table
Meaning
The high table (table shape, or tsukue-gata) is a four-stone formation consisting of two pillar stones connected by a tabletop span across the top. It resembles a table or archway and is one of the most efficient shapes for creating central eye space and structural resilience.
The open interior beneath the table naturally holds potential for eyes while offering multiple directions to expand or connect.
Why it is useful

Natural eye formation: Encloses central territory that easily converts into two distinct eyes when under attack.
Structural strength: Disperses pressure across four interconnected points rather than relying on a single stone.
Versatile in sabaki: Frequently used by running groups to settle quickly inside enemy territory.

Limits

Vulnerable to center peeps: An opponent playing directly under the tabletop can sometimes spoil the eye shape if not countered properly.
Read liberty counts: Ensure that the legs of the table have enough liberties to prevent squeezing tactics.

Example
Black plays at A (ee), bridging the supporting stones to complete the high table shape and guarantee stable center eye potential.

proverbs/Shapes/index.title: Go Shapes
proverbs/Shapes/index.content:
Welcome to the Go Proverb Database.
This is an interactive collection of classic Go sayings. Each entry starts with a proverb, then expands with diagrams and practical explanations.

“Some saying…”

Over time, each proverb page will include:

Interactive board diagrams
Move-by-move examples
Clear commentary on when the proverb applies (and when it does not)

If you are learning or teaching Go, this site is meant to be a practical reference you can return to often.

proverbs/Shapes/keima_cut.title: Keima Cut
proverbs/Shapes/keima_cut.content:
Cutting the Knight’s Move (Keima)
Meaning
The knight’s move (keima) is fast and flexible, but its diagonal connection is inherently fragile. A keima cut takes advantage of this defect by wedging or attaching across the waist of the knight’s jump to sever the two stones.
Cutting the knight’s move is one of the most frequent attacking tesujis in Go, turning a seemingly connected enemy formation into two disconnected, vulnerable targets.
Why it is useful

Splits enemy groups: Destroys the opponent’s coordination and creates two weak groups to attack simultaneously.
Undercuts framework: Tears through territorial boundaries and collapses the opponent’s shape.
Forcing exchanges: Creates multiple cutting points and atari threats that dictate the flow of the game.

Limits

Ensure local strength: Cutting the knight’s move requires adequate supporting stones. If you cut into enemy thickness, your cutting stone can be trapped in a net or ladder.
Beware the counter-crosscut: The opponent will often counter-attack vigorously around the cut point.

Example
White’s stones form a knight’s move. Black targets the waist of the keima at A (cc) or B (cb) to cut White’s stones apart.

proverbs/Shapes/knights_approach.title: Knight's Approach Move
proverbs/Shapes/knights_approach.content:
Knight’s Approach Move (Keima Kakari)
Meaning
The knight’s approach move (keima kakari) is the classic method for challenging an opponent’s corner stone (such as a 3-4 or 4-4 point) from a knight’s move distance.
It strikes an optimal balance between applying pressure on the corner and maintaining agility for your own stone. Depending on the opponent’s reply, the approaching stone can slide into the corner, jump to the outside, or counter-pincer.
Why it is useful

Standard joseki foundation: Leads to well-understood, balanced joseki variations.
Disrupts corner dominance: Prevents the opponent from making an effortless corner enclosure in one move.
High adaptability: Adapts gracefully whether the opponent attaches, pincers, or backs off.

Limits

Vulnerable to sharp pincers: Be prepared to navigate pincer fights if the opponent has strong allies along the side.
Choose high vs low carefully: A low approach (3rd line) seeks a base, while a high approach (4th line) seeks outside influence.

Example
White occupies the corner at ee. Black approaches flexibly with a knight’s move at A (dg) or B (fg) to contest the corner.

proverbs/Shapes/knights_move_slide.title: Knight's Move Slide
proverbs/Shapes/knights_move_slide.content:
Knight’s Move Slide (Suberi)
Meaning
The knight’s move slide (suberi) is a low, gliding move to the second line played after an initial approach to an opponent’s corner. It dives under the opponent’s stones to carve out immediate eye space and establish a stable territorial base.
In classical Go, the slide is the defining move that settles an invading or approaching stone, converting an unsettled position into an independent living group.
Why it is useful

Secures eye base: Establishes guaranteed eye potential along the edge of the board.
Undercuts territory: Shrinks the opponent’s corner territory while expanding your own points.
Settles the group: Often completes a joseki sequence and allows you to transition to whole-board play.

Limits

Avoid when the center is priority: Sliding onto the second line can be slow if outside influence is more urgent.
Watch the clamp: Verify that the opponent cannot clamp or cut off the sliding stone.

Example
White has an imposing wall (gp through jp). Black slides underneath with the knight’s move slide at A (kr), carving out a living base along the bottom side.

proverbs/Shapes/ko_lock.title: Ko Lock
proverbs/Shapes/ko_lock.content:
Ko Lock (Mutual Capture Cycle)
Meaning
A ko lock occurs when two interlocking shapes reach the classic ko state: single stones on each side are alternately in atari, but the fundamental rules of Go forbid immediate recapture to prevent an infinite loop.
When you capture the ko, you “lock” the position in your favor. The opponent is barred from recapturing immediately and must find a viable ko threat elsewhere on the board.
Why it is useful

Ultimate bargaining chip: Turns a local life-and-death struggle into a whole-board tactical exchange.
Leverages outside threats: Allows the player with more ko threats to extract huge concessions across the board.
Tests game reading: Demands precise evaluation of trade values and global balance.

Limits

Never start a ko you cannot win: Evaluate the ko threat count before initiating or locking the ko fight.
Beware local ko threats: Ensure the opponent cannot create endless internal threats within the fighting group.

Example
Black captures the ko stone at A (hf), locking the ko and forcing White to find a suitable ko threat on another part of the board before recapturing.

proverbs/Shapes/ld_3_inrow.title: Straight Three (Life and Death)
proverbs/Shapes/ld_3_inrow.content:
Straight Three (San-moku Narabe)
Meaning
In basic life and death theory, straight three (san-moku narabe) is an enclosed eye space of three empty intersections in a straight line.
The fundamental rule for straight three is: the center point is the vital point for both players.

If the defender plays the center point, the space divides into two real eyes and the group lives.
If the attacker plays the center point, the defender cannot make two eyes and the group dies.

Why it is useful

Foundational tsumego rule: The most basic and important life-and-death model in Go.
Miai symmetry: Playing the center makes the two remaining side points miai for the defender to complete two eyes.
Speed in reading: Instant recognition saves valuable reading time in complex tactical fights.

Limits

First to play wins: Straight three is an unsettled shape; whoever plays at the vital point first decides the fate of the group.
Outside liberties: The center point works unconditionally regardless of outside liberties.

Example
The three-space eye line is contested. Black occupies the central vital point at A (jj), splitting the space into two eyes to live (or killing if Black is the attacker).

proverbs/Shapes/ld_3_inside.title: Bent Three (Life and Death)
proverbs/Shapes/ld_3_inside.content:
Bent Three (Magari San-moku)
Meaning
Bent three (magari san-moku) is an eye space composed of three empty intersections connected in an “L” or bent shape.
Just like straight three, bent three is an unsettled three-space shape whose fate depends entirely on who plays first. The vital point is the central corner vertex (the bend):

If the defender takes the bend, two separate eyes are formed and the group lives.
If the attacker occupies the bend, the defender cannot divide the remaining two spaces and the group dies.

Why it is useful

Unconditional resolution: Identifies the single indispensable point that decides life or death.
Miai eye points: Holding the corner vertex makes the two ends of the “L” symmetrical miai for life.
Corner bent-four relation: Understanding bent three is the prerequisite to mastering the famous bent four in the corner rule.

Limits

Beware corner peculiarities: In the extreme corner of the board, bent three requires careful attention to avoid being caught in a ko trap.

Example
In the bent three formation, Black seizes the crucial bend vertex at A (jj), guaranteeing two eyes and securing life.

proverbs/Shapes/ld_4_inside.title: Square Four & Pyramid Four
proverbs/Shapes/ld_4_inside.content:
Four-Space Eye Shapes (Pyramid / Square Four)
Meaning
Four-space eye shapes have distinct life-and-death classifications depending on their geometry:

Square four (2x2 box): This is a dead shape as it stands. No matter who plays first, it is impossible to make two eyes inside a 2x2 box without the attacker capturing.
Pyramid four (T-shape): An unsettled shape where the vital point is the center of the T. Whoever plays the central intersection controls the life or death of the group.

Why it is useful

Dead shape efficiency: Recognizing that square four is already dead allows you to tenuki and save moves.
Accurate vital point attacks: Directs your attacking stone straight to the center of the T-shape in pyramid four.
Defensive shape guidance: Warns defenders never to let their internal space collapse into a 2x2 square.

Limits

Do not play inside square four needlessly: Since square four is already dead, adding a stone inside wastes a point and a move.
Watch capturing races: Ensure the surrounding wall has enough liberties to avoid being captured before the kill is realized.

Example
Black strikes at the vital center intersection at A (jj), neutralizing the four-space shape and preventing the opponent from forming two living eyes.

proverbs/Shapes/ld_bulkyfive.title: Bulky Five (Life and Death)
proverbs/Shapes/ld_bulkyfive.content:
Bulky Five (Go-moku Nakade)
Meaning
Bulky five (go-moku nakade, or bulky five eye space) is a five-space eye formation shaped like a square four with one extra point attached (resembling a cross or car shape).
Despite having five empty intersections, bulky five is highly vulnerable: there is only one vital point at its center.

If the attacker plays the center vital point, the entire bulky five shape cannot make two eyes and dies.
If the defender plays the center point, the space naturally branches into multiple eyes and lives.

Why it is useful

Single vital point: Concentrates the entire life-and-death calculation into a single, critical intersection.
Classic nakade: The most famous nakade (inside placement) shape taught in classical Go problem study.
Decisive fighting weapon: Enables an attacker to kill large surrounding groups cleanly.

Limits

Sente urgency: Bulky five is an urgent unsettled shape; delaying the vital point move for even one turn can allow the opponent to live or kill.
Do not mistake for flower six: A six-space shape (rabbitty six) has different properties; know your nakade counts.

Example
Black plunges into the central heart of the bulky five at A (jj), preventing White from dividing the space and sealing the doom of the entire group.

proverbs/Shapes/long_knights.title: Large Knight's Move
proverbs/Shapes/long_knights.content:
Large Knight’s Move (Dai-geima)
Meaning
The large knight’s move (dai-geima) steps two intersections forward and one to the side (a 3x2 stride). It is significantly faster and covers more board space than the standard knight’s move (keima).
Because of its broad stride, it is frequently used to approach corner enclosures from a safe distance, reduce opposing frameworks, or extend quickly along the side.
Why it is useful

Vast board coverage: Reaches farther across open terrain with a single move.
Light, elusive shape: Perfect for sabaki and reducing moves where you want to avoid heavy commitment.
Flexible corner approach: Approaching a corner with a large knight’s move keeps distance from the opponent’s pincer attacks.

Limits

Easier to cut: The seam between the stones is wider than a regular keima; the opponent can often attach, push, or wedge through if you do not handle it lightly.
Sacrifice mindset: Be prepared to sacrifice the outer stone if the opponent commits heavily to cutting it.

Example
From the stone at dd, Black leaps across the board with a large knight’s move to A (eg), staking out a broad presence across the quadrant.

proverbs/Shapes/monkey_jump.title: Monkey Jump
proverbs/Shapes/monkey_jump.content:
Monkey Jump (Saru-suberi)
Meaning
The monkey jump (saru-suberi) is a legendary endgame tesuji where a stone leaps from a strong second-line position all the way down to the first line in a large knight’s move (3x2 jump) into the opponent’s territory.
Because the jump lands on the first line backed by the edge of the board and second-line strength, it cannot normally be cut or captured if played under proper conditions. It scoops out 8 to 12 points of territory in sente.
Why it is useful

Massive point swing: The largest standard endgame reduction technique in Go.
Connected and safe: The edge of the board protects the jumping stone, allowing it to connect home smoothly.
Forces passive defense: Compels the opponent into defensive concessions while retaining the initiative.

Limits

Prerequisites must be met: You must have a strong, settled second-line stone. If your supporting stone is weak or short of liberties, the opponent can cut and kill the monkey jump.
Read the counter-clamp: Be prepared to answer the opponent’s defensive clamp or wedge correctly.

Example
From the solid second-line base at jr, Black launches the monkey jump to the first line at A (ms), plunging deep into White’s territory and carving away points in sente.

proverbs/Shapes/multi_stone_capture.title: Capture Several Stones as One Group
proverbs/Shapes/multi_stone_capture.content:
Capture several stones as one group
Meaning
Adjacent enemy stones form one string and share the same liberties. If that string has only one liberty, playing there captures every stone in it at once. Count the liberties of the whole string rather than treating each stone separately.
Practical check
Before playing the capturing move, confirm that:

every target stone is connected to the same string;
the string has no liberty other than the point you plan to occupy; and
your move is legal and does not overlook a larger threat elsewhere.

Removing several stones can do more than gain points. It may connect your own groups, end a semeai, or eliminate cutting stones. However, do not fill liberties automatically: if the enemy string still has another liberty, your move may only put it in atari and give it a chance to escape.

proverbs/Shapes/one_space_jump.title: One Space Jump
proverbs/Shapes/one_space_jump.content:
One-Space Jump
Meaning
The one-space jump (ikken tobi) is the most standard, reliable method for moving into open space or expanding along the side. It moves stones quickly toward the center or along lines without leaving easily exploitable cutting points.
The proverb “The one-space jump is never bad” emphasizes that jumping one space almost always improves group stability, increases liberties, and maintains rapid escape paths without creating urgent local weaknesses.
Why it is useful

Balance of speed and safety: It travels faster than a solid extension while remaining much harder to cut than wider jumps.
Escape route: An essential technique for running weak groups into the center.
Framework expansion: Efficiently stakes out territory and projects influence across the board.

Limits

Beware of the wedge: When an opponent wedges between the stones, ensure your surrounding position can handle the resulting cut and atari sequences.
Direction matters: Always jump toward the open area or friendly strength, not toward enemy thickness.

Example
Black plays the one-space jump at A (eg), extending smoothly into the center while keeping strong connectivity to the original stone.

proverbs/Shapes/opening_heatmap.title: Opening Heatmap
proverbs/Shapes/opening_heatmap.content:
opening_heatmap
Opening idea
In the opening, aim for the key corner points:

4-4 (hoshi): flexible and influence-oriented.
3-4 (komoku): balanced between territory and development.
3-3 (sansan): fast corner territory.

These points are usually the highest-value starting locations on an empty board.
3-4 (komoku) explanation
The 3-4 point emphasizes a stable corner while leaving strong options to extend along one side.
It is a common choice when you want a mix of secure territory and outward development.
3-3 (sansan) explanation
The 3-3 point takes immediate corner territory and keeps the local position compact.
It is efficient for solid points but gives up some early outside influence compared with 4-4.
Demo

proverbs/Shapes/parallelogram.title: Parallelogram
proverbs/Shapes/parallelogram.content:
Parallelogram
Meaning
The parallelogram (or diamond shape) is a coordinated arrangement where four stones form a flexible, diagonal quadrilateral across the board. Rather than clumping together in a rigid wall, the stones maintain dynamic diagonal and knight-move relationships.
This geometric synergy allows the group to adapt quickly—expanding into a large moyo, shifting defense to any threatened corner, or connecting easily across open terrain.
Why it is useful

Dynamic balance: Combines wide board coverage with mutual diagonal reinforcement.
High adaptability: Can shift from territorial expansion to group defense depending on the opponent’s approach.
Efficient stone economy: Uses four stones to influence a large quadrant without overconcentration.

Limits

Avoid loose gaps: Because the connections are diagonal, read carefully to ensure the opponent cannot cut through with a well-placed wedge.
Maintain sente: Do not spend extra moves perfecting the geometry if a larger urgent move is available on the whole board.

Example
Black coordinates the formation by playing at A (ie) or B (ee), weaving the stones into a balanced parallelogram shape with broad center influence.

proverbs/Shapes/pass_when_no_legal_move.title: Pass When No Legal Move
proverbs/Shapes/pass_when_no_legal_move.content:
Pass When No Legal Move
Meaning
In Go, passing is a legal option on any turn, signaling that no advantageous, necessary, or profitable move remains. When both players pass consecutively, the game ends and territory is counted.
The proverb reminds players not to play unnecessary moves inside their own territory (which reduces score under Japanese rules or wastes moves) or fill neutral points (dame) that put their own living groups in self-atari or shortage of liberties.
Why it is useful

Preserves territory: Avoids placing self-destructive stones inside established boundaries.
Prevents dame accidents: Eliminates reckless filling of neutral liberties that could trigger unexpected captures.
Recognizes game completion: Helps players accurately evaluate when the endgame is fully settled.

Limits

Ensure all defects are resolved: Before passing, confirm that all cutting points, seki situations, and boundary weaknesses are completely secure.
Confirm opponent’s status: Ensure dead stones can be removed cleanly without requiring an additional defensive stone.

proverbs/Shapes/ponnuki.title: Ponnuki
proverbs/Shapes/ponnuki.content:
ponnuki
Example

Meaning
A ponnuki is the diamond-shaped formation left when four stones capture a
single opposing stone. The name means “to pull out,” describing the captured
stone being removed from the center of the shape. In the example, Black can
play at A to capture the white stone and complete the ponnuki.
The shape is powerful because its stones face outward in four directions. They
have many liberties, support one another, and can influence
several parts of the board at once. This strength is summarized by the proverb:
“A ponnuki is worth thirty points.”
Why it is useful

Outward influence: each stone helps Black develop toward a different area.
Strong shape: the four stones are difficult to cut or attack effectively.
Fighting support: nearby stones can use the ponnuki’s strength when
attacking, invading, or escaping.
Efficient capture: removing the center stone may solve a local weakness
while building thickness for play elsewhere.

The proverb’s “thirty points” is not a literal value. It is a reminder to count
the resulting influence and fighting strength, not only the one captured stone.
Limits
A ponnuki is most valuable in an open area where its influence has room to
work. Near a secure edge or among already strong stones, it may be
overconcentrated. Do not make the shape
automatically: compare the capture with larger moves, and check whether the
opponent can sacrifice the center stone to gain sente or profit
elsewhere.

proverbs/Shapes/read_your_opponents_best.title: Read Your Opponent's Best Move First
proverbs/Shapes/read_your_opponents_best.content:
Read your opponent’s best move first.
Before you choose a move, run a quick test:
“If I play here, what is my opponent’s strongest reply?”
This single habit improves both attack and defense:

It filters out attractive moves that fail to a simple tactical answer.
It reveals urgent defects in your own position before they become costly.
It helps you choose plans that still work against accurate resistance.

A deeper reading principle:
Your opponent’s best move is often your best move, too.
If their sharpest reply takes a key point, ask whether you should take that point first—or remove its power—before continuing your original plan.
In practice:

Name 2-3 realistic candidate moves.
For each candidate, read your opponent’s strongest local and whole-board continuation.
Compare outcomes after best play, not hopeful play.
Prefer the move that leaves you stable shape, initiative, or a forcing follow-up.

Practical checks while reading:

If their best reply attacks your weakness, fixing that weakness may be first priority.
If their best reply is a large shared point, that point is likely urgent for both sides.
If their best reply seizes sente, favor lines that keep the initiative with you.

proverbs/Shapes/remove_eye1.title: Destroying Side Eyes
proverbs/Shapes/remove_eye1.content:
Destroying Side Eyes
Meaning
An eye along the side or edge depends on controlling the diagonal corner intersections. When an attacker occupies or wedges through these diagonal control points, the internal eye collapses into a false eye (kake-me).
A false eye provides no permanent life; when the outer liberties are filled, the defending stones around a false eye will eventually be placed in atari and captured.
Why it is useful

Exposes false eyes: Reveals that a group believed to be alive is actually dead or must fight a desperate ko.
Reduces liberties: Forces the defender to fill their own internal liberties to protect against atari.
Simplifies endgame capturing: Cleans up contested border stones in late-game tsumego.

Limits

Timing the falsification: Make sure the defender cannot capture your destroying stone in sente and make a real eye elsewhere.
Count liberties: Verify that your attacking perimeter has more liberties than the enclosed group.

Example
White’s side group seeks two eyes. Black plunges into the critical diagonal point at A (ai), degrading White’s eye into a false eye and deciding the group’s fate.

proverbs/Shapes/respond_to_armpithit.title: Respond to Armpit Hit
proverbs/Shapes/respond_to_armpithit.content:
Respond to Armpit Hit
Meaning
When an opponent hits your fourth-line stone with an armpit hit from underneath, responding correctly determines whether you retain commanding influence or get flattened.
The standard responses are either to stand tall (extend upward to preserve height and center dominance) or to hane across the head of the intruding stone to pin it against the edge and capture it or force it into awkward crawling.
Why it is useful

Maintains structural height: Prevents the opponent from dictating the shape and keeps your outside development intact.
Punishes overextension: If the armpit hit lacks nearby allies, an aggressive hane can trap the invading stone against the side.
Sets up future attacks: Keeps your stones thick, creating a formidable base to attack neighboring enemy groups.

Limits

Avoid passive submissiveness: Simply connecting flatly or backing away lets the opponent achieve effortless sabaki at your expense.
Mind your cutting points: If you choose to hane, verify that the resulting cut does not leave you short of liberties.

Example
White has played underneath at kq. Black responds by pushing or extending at A (jq) or B (kp), maintaining stature and preserving outside strength.

proverbs/Shapes/respond_to_attatchment.title: Respond to Attachment
proverbs/Shapes/respond_to_attatchment.content:
Respond to attachment
What it means
An attachment puts an opposing stone directly beside one of yours. The usual active response is a hane: play diagonally around the attaching stone so that your stones bend around it. This restricts the opponent’s movement and often keeps the initiative.
Choosing a response
Hane is a useful first move to consider, not an automatic rule. Read the nearby cuts and liberties before playing it. Hane is most attractive when your stones are strong enough to fight and the move presses the opponent toward an area where you are already strong.
Extend instead when hane would leave a severe cutting point, begin an unfavorable capturing race, or make an important group heavy. In some positions, playing elsewhere may also be larger than answering the attachment.
Before responding, ask:

Can either side cut after the hane?
Which direction do I want to push the opponent?
Are my nearby stones strong enough for the resulting fight?
Does extending create a safer, more efficient shape?

The proverb identifies the fighting response to examine first; reading determines whether it works.

proverbs/Shapes/respond_to_shoulderhit.title: Respond to Shoulder Hit
proverbs/Shapes/respond_to_shoulderhit.content:
Respond to Shoulder Hit
Meaning
When the opponent plays a shoulder hit against your third-line stone, the fundamental and most reliable response is to push along the side (extending forward on the third line).
The proverb encourages players not to panic when pressed: third-line territory is solid, profitable, and secure. By pushing ahead naturally, you collect guaranteed territory on the third line while keeping your group’s liberties high.
Why it is useful

Guaranteed profit: Every push takes 4th-line influence away while cementing 3rd-line cash points.
Preserves group health: Keeps your stones connected and prevents the opponent from wrapping around with a painful bend.
Keeps counter-chances: After pushing two or three times, you often have the opportunity to turn, jump, or tenuki effectively.

Limits

Know when to stop pushing: Pushing too many times along the third line can let the opponent build unassailable center thickness. Transition to a turn or tenuki once stable.
Do not submissively hane underneath: Haning on the second line under pressure is usually a blunder that ruins your shape.

Example
White presses with a shoulder hit at kp. Black responds calmly by pushing at A (jp) or turning at B (kq), banking solid third-line territory.

proverbs/Shapes/shoulderhit.title: Shoulder Hit
proverbs/Shapes/shoulderhit.content:
Shoulder Hit (Kata-tsuki)
Meaning
The shoulder hit (kata-tsuki) is a diagonal contact move played against an opponent’s stone from above (for example, playing on the fourth line against a third-line stone).
It is one of the most celebrated reduction techniques in modern Go. By pressing down from the outside, you trade third-line territory to the opponent in exchange for dominant center influence, outward thickness, and tempo control.
Why it is useful

Supreme reduction weapon: Safely caps and restricts the expansion of an opponent’s side or corner framework.
Effortless influence: As the opponent crawls along the lower line to take points, you build a magnificent wall facing the center.
Hard to counterattack: Because it is played from above and touches diagonally, the shoulder hit rarely gets trapped or heavily punished.

Limits

Gives solid territory: Remember that pushing an opponent on the third line gives them secure points. Only play it when your center influence is worth more than the points surrendered.
Direction is everything: Hit the shoulder on the side where your developing framework will benefit most.

Example
White occupies the third line at jq. Black executes the shoulder hit at A (ip) or B (kp), pressing White down while building center power.

proverbs/Shapes/side_false_eye_1.title: Side False Eye
proverbs/Shapes/side_false_eye_1.content:
Side False Eye (Kake-Me)
Meaning
A side false eye occurs along the edge of the board when a group’s eye shape is missing a crucial corner support stone. Because the edge restricts the number of diagonal supports available, a single enemy stone at the boundary can turn an apparent eye into an unusable false eye.
Recognizing false eyes early is vital: relying on a false eye for survival leads to sudden, catastrophic group collapse when the outer liberties run out.
Why it is useful

Tactical clarity: Allows the attacker to correctly assess that the defending group is not alive.
Prepares the squeeze: Sets up a future atari that forces the opponent to connect inside their own eye space.
Prevents opponent bluffing: Stops the defender from playing tenuki based on false assumptions of safety.

Limits

Avoid careless defense: When defending, always protect the diagonal vertex to turn a potential false eye into a real one.
Beware snapbacks: Read local capturing combinations (oi-otoshi / snapbacks) carefully around the false eye.

Example
White’s eye at the side is compromised. Black plays at A (ak), clamping down on the diagonal vertex to confirm the false eye and seal White’s defeat.

proverbs/Shapes/solid_connection.title: Solid Connection
proverbs/Shapes/solid_connection.content:
Solid Connection
Meaning
A solid connection (tsugi) is the direct placement of a stone adjacent to friendly stones to leave zero internal cutting points. Unlike indirect connections such as the bamboo joint or tiger’s mouth, a solid connection gives the opponent no tactical entry point whatsoever.
While it is the least ambitious connection in terms of speed, it eliminates all lingering aji and creates thick, reliable shape that supports heavy fighting nearby.
Why it is useful

Zero cutting defects: Eliminates all double-atari and crosscut threats locally.
Creates thickness: Solidly connected stones cannot be squeezed, providing a strong base of thickness to attack surrounding enemy groups.
Simplifies reading: Leaves no complex tactical complications for the opponent to exploit later in the game.

Limits

Can be slow: Playing a solid connection when a lighter connection (like a bamboo joint or hanging connection) is sufficient can cost a valuable move in sente.
Overconcentration: Avoid adding solid connections to groups that are already safe and stable.

Example
In the diagram, Black plays at A (fd) to connect two stones solidly, completely removing White’s cutting threats and cementing Black’s group.

proverbs/Shapes/steel_post.title: Steel Post
proverbs/Shapes/steel_post.content:
Steel Post
Meaning
The steel post (also known as an iron pillar or solid downward extension) is a direct, vertical descent of a stone to the adjacent line, usually played toward the edge of the board.
It turns a floating or loose stone into an immovable anchor. By dropping straight down, it firmly seals off an edge, prevents sliding moves like the monkey jump, and creates unassailable thickness.
Why it is useful

Rock-solid base: Eliminates undercutting moves and solidifies side or corner territory completely.
Denies counter-attacks: Gives the opponent no contact tesuji or leaning plays to build momentum.
Increases liberties: Adds crucial liberties directly, turning a contested flank into a secure bastion.

Limits

Can be heavy: If played too early in the opening, it may be overly conservative compared to faster extensions.
Gote risk: The move is often defensive and settles a local situation in gote, so time it when defending is truly urgent.

Example
In the diagram, Black plays the steel post at A (hq), reinforcing the group downward toward the edge to anchor the side territory and prevent enemy incursions.

proverbs/Shapes/tiger_mouth1.title: Tiger's Mouth
proverbs/Shapes/tiger_mouth1.content:
Tiger’s Mouth (Hanging Connection)
Meaning
The tiger’s mouth (kake-tsugi, or hanging connection) is a three-stone triangular formation with an open center. It acts as an active, threatening connection: if the opponent dares to step inside the mouth to cut, they are immediately placed in atari and can be captured on the following turn.
It is superior to a solid connection when you want to develop outward eye space and maintain active board presence while still guarding a cut.
Why it is useful

Automatic cut deterrent: Prevents direct enemy cuts without needing a heavy solid connection.
Eye space generator: Directly outlines a potential eye inside the pocket of the shape.
Maintains active shape: Extends influence in two directions while staying light and resilient.

Limits

Ko threats and throw-ins: Be wary of throw-in moves that sacrifice a stone into the mouth to squeeze liberties or create a false eye.
Shortage of liberties: If the surrounding stones have only 2 liberties, the tiger’s mouth may not generate a safe atari.

Example
Black plays at A (bc), forming a tiger’s mouth that protects the corner and creates an instant atari threat against any White intrusion at cc.

proverbs/Shapes/tiger_mouth2.title: Tiger's Mouth (Alternative Orientation)
proverbs/Shapes/tiger_mouth2.content:
Tiger’s Mouth (Corner / Side Defense)
Meaning
This variation of the tiger’s mouth illustrates how the hanging connection adapts to the edge of the board. By curving stones around an open intersection facing the side, you establish a resilient defensive perimeter that deters enemy entry and secures local eye potential.
Like its center counterpart, any enemy piece entering the tiger’s jaw is subjected to immediate capture or severe tactical punishment.
Why it is useful

Flexible side stability: Secures flank territory and eyes without overcommitting stones.
Defensive efficiency: Protects cutting points while simultaneously expanding the group’s breathing room.
Speed in joseki: Frequently appears in standard joseki sequences to maintain sente.

Limits

Do not ignore outside weaknesses: Ensure the tail of the tiger’s mouth is not vulnerable to an outside hane or double atari.
Read liberties carefully: Always check that your group has enough liberties to execute the capture if the opponent cuts into the mouth.

Example
Black plays at A (cb), completing the tiger’s mouth along the top edge to defend against cuts and solidify side eye space.

proverbs/Shapes/two_space_jump.title: Two Space Jump
proverbs/Shapes/two_space_jump.content:
Two-Space Jump
Meaning
The two-space jump (niken tobi) extends two intersections away from an existing stone. It is faster and covers more ground than a one-space jump, making it popular in the opening for staking out wider territory or building large moyos.
However, because of the wider two-point gap, it contains latent cutting aji and requires adequate supporting stones or whole-board coordination.
Why it is useful

Rapid development: Covers territory quickly and applies broader pressure on opponent frameworks.
Flexible spacing: Works exceptionally well along the third or fourth line when extending from stable corner formations.
Light play: Useful in sabaki when seeking rapid expansion without committing heavy stones.

Limits

Vulnerable to peep and wedge: An opponent can often peep at the gap or wedge through if nearby support is lacking.
Not for urgent defense: When running under heavy attack, a two-space jump is often too loose; prefer a one-space jump instead.

Example
Black plays at A (eh), making a two-space jump to quickly stake out territory and project outward influence across the board.

proverbs/Shapes/vertical_eye.title: Vertical Eye Shape
proverbs/Shapes/vertical_eye.content:
Vertical Eye Shape (Linear Eye)
Meaning
The vertical eye shape is a sturdy two-line formation along the second and third lines that creates a deep, secure eye pocket. By aligning stones vertically against the edge, you construct a wall that the opponent cannot easily falsify or squeeze.
It is a core structural pattern used by side groups to guarantee life when fighting in tight, restricted corridors.
Why it is useful

Guaranteed eye space: Provides a deep, unassailable eye pocket along the board boundary.
Increases vertical liberties: Gives the group sufficient breathing room to win local capturing races (semeai).
Defends against undercuts: Blocks slides and clamps from stealing the group’s foundation.

Limits

Must have a second eye: One eye—no matter how solid—does not make life; ensure the group has a second eye or an escape route.
Do not overcommit: Once the eye is unconditionally secure, avoid playing additional inside moves.

Example
Black plays at A (bi), completing the vertical column to solidify the eye pocket and ensure unconditional local survival.

proverbs/Shapes/wall_extension_2.title: wall_extension_2
proverbs/Shapes/wall_extension_2.content:
﻿---
title: “Wall Extension: 2-Stone Wall”
tags:

Shape
Fuseki
Extension
Proverb


Extension From a Two-Stone Wall
Meaning
The classic Go proverb for side extensions dictates: “Extend two spaces from one stone, three spaces from a two-stone wall, four spaces from a three-stone wall.” (The “N + 1 rule”).
A solid wall of two stones has enough structural power and liberties to support an extension of exactly three spaces along the side. This distance maximizes territorial scope while keeping the extension completely secure against invading cuts.
Why it is useful

Optimal territorial efficiency: Stretches your side development to the furthest safe limit.
Immune to direct cuts: A three-space jump from two stones has enough backup that any enemy invasion can be attacked profitably.
Coordinates third and fourth lines: Can be placed on the third line for secure points or fourth line for center expansion.

Limits

Do not overextend: Extending four spaces from only two stones leaves a vulnerable gap that can be invaded.
Adapt to enemy thickness: If the adjacent corner is held by strong enemy stones, shorten the extension to two spaces.

Example
Black forms a two-stone wall at ch-dh. Black makes the ideal three-space extension to A (ck) or B (dk) to develop the side.

proverbs/Shapes/wall_extension_3.title: wall_extension_3
proverbs/Shapes/wall_extension_3.content:

title: “Wall Extension: 3-Stone Wall”
tags:

Shape
Fuseki
Extension
Thickness


Extension From a Three-Stone Wall
Meaning
Building on the fundamental “N + 1 rule”, a solid wall of three stones possesses immense local thickness. Because of this formidable power, the wall can safely support an extension of four spaces along the side.
This wide extension stakes out a vast territorial framework while deterring the opponent from entering the corridor between the wall and the extension stone.
Why it is useful

Dominates the entire side: Four spaces covers nearly a third of the entire side of the board.
Severe attacking potential: If the opponent invades the four-space gap, your three-stone wall acts as an immovable anvil against which the invader can be crushed.
Harmonious fuseki structure: Serves as the cornerstone of large moyo strategies.

Limits

Watch the invasion timing: If you delay following up, an opponent may invade deeply to test your attack. Be prepared to attack rather than trying to defend passively.
Maintain connection support: Ensure the wall itself cannot be cut or pressured from behind.

Example
Black possesses a three-stone wall (ch-dh-eh). Black extends four spaces down the side to A (cl) or B (dl), establishing a grand framework.

Extension From a Four-Stone Wall
Meaning
In Go opening theory, a four-stone solid wall is the pinnacle of linear strength. In accordance with the “N + 1 rule”, a wall of four stones easily supports a dramatic five-space extension along the side.
A five-space extension reaches across the entire flank of the board, claiming immense territory and projecting immense center power. Any enemy stone attempting to survive inside this corridor will face overwhelming attacking force.
Why it is useful

Massive framework: Secures an entire board edge and turns it into a dominant territorial zone.
Maximum stone efficiency: Exploits the absolute safety of the four-stone wall to stretch stones to their utmost reach.
Unassailable thickness: The four-stone wall provides an infinite reservoir of liberties for any ensuing fight.

Limits

Prepare to attack: The opponent will almost certainly invade a five-space gap. Treat the invasion not as a loss of territory, but as an opportunity to attack for profit elsewhere.
Avoid playing too flat: Extending on the fourth line often yields superior center synergy compared to staying flat on the third line.

Example
Black’s wall spans four stones (ch through fh). Black extends a full five spaces down the side to A (dm), completing an expansive side framework.

proverbs/Shapes/wedge.title: Wedge
proverbs/Shapes/wedge.content:
Wedge
What is a wedge?
A wedge is a stone played directly between two opposing stones. It prevents them from connecting cleanly and may split them into two groups that must be handled separately.
The move is severe because both opposing stones touch the wedge. That also means the wedge stone can come under immediate pressure from either side, so wedging is not automatically safe.
Read before you wedge
Before playing the wedge, read the opponent’s strongest replies:

Atari from either side: Can you answer without losing the wedge or a nearby cutting stone?
A counter-cut: If the opponent gives up one stone, can they cut elsewhere or trap your stones?
A ladder or net: After the local exchanges, does a resulting chase work in your favor?
A sacrifice: Is separating the stones still valuable if the opponent abandons one and gains outside strength?

Play the wedge when your nearby stones support it and at least one favorable continuation works. If neither side can be handled, the wedge only creates a weak stone in contact with two opponents.
Common mistake
Do not wedge just because the point is available. Read the forcing sequence first, including replies from both directions. When the opponent can choose which side to press, overlooking one variation can reverse the attack.
Example
Black can play at A, directly between the two white stones. The move separates them, but Black must first read White’s ataris and decide which side to fight.

proverbs/Strategies/a_good_move_is_one_t.title: A Good Move Is One That Creates Multiple Threats
proverbs/Strategies/a_good_move_is_one_t.content:
Core Meaning
A move that creates two or more distinct threats is far stronger than a move with a single purpose. Since your opponent can only respond once, at least one threat will remain effective—giving you a clear advantage.

Kikashi Connection
Moves with strong kikashi qualities are especially powerful because they are:

Forcing – ignoring them leads to immediate damage
Efficient – they improve your shape while worsening your opponent’s
Generative – they leave behind useful aji (latent potential) for later
