A true kikashi move forces your opponent to handle multiple problems at once—life, connection, capture, or territory—with a single response.

Classic Go Examples






























Threat TypeExample MoveOpponent’s DilemmaCapture + CutClamping (hasami-tsuke) on the second lineSave the stone or prevent a cutLife + Eye TheftHane inside the eye spaceDefend capture or preserve eye shapeSente + Ko ThreatDistant atari creating a cutAnswer locally (lose sente) or face future complicationsConnection + AttackShoulder hit between weak groupsStrengthen one side or rescue the other

Why This Works

One move limit – A single reply cannot solve multiple problems
Decision pressure – Even strong players may misjudge priorities
Initiative control – You often retain sente
Lasting value – Unresolved weaknesses and aji remain


Counterexample
A single-purpose move—like a basic connection or simple extension—is easy to answer. The opponent responds efficiently and often takes the initiative, leaving you with little gain.

Proverb Variants

“A move with two purposes is twice as good.”
“Kikashi is multi-threat forcing.”
“Don’t make one threat—make many.”

proverbs/Strategies/a_monkey_jump_late_i.title: A Monkey Jump Late in the Game Can Be Devastating
proverbs/Strategies/a_monkey_jump_late_i.content:
Core Meaning
A late-game Monkey Jump can inflict surprisingly large territorial damage, especially when your opponent is not prepared for it. Even small-looking moves on the third line can swing the score.

Tesuji & Sente Connection
The monkey jump is a classic Tesuji because it is:

Precise – it targets the exact weakness in your opponent’s endgame shape
Forcing – it often demands an immediate response
Efficient – it gains points while limiting your opponent’s options

When played at the right moment, it frequently keeps or regains Sente, allowing you to continue dictating the flow of the endgame.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationMonkey Jump EffectOpponent’s DilemmaSecured side territorySlides under the boundaryBlock low (lose points) or allow deeper invasionLoose endgame defenseExploits a gap on the third lineDefend locally or accept territorial lossOverconfident boundaryReduces more than expectedProtect edge or preserve sente elsewhereTight yose positionGains unexpected extra pointsRespond (lose initiative) or concede profit

Why This Works

Endgame complacency – players often underestimate small moves
Hidden aji – weaknesses remain even in “settled” positions
Timing sensitivity – played too early it’s small; too late it disappears
Initiative swing – it can steal or maintain sente at a critical moment


Counterexample
If your opponent has already sealed the boundary tightly, the monkey jump becomes small or ineffective. Playing it blindly can turn into a low-value move that loses sente.

Proverb Variants

“The monkey jump steals points in plain sight.”
“Small moves decide big games.”
“Never ignore third-line endgame tesuji.”

proverbs/Strategies/a_peep_forces_the_op.title: A Peep Threatens To Cut And Creates Future Weaknesses
proverbs/Strategies/a_peep_forces_the_op.content:
Core Meaning
A Peep is a forcing move that threatens to cut an opponent’s stones apart. Because cuts are dangerous, the opponent is usually compelled to respond immediately. Even after defending, the exchange often leaves behind weaknesses and lingering aji that can be attacked later.

Tesuji & Sente Connection
The peep is a fundamental Tesuji because it is:

Forcing – ignoring it may lead to separation or collapse
Light – it applies pressure without heavy commitment
Preparatory – it creates future attacking opportunities
Disruptive – it interferes with efficient shape and development

Well-timed peeps frequently preserve or gain Sente, allowing you to pressure weak points while controlling the pace of the game.

Classic Go Examples



































SituationPeep EffectOpponent’s DilemmaLoose connectionThreatens to separate stonesConnect securely or risk being cutDefensive formationCreates cutting ajiReinforce shape or accept future weaknessRunning groupInterrupts smooth escapeDefend locally or suffer attack laterDeveloping frameworkDisrupts coordinated expansionStrengthen shape or weaken influenceBorder confrontationForces a submissive responseProtect shape or lose sente

Why This Works

Cuts are severe – separated stones become vulnerable
Forcing exchanges shape the future – even small moves create lasting impact
Aji remains after defense – weaknesses may persist beneath solid connections
Shape pressure creates inefficiency – responses often become heavy or passive
Initiative matters – forcing moves help maintain tempo and control


Counterexample
A peep against stones that are already perfectly connected may accomplish little. Repeated meaningless peeps can become inefficient and may surrender initiative without creating useful weaknesses.

Proverb Variants

“Every peep asks a dangerous question.”
“Threaten the cut, control the flow.”
“A forcing move today creates weakness tomorrow.”
“A peep today becomes a cut tomorrow.”

proverbs/Strategies/a_thick_position_is_.title: Thickness Is Better Than Weak Territory
proverbs/Strategies/a_thick_position_is_.content:
Core Meaning
Solid, strong positions with influence are often more valuable than fragile territory. Thickness provides stability, attacking power, and flexibility, while weak territory may require constant defense.

Strategic Connection
Thickness is prized in Go because it is:

Stable – strong shapes are difficult to attack
Influential – they project power outward across the board
Flexible – they support both attack and defense efficiently

A thick position often allows you to play aggressively elsewhere with confidence, since your stones already work well together.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationThick Position BenefitWeak Territory ProblemStrong wall facing centerBuilds outward influenceSmall territory becomes overconcentratedFighting positionSupports attacks on weak groupsWeak territory invites counterattacksExpanding moyoControls future developmentThin shape collapses under pressureEndgame transitionProvides safe sente opportunitiesFragile borders require constant defense

Why This Works

Strength creates freedom – secure groups reduce defensive burdens
Influence scales – thickness affects large areas of the board
Weakness attracts attack – thin territory becomes a target
Initiative advantage – strong positions help maintain tempo


Counterexample
Thickness without purpose can become inefficient overconcentration. Building excessive strength in already secure areas may waste moves and allow the opponent to take larger points elsewhere.

Proverb Variants

“Strong stones build future territory.”
“Influence outlives fragile profit.”
“Thickness gives confidence to attack.”

proverbs/Strategies/a_weak_group_running.title: A Running Weak Group Weakens The Whole Board
proverbs/Strategies/a_weak_group_running.content:
Core Meaning
A weak group forced to run across the board becomes a burden on all your surrounding stones. Constant defense drains moves, loses initiative, and gives your opponent attacking opportunities everywhere.

Strategic Connection
Weak groups are dangerous because they are:

Heavy – they demand repeated defensive moves
Restrictive – they limit your strategic freedom
Vulnerable – they become targets for attacks and forcing moves

Strengthening weak groups early often preserves Sente and prevents the opponent from building influence while chasing your stones.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationWeak Group ProblemOpponent’s OpportunityRunning without eyesRequires constant defenseAttack while building outside influenceSeparated stonesCannot support each otherSplit and pressure multiple groupsThin invasionEscapes inefficientlyGain territory and momentum simultaneouslyCenter chaseDrifts into unfavorable fightsStrengthen surrounding positions during attack

Why This Works

Running stones lose efficiency – defensive moves rarely gain territory
Attacks build strength – the pursuer profits while chasing
Weakness spreads – nearby groups may become burdened as well
Initiative matters – defending too late often loses tempo


Counterexample
Over-defending groups that are already safe can become inefficient. Sometimes light, flexible play is better than investing too many moves into absolute security.

Proverb Variants

“One weak group invites attacks everywhere.”
“Running stones burden the whole board.”
“Defend weakness before it spreads.”

proverbs/Strategies/always_check_if_your.title: Always Check Whether Your Groups Are In Atari
proverbs/Strategies/always_check_if_your.content:
Core Meaning
A group in Atari has only one liberty remaining and is in immediate danger of capture. Constantly checking the liberty count of your stones is one of the most fundamental survival skills in Go.

Tactical Connection
Recognizing Atari is essential because it is:

Urgent – ignoring it usually loses stones immediately
Foundational – liberty awareness underlies all fighting
Preventive – early recognition avoids larger disasters later

Strong players continuously monitor both their own groups and their opponent’s groups for Atari opportunities.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationAtari DangerCorrect ResponseSmall chain surroundedOnly one liberty remainsExtend to safety or connect to alliesCutting fightStones become separatedEscape before the cut becomes fatalLadder sequenceRepeated Atari pressureRead ahead before committingCorner capture raceLiberties disappear rapidlyCount carefully and defend in time

Why This Works

Captured stones are permanent losses – mistakes can decide the game quickly
Liberty counting guides tactics – many Tesuji depend on precise counts
Early defense is cheaper – saving stones late is often difficult
Awareness creates opportunities – spotting enemy Atari enables attacks


Counterexample
Not every Atari must be answered directly. Sometimes sacrificing stones for compensation elsewhere is strategically correct, especially if saving them would become inefficient or heavy.

Proverb Variants

“Count liberties before making plans.”
“An unseen Atari becomes a sudden loss.”
“The first rule of fighting is to stay alive.”

proverbs/Strategies/always_count_liberti.title: Count Liberties Carefully In Capturing Races
proverbs/Strategies/always_count_liberti.content:
Core Meaning
Capturing races are won by accurate liberty counting. Understanding exactly how many liberties each group has is essential for deciding whether to attack, defend, or abandon the fight.

Tactical Connection
Liberty counting is a core fighting skill because it is:

Essential – survival often depends on a single liberty
Analytical – correct reading prevents tactical mistakes
Reliable – accurate counts reveal the true status of groups

Strong players count liberties before committing to complicated fights instead of relying on guesswork.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationLiberty Count ImpactFighting ConsequenceDirect semeaiOne group has fewer libertiesThe weaker group dies firstShared liberty fightMove order becomes criticalIncorrect sequence loses the raceRunning battleExternal liberties determine lifeEscape route may decide the outcomeCorner struggleEye shape affects effective countFalse eyes reduce survival chances

Why This Works

Capturing races are numerical – exact counts determine results
Move order matters – each liberty changes timing immediately
Reading prevents blunders – miscounting leads to avoidable losses
Shape influences liberties – strong shape increases survival chances


Counterexample
Liberty count alone does not always decide the fight. Ko threats, snapbacks, ladders, and outside reinforcements can dramatically alter the outcome.

Proverb Variants

“Count first, fight second.”
“Every liberty matters in a semeai.”
“The group with one more liberty controls the fight.”

proverbs/Strategies/an_empty_triangle_is.title: An Empty Triangle Is Usually Inefficient
proverbs/Strategies/an_empty_triangle_is.content:
Core Meaning
The empty triangle is one of the most famous examples of bad shape in Go. Three stones clustered tightly together often waste moves, reduce liberties, and create inefficient development.

Shape Connection
The empty triangle is considered poor shape because it is:

Overconcentrated – too many stones perform too little work
Slow – it develops inefficiently compared to lighter shapes
Restricted – it limits future flexibility and movement

Good shape aims for efficiency, balance, and maximum effectiveness from every stone.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationEmpty Triangle ProblemBetter AlternativeConnecting stonesUses an extra move inefficientlyExtend more lightly for flexibilityRunning groupCreates slow heavy shapeUse knight’s moves or diagonal connectionsFighting positionReduces liberties unnecessarilyPreserve stronger liberty countCenter developmentLimits outward influenceBuild broader and more active shape

Why This Works

Efficiency matters – every move should accomplish multiple goals
Shape affects strength – cramped formations become heavy
Liberties are reduced – tighter shapes are easier to attack
Flexibility wins fights – lighter stones adapt more easily


Counterexample
An empty triangle is not always bad. In tactical situations, it may be the strongest move to capture stones, secure a connection, or win a critical fight immediately.

Proverb Variants

“Bad shape wastes good moves.”
“The empty triangle is heavy and slow.”
“Strong shape values efficiency over closeness.”

proverbs/Strategies/an_empty_triangle_is.title: Avoid Empty Triangles And Inefficient Shape
proverbs/Strategies/an_empty_triangle_is.content:
Core Meaning
The empty triangle is a classic example of inefficient shape. While it may look solid, it often wastes moves, reduces liberties, and limits the effectiveness of your stones across the board.

Shape Connection
The empty triangle is usually considered bad shape because it is:

Overconcentrated – too many stones defend the same area
Heavy – the shape becomes slow and difficult to use efficiently
Inflexible – it limits future movement and development

Efficient shapes spread naturally while maintaining strength and mobility.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationEmpty Triangle ProblemBetter Shape AlternativeSimple connectionUses one move too manyExtend lightly with better spacingRunning stonesCreates heavy movementUse diagonal or knight’s connectionsFighting sequenceReduces available libertiesPreserve flexibility and escape routesBuilding influenceCompresses stones too tightlyExpand outward with efficient shape

Why This Works

Efficiency wins long games – wasted moves reduce overall potential
Shape affects mobility – heavy stones are easier to pressure
Liberties matter in fights – cramped formations weaken tactical strength
Flexibility creates options – lighter shapes adapt better to changing positions


Counterexample
An empty triangle can still be correct in tactical situations. If it captures stones, prevents a cut, wins a capturing race, or secures life immediately, efficiency may become less important than certainty.

Proverb Variants

“Good shape uses every stone wisely.”
“The empty triangle is solid but slow.”
“Efficiency matters more than appearance.”

proverbs/Strategies/are_any_of_your_grou.title: Always Check Whether Your Groups Are In Atari
proverbs/Strategies/are_any_of_your_grou.content:
Core Meaning
A group in Atari has only one liberty remaining and can be captured on the next move if left undefended. Constant awareness of Atari is essential for avoiding sudden tactical losses.

Tactical Connection
Recognizing Atari is a fundamental fighting skill because it is:

Urgent – ignored Atari usually leads to immediate capture
Preventive – early awareness avoids larger disasters
Foundational – liberty counting supports all tactical reading

Strong players continually check both their own stones and their opponent’s stones for Atari opportunities.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationAtari DangerProper ResponseSmall isolated groupOnly one liberty remainsExtend or connect to safetyCutting fightStones become separatedDefend before the cut becomes fatalLadder attackRepeated Atari pressureRead carefully before committingCorner struggleLiberties disappear rapidlyCount accurately and defend in time

Why This Works

Captured stones are irreversible – simple oversights lose games quickly
Liberty awareness guides tactics – many Tesuji rely on precise counts
Defense is easier early – delayed responses often become inefficient
Atari creates opportunities – threatening capture can force mistakes


Counterexample
Not every Atari needs to be answered directly. Sometimes sacrificing stones for outside influence, sente, or larger strategic gains is the better choice.

Proverb Variants

“One liberty away from disaster.”
“Always count before you fight.”
“The careless player overlooks Atari.”

proverbs/Strategies/attack_your_opponent.title: Attack Weak Groups Before Defending Your Own
proverbs/Strategies/attack_your_opponent.content:
Core Meaning
In many fights, the best defense is active pressure. Attacking your opponent’s weak groups can force them to respond, giving you time and opportunities to strengthen your own positions naturally.

Strategic Connection
Attacking weak groups is powerful because it is:

Forcing – weak groups demand immediate attention
Efficient – attacking while defending gains multiple benefits
Initiative-driven – pressure helps maintain Sente

Strong players often strengthen their own stones indirectly by attacking nearby weaknesses instead of defending passively.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationAttacking BenefitOpponent’s ProblemTwo weak groups nearbyAttack one while stabilizing yoursDefend under pressureRunning fightGain outside influenceEscape inefficientlyCenter attackBuild strength naturallyLose territory while defendingThin enemy formationForce submissive shapeRespond repeatedly and lose initiative

Why This Works

Pressure creates tempo – forcing moves limit enemy choices
Attacking builds strength – nearby stones become stronger naturally
Weak groups are burdens – the defender loses flexibility
Initiative matters – active play controls the flow of the game


Counterexample
Ignoring your own critically weak groups can be disastrous. If your stones are close to collapse or capture, immediate defense may be more urgent than counterattacking.

Proverb Variants

“Attack is often the best defense.”
“Pressure weak groups to gain time.”
“Strong attacks strengthen your own stones.”

proverbs/Strategies/avoid_over.title: Avoid Overconcentration And Balance Your Stones
proverbs/Strategies/avoid_over.content:
Core Meaning
Overconcentration wastes moves by placing too many stones in areas that are already strong. Efficient play spreads influence across the board, allowing each stone to contribute actively to both attack and defense.

Strategic Connection
Balanced stone placement is valuable because it is:

Efficient – each move develops useful influence
Flexible – lighter formations adapt more easily
Expansive – spreading strength controls larger areas

Good players avoid clustering stones unnecessarily and instead aim for harmony between territory, influence, and mobility.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationOverconcentration ProblemBetter Strategic ChoiceReinforcing safe areaAdds strength where none is neededPlay larger points elsewhereHeavy local defenseCreates cramped inefficient shapeDefend lightly while expanding outwardCenter formationLimits overall influenceSpread stones for broader board controlRunning battleDefensive clustering loses tempoUse flexible Sabaki to stay light

Why This Works

Efficiency increases board value – fewer stones accomplish more
Influence grows outward – balanced formations affect wider areas
Heavy groups invite attack – clustered stones become slow and passive
Flexibility preserves initiative – lighter positions respond better to change


Counterexample
Avoiding concentration too rigidly can leave weak or disconnected groups. In tactical situations, solid reinforcement may be necessary to secure life, connection, or stability.

Proverb Variants

“Too many stones in one place become inefficient.”
“Balanced influence is stronger than crowded strength.”
“Light shape gives freedom across the board.”

proverbs/Strategies/avoid_over_2.title: Avoid Overconcentration And Spread Stones Efficiently
proverbs/Strategies/avoid_over_2.content:
Core Meaning
Overconcentration occurs when too many stones perform the same job in a small area. Efficient play spreads strength naturally, creating flexible positions that remain light, active, and adaptable.

Strategic Connection
Efficient stone placement is important because it is:

Flexible – balanced shapes adapt easily to changing fights
Efficient – each stone contributes maximum value
Light – loose formations are harder to attack severely

Good Sabaki emphasizes mobility and coordination rather than excessive reinforcement.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationOverconcentration ProblemBetter AlternativeReinforcing safe areaWastes moves on already strong stonesExpand toward larger areasHeavy defensive shapeCreates slow clustered formationsUse lighter connections and flexible shapeCenter developmentCompresses influence unnecessarilySpread stones for broader controlRunning groupAdds defensive stones repeatedlyEscape lightly while maintaining balance

Why This Works

Efficiency creates larger potential – fewer moves achieve more influence
Flexible stones stay active – light shapes adapt during fighting
Heavy groups become targets – clustered stones are easier to pressure
Balanced shape improves Sabaki – mobility reduces defensive burden


Counterexample
Avoiding concentration too aggressively can create thin, weak positions. Sometimes solid reinforcement is necessary during tactical fights or life-and-death situations.

Proverb Variants

“Spread strength, not stones blindly.”
“Light shape survives heavy attacks.”
“Efficiency comes from balance and flexibility.”

proverbs/Strategies/avoid_playing_deep_i.title: Avoid Deep Early Invasions In The Fuseki
proverbs/Strategies/avoid_playing_deep_i.content:
Core Meaning
Deep invasions during the early Fuseki are often premature. Before the board develops fully, invading too deeply can create weak groups that lack support, influence, and safe escape routes.

Strategic Connection
Early invasions are risky because they are:

Isolated – surrounding support is often insufficient
Heavy – weak invading groups require repeated defense
Premature – larger strategic opportunities may still exist elsewhere

Strong Fuseki play values balance, influence, and development before committing to dangerous reductions or invasions.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationDeep Invasion ProblemBetter Strategic ChoiceEarly corner frameworkInvader becomes surrounded quicklyDevelop outside influence firstStrong enemy moyoEscape routes are limitedReduce lightly instead of invading deeplyUnsettled boardWeak groups appear too earlyStrengthen nearby stones before invadingLarge-scale FusekiOpponent gains attacking influencePlay wider extensions and approach moves

Why This Works

Weak groups become burdens – early invasions often need constant defense
Influence matters early – giving the opponent strength can be costly
Timing is critical – invasions work better after outside support develops
Flexibility preserves initiative – lighter reductions avoid heavy fighting


Counterexample
Some early invasions are correct when the opponent’s framework is still thin or incomplete. Skilled invasions can exploit weak shapes before territory becomes fully secure.

Proverb Variants

“Invade deeply only with support.”
“Premature invasions create unnecessary weakness.”
“In Fuseki, influence comes before reckless invasion.”

proverbs/Strategies/avoid_playing_moves_.title: Avoid Fixing Your Opponent’s Weaknesses
proverbs/Strategies/avoid_playing_moves_.content:
Core Meaning
Moves that accidentally strengthen your opponent can erase attacking opportunities and surrender initiative. Strong play pressures weaknesses instead of helping the opponent repair them for free.

Strategic Connection
Avoiding helpful moves is important because it preserves:

Pressure – weak groups remain targets for attack
Initiative – forcing the opponent to defend maintains Sente
Efficiency – unnecessary contact often strengthens enemy shape

Good players carefully consider whether a move improves the opponent’s Sabaki or fixes defects that could have remained exploitable.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationMistakeBetter AlternativeAttacking weak groupPushes opponent into strong shapeAttack from a distance to limit flexibilityContact fightingForces efficient enemy connectionMaintain outside pressure insteadDefensive reductionReinforces enemy territoryReduce lightly without strengthening shapeRunning battleHelps opponent escape naturallyBlock escape routes before attacking

Why This Works

Weakness creates leverage – unsettled groups restrict enemy freedom
Sabaki thrives on efficiency – helping shape development aids survival
Initiative matters – forcing defense preserves momentum
Strong attacks deny comfort – pressure is most effective before stabilization


Counterexample
Sometimes strengthening the opponent slightly is acceptable if it secures a larger strategic gain elsewhere. Sacrificing local pressure for global efficiency can still be correct.

Proverb Variants

“Do not repair the enemy’s shape for free.”
“Pressure weak groups before they settle.”
“Helping your opponent often loses initiative.”

proverbs/Strategies/balance_territory_an.title: Balance Territory And Influence
proverbs/Strategies/balance_territory_an.content:
Core Meaning
Strong Go strategy requires balancing secure territory with outward influence. Focusing too heavily on one while neglecting the other can create weaknesses in both local and global positions.

Strategic Connection
Balance matters because:

Territory provides reliable points and stability
Influence creates future potential and attacking power
Harmony between the two produces flexible, resilient positions

Good players adapt according to the board situation instead of pursuing only immediate profit or only large-scale frameworks.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationImbalance ProblemBalanced ApproachGreedy territorial playBecomes low and overconcentratedLeave room for outside influenceExcessive moyo buildingGives away secure pointsConvert influence into reliable territoryStrong attacking wallGains influence but no profitUse thickness to secure territory laterEarly Fuseki expansionToo wide and vulnerableCombine development with solid foundations

Why This Works

Territory wins games – secure points matter in the final count
Influence shapes the future – strong positions affect large areas
Flexibility prevents weakness – balanced positions adapt better
Efficiency combines both goals – strong shape can attack and profit simultaneously


Counterexample
Some board positions justify imbalance temporarily. A player behind in territory may need to emphasize influence and attacking potential, while a player ahead may prefer secure territorial play.

Proverb Variants

“Territory gives profit; influence gives power.”
“Balance creates flexibility.”
“Too much greed weakens the whole board.”

proverbs/Strategies/be_cautious_not_gree.title: Be Cautious, Not Greedy
proverbs/Strategies/be_cautious_not_gree.content:
Core Meaning
When holding an advantage, solid and careful play is often stronger than greedy overextension. Trying to gain too much at once can create weaknesses that allow the opponent to recover momentum.

Strategic Connection
Cautious play is effective because it is:

Stable – strong positions are difficult to attack
Efficient – secure gains are more valuable than risky overplays
Controlled – careful moves preserve your lead and initiative

In handicap games especially, maintaining balance and avoiding unnecessary complications is often more important than maximizing territory immediately.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationGreedy MistakeCautious AlternativeEarly territorial leadOverextends into enemy strengthConsolidate influence and secure weak groupsStrong attacking wallChases too deeply for extra profitAttack lightly while protecting shapeInvading moyoPushes recklessly for maximum gainReduce safely and remain flexibleWinning positionStarts unnecessary fightsSimplify the board and preserve stability

Why This Works

Overplay creates weakness – greed often leads to thin shape
Strong positions need stability – secure groups preserve advantages
Complicated fights increase risk – unnecessary battles invite mistakes
Patience wins games – steady profit accumulates over time


Counterexample
Playing too cautiously can become passive and allow the opponent to recover. Sometimes active pressure or calculated aggression is necessary to maintain control.

Proverb Variants

“Protect your lead before seeking more.”
“Greed creates weakness.”
“Solid play turns advantage into victory.”

proverbs/Strategies/big_moves_before_sma.title: Play Big Moves Before Small Moves
proverbs/Strategies/big_moves_before_sma.content:
Core Meaning
In Go, the largest moves should usually be played before smaller local gains. Prioritizing major points, valuable Miai, and strong Sente opportunities creates greater overall board efficiency and strategic momentum.

Strategic Connection
Big moves are important because they are:

Efficient – they influence large areas of the board
Urgent – delaying them may allow the opponent to claim them first
Flexible – large-scale moves often create multiple future possibilities

Strong players constantly compare move value and avoid becoming distracted by small local plays too early.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationBig Move ValueSmall Move ProblemOpen side extensionExpands territory and influenceSmall local defense gains littleLarge endgame pointSecures major territorial swingTiny yose move wastes initiativeMiai opportunityForces opponent into difficult choiceLocal adjustment lacks urgencySente attackMaintains tempo and board controlGote move loses initiative unnecessarily

Why This Works

Large moves shape the whole board – early priorities affect future strategy
Efficiency matters – one big move can outperform several small ones
Initiative is valuable – Sente keeps pressure on the opponent
Timing determines value – delayed large points often disappear


Counterexample
Ignoring urgent tactical weaknesses for the sake of a “big move” can be disastrous. Saving a weak group or responding to a severe threat may outweigh larger strategic opportunities.

Proverb Variants

“Play where the board is largest.”
“Big points disappear quickly.”
“Do not trade initiative for tiny profit.”

proverbs/Strategies/build_flexible_shape.title: Build Flexible Shapes Instead Of Rigid Territory
proverbs/Strategies/build_flexible_shape.content:
Core Meaning
Flexible shapes adapt more effectively to changing board conditions than rigid territorial formations. Strong shape balances stability with mobility, allowing stones to attack, defend, expand, or reduce as needed.

Strategic Connection
Flexible formations are valuable because they are:

Adaptable – they respond smoothly to attacks and invasions
Efficient – stones work together without becoming overconcentrated
Resilient – light shape is harder to trap or exploit

Rigid territory may appear secure, but inflexible positions often become vulnerable once the opponent applies pressure.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationFlexible Shape BenefitRigid Territory ProblemExpanding moyoAllows future adjustmentSolid borders become overconcentratedRunning groupsEscapes lightly and efficientlyHeavy defensive shape loses mobilityBorder defenseAdapts to invasions naturallyFixed walls create exploitable weaknessesFighting positionSupports attack and defenseCramped territory limits tactical options

Why This Works

Adaptability preserves strength – flexible stones respond to changing threats
Overconcentration wastes moves – rigid formations often duplicate effort
Light shape survives pressure – mobile groups are difficult to attack severely
Influence creates options – outward strength supports future development


Counterexample
Excessive flexibility without solid foundations can create thin and weak positions. Some situations require firm territorial defense instead of loose development.

Proverb Variants

“Flexible shape survives changing battles.”
“Rigid territory invites pressure.”
“Strength comes from adaptability, not stiffness.”

proverbs/Strategies/build_territory_natu.title: Build Territory Naturally Around Existing Stones
proverbs/Strategies/build_territory_natu.content:
Core Meaning
Strong territory often grows naturally from stones that are already well placed. Instead of forcing risky invasions or distant expansions, use your existing strength to develop stable and efficient areas of control.

Strategic Connection
Natural territorial growth is effective because it is:

Efficient – existing stones already provide support
Stable – connected positions are harder to attack
Expansive – small extensions can develop into large frameworks

In handicap games especially, nearby expansions around handicap stones can quietly build powerful territorial potential.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationNatural Development BenefitForced Play ProblemHandicap corner stoneSupports easy side expansionDistant invasion becomes unsupportedStrong wall formationConverts influence into territoryOverextending creates weak groupsSide frameworkBuilds territory graduallyGreedy enclosure invites reductionStable connected shapeExpands safely and efficientlyThin development risks attack

Why This Works

Strong stones support expansion – nearby influence protects growth
Efficiency matters – connected stones accomplish more together
Natural territory is resilient – stable formations resist invasion
Patience creates profit – steady development often outperforms greed


Counterexample
Building only near existing stones can become overly passive or overconcentrated. Sometimes larger strategic opportunities elsewhere on the board are more important.

Proverb Variants

“Strong stones grow strong territory.”
“Expand naturally from existing strength.”
“Small extensions can become large frameworks.”

proverbs/Strategies/connect_your_stones_.title: Connect Your Stones Methodically
proverbs/Strategies/connect_your_stones_.content:
Core Meaning
Strong connections create stable positions and reduce tactical weaknesses. By connecting stones carefully and methodically, you build resilient formations that are difficult to cut apart or attack severely.

Strategic Connection
Solid connections are valuable because they are:

Stable – connected groups support each other naturally
Efficient – strong chains reduce the need for constant defense
Reliable – fewer cutting points mean fewer tactical dangers

In handicap games especially, existing handicap stones often provide natural anchors for building strong connected frameworks.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationMethodical Connection BenefitRisky AlternativeNearby handicap stonesForms strong territorial frameworkOverextending creates cutting weaknessesRunning groupEscapes safely with supportThin jumps invite attackFighting positionRemoves tactical vulnerabilitiesIgnoring cuts leads to separationSide expansionBuilds stable influence graduallyLoose shape collapses under pressure

Why This Works

Connected stones share strength – groups defend each other efficiently
Cuts create weakness – separated groups become attack targets
Stability preserves initiative – strong shape reduces defensive burden
Simple shape avoids mistakes – reliable connections improve consistency


Counterexample
Overconnecting can become inefficient and overconcentrated. In some situations, lighter and more flexible play is better than making every connection completely solid.

Proverb Variants

“Connected stones are strong stones.”
“Prevent cuts before they appear.”
“Strong chains reduce future problems.”

proverbs/Strategies/control_the_center_t.title: Control The Center To Influence The Whole Board
proverbs/Strategies/control_the_center_t.content:
Core Meaning
A strong central presence gives influence across multiple areas of the board simultaneously. Control of the center increases flexibility, supports attacks, and allows rapid response to changing developments.

Strategic Connection
Central influence is powerful because it is:

Flexible – central stones can assist many regions at once
Expansive – influence radiates outward in every direction
Supportive – center strength helps both attack and defense

Unlike corner territory, central influence is less about immediate points and more about long-term control and mobility.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationCentral Influence BenefitOpponent’s DifficultyRunning attackSupports pressure from multiple sidesEscaping groups lack safe directionLarge moyo frameworkExpands territorial potentialInvasions become dangerousBoard-wide fightingReinforces nearby weak groupsOpponent struggles to coordinate efficientlyMidgame transitionEnables quick directional changesLocalized play becomes restricted

Why This Works

Center stones affect many areas – influence spreads naturally outward
Mobility creates strength – central positions react quickly to threats
Attacks become stronger – nearby support limits enemy escape routes
Flexibility improves efficiency – one strong framework supports multiple plans


Counterexample
Center influence without territorial value can become too abstract. If influence is not converted into territory, attack potential, or strategic advantage, the opponent may simply take secure points elsewhere.

Proverb Variants

“The center connects the whole board.”
“Influence radiates outward from strength.”
“Central control creates strategic freedom.”

proverbs/Strategies/coordinate_your_ston.title: Coordinate Your Stones To Support Each Other
proverbs/Strategies/coordinate_your_ston.content:
Core Meaning
Stones placed in isolation are easily surrounded and overwhelmed, but stones that coordinate across distances multiply each other’s strength. In Go, true efficiency comes from synergy: every move should harmonize with your existing stones, building mutual pathways for connection, escape, and territorial development.
When your stones support each other, your entire board position becomes resilient and flexible, denying the opponent easy cutting targets.

Strategic Connection
Coordinating your stones is fundamental because it is:

Synergistic – two cooperating groups are vastly stronger than two independent groups
Economical – fewer stones are needed for defense when mutual support exists
Attacking-ready – coordinated positions project crossfire that makes enemy invasions perilous

A well-coordinated position lets you pivot between territory and attack effortlessly.

Classic Go Examples






























SituationUncoordinated PlayCoordinated AlternativeExpanding from a cornerPlacing an isolated stone far awayExtending at an optimal distance from your enclosureUnder center attackRunning in separate directionsMoving toward friendly thickness to link upInvading enemy moyoCreating a lone, heavy targetLightly reducing while keeping an eye on friendly alliesDeveloping frameworksClumping stones on one sideBalancing third- and fourth-line stones across the board

Why This Works

Mutual support deters cuts – stones that see each other can connect or counterattack easily.
Amplifies thickness – multiple stones working together project formidable power across open terrain.
Improves efficiency – stones accomplish territorial and defensive duties simultaneously.
Preserves sente – coordinated stones rarely need submissive, defensive reinforcements.


Counterexample
Do not confuse coordination with overconcentration. Placing stones too close together in an effort to support each other wastes moves and builds heavy, inefficient clumps. Support should be maintained across flexible distances.

Proverb Variants

“Stones that work together never walk alone.”
“Coordinate your stones; do not scatter your forces.”
“Mutual support is the mother of good shape.”

proverbs/Strategies/coordinate_your_ston.title: Stones Working Together Create Solid Connection
proverbs/Strategies/coordinate_your_ston.content:
Core Meaning
Go is not a game of individual stones; it is a game of connected teams. When stones work in concert, they form unbreakable chains of connection and mutual protection.
A move that might look modest locally becomes brilliant when it provides a lifeline to an adjacent group or establishes a pincer coordination across the side. Always ask how a new stone communicates with the stones already on the board.

Tactical Connection
Stones working together provide:

Structural integrity – prevents the opponent from finding separating cuts
Shared liberties – connected chains resist squeezing and atari sequences
Unified direction – channels whole-board influence toward a single strategic goal


Classic Go Examples






























SituationDisconnected RiskCoordinated PlaySide extensionPlaying a floating stone with no baseExtending within reach of a corner shimariEscaping from a capJumping blindly into enemy territoryJumping toward friendly waiting stonesFlank fightingLeaving cutting gaps between groupsUsing bamboo joints or solid connectionsCenter influenceBuilding disconnected wallsAligning walls to face each other across the center

Why This Works

Unity creates safety – a single united army is nearly impossible to capture.
Halves defensive burden – defending one connected group requires half the moves of defending two separate groups.
Restricts enemy sabaki – coordinated stones leave no gaps for enemy counter-play.


Counterexample
Sometimes playing an independent stone away from friendly allies is necessary to make a timely reduction or take an urgent whole-board point, provided you are prepared to treat the stone lightly.

Proverb Variants

“United stones stand; divided stones fall.”
“Connect your stones before you conquer the board.”
“Good stones speak to each other across the grid.”

proverbs/Strategies/corners_first_then_s.title: Corners First, Then Sides, Then Center
proverbs/Strategies/corners_first_then_s.content:
Core Meaning
The golden rule of the Go opening is: “Corners first, then sides, then center.” The geometry of the board makes corners the most efficient place to make territory: you only need two walls of stones to enclose a corner, because the two board edges provide free boundaries.
Enclosing a side requires three walls, while enclosing the center requires four walls on all sides. Securing the corners early lays the foundation of secure points before venturing into the open center.

Strategic Connection
The corner-side-center progression governs opening efficiency:

Corners (Maximum efficiency) – fewest stones required per point of territory
Sides (Moderate efficiency) – excellent for extending corner influence and settling bases
Center (Lowest efficiency) – vast and porous, best used for fighting rather than direct point-making


Classic Go Examples






























StagePriority AreaStrategic ObjectiveMoves 1–8Empty CornersStake out 4-4, 3-4, or 3-3 starting pointsMoves 9–25Approaches & EnclosuresEnclose corners (shimari) or approach enemy cornersMoves 25–50Side ExtensionsExtend along side star points to convert corner frameworksMoves 50+Center DevelopmentExpand moyos or contest center boundaries

Why This Works

Board edges are free shields – corners require only two stones to establish a viable base.
Guaranteed eye space – corner groups make two eyes far more easily than center stones.
Stability creates freedom – safe corners grant the tactical confidence to fight aggressively elsewhere.


Counterexample
Do not cling exclusively to low corner territory if the opponent is allowed to construct an unstoppable, monolithic center moyo. Balance corner profit with adequate outside presence.

Proverb Variants

“Corners are gold, sides are silver, the center is grass.”
“Win the corners, guide the sides, fight in the center.”
“First the corner, then the edge, last the vast plain.”

proverbs/Strategies/do_not_attach_to_str.title: Do Not Attach To Strong Stones Without Clear Purpose
proverbs/Strategies/do_not_attach_to_str.content:
Core Meaning
Contact plays (tsuke) have a universal rule in Go: attaching to an opposing stone makes it stronger. When you attach, the opponent naturally extends or hanes, increasing their liberties and solidifying their shape.
Therefore, attaching carelessly to an opponent’s already strong group is an unmitigated disaster: you reinforce their strength while leaving your own attaching stone weak and outnumbered.

Strategic Connection
When attachment is and isn’t justified:

Forbidden – attaching to strong enemy walls when trying to attack or make normal territory
Permitted (Sabaki) – attaching to strong stones when you are desperately weak and need to sacrifice lightly to settle
Permitted (Endgame) – specific boundary tesujis where the follow-up is read out completely


Classic Go Examples

























ScenarioCareless Attachment (Bad)Correct TechniqueAttacking an enemy groupAttaching directly to their stonesCapping or pincering from 1–2 spaces awayApproaching a solid enclosureAttaching to their corner stoneMaking a loose, flexible approach from a safe distanceSettling a weak invading groupExtending slowly into a netAttaching deliberately to crosscut and make sabaki

Why This Works

Action causes reaction – contact moves force the defender to add stones and grow thicker.
Reinforces enemy bastions – making an already strong group even stronger ruins your whole-board prospects.
Sacrifice logic – attachment only works when you actively want the opponent to become heavy while you slip away.


Counterexample
In sabaki operations deep inside enemy territory, attaching to the opponent’s strongest stone is the standard technique! Because their stone is already strong, making it slightly stronger doesn’t matter, while you get the leverage needed to shape your eyes.

Proverb Variants

“Attach to defend; keep distance to attack.”
“Do not touch strong stones.”
“Contact breeds strength; do not feed the beast.”

proverbs/Strategies/do_not_chase_your_op.title: Do Not Chase Too Aggressively; They Will Make Shape
proverbs/Strategies/do_not_chase_your_op.content:
Core Meaning
When you chase an opponent’s fleeing stones with unrestrained aggression, you frequently give them the exact contact points they need to make good shape.
A running group in open space has no eyes and struggles for direction. But as soon as you press too tightly against it, the opponent can use hane, crosscuts, and counter-attachments to establish eye shape and spring counter-attacks.

Tactical Connection
The perils of overzealous chasing:

Creates sabaki opportunities – gives the defender leverage to sacrifice and make eyes
Exposes cutting defects – aggressive chasers often outrun their own supply lines
Surrenders the initiative – a successful enemy counter-hane can reverse the attack instantly


Classic Go Examples

























SituationOverzealous PursuitPrudent Attacking MoveEyeless enemy group fleeingPlaying contact moves to block escapeLeaping ahead with a loose cap to steer itChasing along the sidePushing directly from behindExtending parallel on the higher line to build influenceOpponent counter-cutsPanicking and playing multiple atarisConnecting your cutting stones calmly to maintain thickness

Why This Works

Stones need leverage to make shape – without contact, making eyes in open space is arduous.
Loose nets catch big fish – keeping distance seals escape routes while leaving the defender nothing to lean on.
Thickness endures – patient attacks ensure your own group never becomes a counter-target.


Counterexample
If the opponent’s stones are trapped against the edge of the board with nowhere to run, tight contact ataris that capture the stones on the spot are completely warranted.

Proverb Variants

“Do not crowd the runner.”
“Distance kills; contact heals.”
“Attack with an open net, not a tight fist.”

proverbs/Strategies/do_not_push_from_beh.title: Do Not Push From Behind
proverbs/Strategies/do_not_push_from_beh.content:
Core Meaning
The proverb “Do not push from behind” (ushiro kara osu na) warns against crawling directly behind an opponent’s line of stones. When two lines of stones race alongside each other, the player who is one step ahead has the initiative: they can turn (bend) or hane at will.
If you push from behind, every move you play gives the opponent a free head start, strengthening their wall and allowing them to dictate the direction of the game while you remain one step behind in gote.

Tactical Connection
Pushing from behind causes:

Structural inferiority – the opponent is always one step ahead in liberties and reach
Wall gift – you build a powerful, solid wall for the opponent at your own expense
Head of stones danger – allows the opponent to deliver a devastating hane at the head


Classic Go Examples

























Race on the BoardBlunder (Pushing Behind)Strategic Master MoveSide running battlePushing along the 3rd line while opponent is on the 4thJumping ahead or playing elsewhere (tenuki)Center escapePushing directly into the enemy’s tailCapping or knight’s move leaping ahead to seize the frontEdge crawlingCrawling on line 2 while opponent walks on line 3Turning or jumping out to break the pattern

Why This Works

The lead stone dictates the turn – the frontrunner decides when to bend and seal the border.
Pushing strengthens the defender – touching stones gives the opponent effortless, solid connections.
Tempo loss – pushing from behind is inherently passive and reactive.


Counterexample
If pushing from behind directly captures cutting stones, prevents a fatal disconnection of your own group, or wins an immediate capturing race, pushing is tactically justified.

Proverb Variants

“Pushing from behind builds the enemy’s palace.”
“Stay one step ahead; never follow the tail.”
“He who pushes from behind walks in shadows.”

proverbs/Strategies/do_not_rush_into_fig.title: Do Not Rush Into Fights Too Early
proverbs/Strategies/do_not_rush_into_fig.content:
Core Meaning
The opening (fuseki) is a time for staking claims, creating frameworks, and establishing harmonious coordinate relationships among your stones. Rushing into violent, full-board fighting on move 10 destroys whole-board harmony and creates weak groups before bases are established.
Patience in the opening yields stable positions with high liberties that provide the launchpad for decisive middle-game fighting.

Strategic Connection
Opening discipline requires:

Broad vision – look at all four corners and sides before engaging locally
Solid bases – build two-space extensions and enclosures before brawling
Avoiding needless battles – let the opponent overextend while you take secure territory


Classic Go Examples

























StagePremature Brawl (Bad)Mature Opening Play (Good)Empty board with open cornersCrosscutting an opponent’s approach stoneResponding with a standard corner josekiOpponent extends along sideDiving in with an unsupported invasionEnclosing your own corner (shimari)Unsettled stonesStarting a second fight elsewhereSettling the first group with a base or jump

Why This Works

Open corners have higher point yields – early fighting yields 2–4 points; corners yield 15–20.
Prevents floating groups – fighting without bases turns stones into vulnerable targets.
Sets the stage for victory – thick opening formations win middle-game fights naturally.


Counterexample
If the opponent plays a flagrant opening mistake that can be punished with a simple refutation without compromising your own stones, execute the punishment calmly.

Proverb Variants

“First cultivate the field, then harvest the grain.”
“A calm opening precedes a victorious middle game.”
“Do not draw your sword on an empty plain.”

proverbs/Strategies/do_not_waste_moves_e.title: Every Stone Should Have A Purpose
proverbs/Strategies/do_not_waste_moves_e.content:
Core Meaning
In Go, every single stone placed on the board represents one turn of investment. A wasted move—a stone played aimlessly without defending a weakness, expanding territory, attacking an enemy group, or claiming sente—is an outright gift of a free turn to the opponent.
Strong players play with intense intentionality: every stone must perform a clear function, and the very best stones perform two or three functions simultaneously.

Strategic Connection
Stone purpose and efficiency:

Multitasking – ideal moves combine attack with territorial expansion
No phantom moves – avoid placing stones in areas where nothing is at stake
Strategic coherence – ensure each move directly advances your whole-board plan


Classic Go Examples

























Move TypeWasted Move (No Purpose)Purposeful MoveDefendingAdding a stone inside an unconditionally alive cornerExpanding along the side to create an eye baseAttackingPlaying a single peep that opponent easily connectsCapping to steer the enemy group toward your thicknessEndgameFilling a neutral dame point prematurelyPlaying a second-line sente hane-and-connect

Why This Works

Stone economy determines the winner – 100 purposeful stones beat 100 casual stones every time.
Maintains momentum – purposeful moves force the opponent to react, keeping sente.
Creates synergy – stones with distinct roles combine into a formidable whole-board web.


Counterexample
Sometimes playing a simple, solid, seemingly modest connection is the highest-purpose move on the board because it prevents a catastrophic future cut.

Proverb Variants

“Do not cast stones into the void.”
“One move, two purposes; two moves, three gains.”
“Every stone is a soldier; give each an order.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_chase_your_opp.title: Don't Chase Your Opponent's Stones Too Much
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_chase_your_opp.content:
Core Meaning
Attacking is one of the greatest pleasures in Go, but chasing an opposing group too aggressively often backfires. When you chase stones too closely with contact moves or overextended jumps, you inadvertently give the opponent leverage to make good shape and counter-attack.
The true purpose of an attack is not to kill, but to profit elsewhere—building solid territory or outside thickness while the defender struggles to stay alive.

Tactical Connection
Overzealous pursuit causes:

Self-weakening – pushing too hard leaves your own cutting defects exposed
Opponent sabaki – close contact allows the defender to crosscut or hane to settle
Loss of whole-board balance – tunnel vision on one group neglects larger open areas


Classic Go Examples

























ScenarioFlawed AggressionSound Attacking StrategyRunning group in centerAttaching directly to try to captureCapping from a distance to steer it toward your thicknessDragon escapingChasing blindly with cutting movesBuilding territory along the side while keeping the group eyelessOpponent invades moyoFrantically trying to kill every stoneSqueezing the invasion to secure guaranteed perimeter points

Why This Works

Cornered stones fight hardest – an opponent facing death will find sharp, desperate counter-tesujis.
Contact creates strength – touching enemy stones gives them liberties and shape-making opportunities.
Indirect profit wins games – surrounding territory while attacking yields guaranteed leads.


Counterexample
If the opponent’s group has zero eyes, lacks escape routes, and a clean, read-out killing sequence exists without creating counter-weaknesses, you should strike decisively to capture.

Proverb Variants

“Attack from a distance; do not touch what you wish to kill.”
“Do not chase the rabbit into its burrow.”
“Profit from the chase; do not gamble on the kill.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_cram_too_many_.title: Don't Cram Too Many Stones In One Area
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_cram_too_many_.content:
Core Meaning
Overconcentration (korigatachi) is the disease of putting too many stones in one area to do the work that fewer stones could accomplish. Cramming stones into a tight cluster wastes moves, yields minimal territory, and leaves the rest of the board wide open for the opponent to claim.
Stones must be deployed with maximum breathing room and scope, balancing solid connections with expansive board coverage.

Strategic Connection
Avoiding overconcentration ensures:

Stone efficiency – every stone works at maximum capacity
Whole-board balance – prevents falling behind in the global territory race
Dynamic flexibility – lighter structures adapt more easily to changing board conditions


Classic Go Examples

























MistakeProblemSolutionAdding extra stones to a living groupGenerates zero additional pointsPlay tenuki to seize a large side pointClumping around a captured stoneCreates slow, heavy shapeExtend outward or jump into the centerMaking multiple tight solid connectionsOverconcentrated, slow defenseUse one-space jumps or bamboo joints

Why This Works

Go is a game of stone economy – 10 stones making 10 points loses to 10 stones making 30 points.
Broad influence deters invasions – spaced-out stones project a wider protective net.
Light stones have fewer burdens – if a loose stone is attacked, it can be sacrificed or handled flexibly.


Counterexample
In life-and-death emergencies or tight tactical capturing races (semeai), adding close, solid stones is essential to prevent immediate tactical collapse.

Proverb Variants

“Overconcentration is the road to defeat.”
“Do not put all your eggs in one corner.”
“Spread your wings; do not huddle in fear.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_forget_endgame.title: Don't Forget Endgame Moves
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_forget_endgame.content:
Core Meaning
Many games won in the opening or middle game are squandered in the endgame (yose). Players often relax once major battles subside, neglecting crucial second- and third-line boundary plays.
A sharp endgame sequence—especially one executed in sente—can easily swing 15 to 30 points, completely overturning the outcome of a close match.

Strategic Connection
Endgame mastery requires:

Sente prioritization – play double-sente, then sente, then reverse-sente, and finally gote
Accurate counting – calculate point values of boundary closures before playing
Relentless vigilance – look for undercuts like the monkey jump and second-line hane-connects


Classic Go Examples






























Endgame MoveValue & PriorityTypical MistakeDouble Sente boundaryAbsolute top priorityOverlooking it and allowing opponent to play it in senteMonkey jump reduction8–12 pointsPlaying small 2-point gote moves in the center insteadSecond-line hane and connect4–6 points in senteForgetting to connect and suffering a back-rank cutSecuring side bordersFirm pointsPlaying neutral dame moves prematurely

Why This Works

Every point counts equally – an endgame point won is identical in value to an opening point.
Sente moves cost nothing – forcing the opponent to respond leaves you with both the profit and the next turn.
Endgame mistakes are permanent – with few open points left, late-game losses cannot be recovered elsewhere.


Counterexample
Do not plunge into small 1- or 2-point endgame plays while an unsettled dragon is still fighting for life in the center. Life and death always takes precedence over yose.

Proverb Variants

“Yose decides the victor.”
“Sente in the endgame is worth double.”
“Count the small points; they build the mountain.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_go_fishing_whi.title: Don't Go Fishing While Your House Is On Fire
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_go_fishing_whi.content:
Core Meaning
This vivid proverb warns against greed in the face of mortal danger. “Going fishing” represents wandering off to chase small captures or speculative territory on the side, while “your house is on fire” represents your own weak group being on the verge of capture.
No matter how attractive an outside point looks, saving an urgent, dying group must always take precedence. If your group dies, whatever you caught while “fishing” will never compensate for the loss.

Strategic Connection
Urgency always trumps size:

Survival first – dead groups surrender both points and immense enemy thickness
Extinguish the blaze – reinforce your weak stones before looking for whole-board profit
Discipline over greed – resist the temptation to take tenuki when under lethal attack


Classic Go Examples

























House on Fire (Urgent)Going Fishing (Distraction)Correct ActionGroup has only 2 libertiesApproaching an open cornerExtend to safety or connect immediatelyOpponent peeps at a vital cutTaking an endgame slide on the sideConnect the cut firmlyLarge center dragon eyelessTaking second-line side territoryJump into the center to connect or make eyes

Why This Works

The cost of death is catastrophic – losing a 10-stone group is a 40-point swing that ends the game.
Defense preserves initiative later – once your house is secure, you can fish in peace.
Enemy thickness will punish you – ignoring an urgent defense gifts the opponent unconditional power across the board.


Counterexample
If your endangered stones are genuinely light, small, and easily disposable (e.g. 1–2 stones with zero strategic significance), you can intentionally sacrifice them to take a massive whole-board prize.

Proverb Variants

“Urgent moves before big moves.”
“Put out the fire before you count your gold.”
“A burning house has no room for guests.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_help_your_oppo.title: Don't Help Your Opponent Fix Their Weak Groups
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_help_your_oppo.content:
Core Meaning
When your opponent leaves behind cutting points, bad shape, or unsettled stones, do not play moves that force them to fix their defects. Beginners often play careless peeps or ataris that simply prompt the opponent to connect solidly, eliminating all lingering aji.
Leave the opponent’s weaknesses unplayed until the exact moment when exploiting them produces maximum tactical profit.

Strategic Connection
Preserving enemy defects requires:

Patience with aji – keep threats in reserve to use as ko threats or steering tools
Avoiding thank-you moves – don’t play moves that make the opponent happy to respond
Maximizing leverage – the threat of a cut is often more potent than the cut itself


Classic Go Examples

























Enemy WeaknessCareless Play (Helping Opponent)Disciplined PlayOpponent has a loose knight’s movePeeping immediately and forcing a solid connectionLeaving the cut open and attacking the whole group from afarOpponent stone has 2 libertiesPlaying atari and letting them connect to safetySurrounding the stone or using it as a ladder threatBroken eye shapeForcing a contact move that allows them to make eyesKeeping the boundary open and attacking for profit

Why This Works

Threats restrict enemy movement – as long as a cut exists, the opponent must play cautiously.
Premature play destroys aji – once the opponent connects, your leverage vanishes forever.
Saves ko threats – unplayed defects serve as invaluable assets during future ko fights.


Counterexample
If an immediate peep or cutting strike cuts the group apart decisively, captures critical stones, or secures immediate life for your own group in sente, strike without hesitation.

Proverb Variants

“The threat is stronger than the execution.”
“Do not repair the enemy’s fences.”
“Preserve the aji; do not give thank-you moves.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_let_your_group.title: Don't Let Your Groups Become Lonely
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_let_your_group.content:
Core Meaning
A “lonely” group is an isolated collection of stones stranded far from friendly allies with no base on the edge and no clear escape route into the center. Lonely groups become natural prey: the opponent can attack them relentlessly, building territory and strength while you scramble merely to survive.
Always keep lines of communication open between your groups or ensure every group has a clear plan for making a local base.

Strategic Connection
Preventing loneliness requires:

Proactive connection – link stones before enemy walls sever your escape routes
Base formation – secure a two-space extension along the side whenever possible
Central vision – keep a path open toward the open sky of the center


Classic Go Examples

























Board ScenarioLonely MistakeHealthy StrategyDeep invasionStaying inside to fight without an exitLeaping into the center with a one-space jumpCorner under siegeLetting the opponent seal the group in goteBending or jumping out into the centerSplit forces on the sideAllowing the opponent to wedge between groupsConnecting via a bamboo joint or diagonal move

Why This Works

Lonely groups hemorrhage points – running for life forces you to play passive gote moves.
Opponent gains free territory – chasing a lonely group allows the attacker to build walls effortlessly.
Two eyes are harder in isolation – surrounded groups must find eyes in cramped, hostile territory.


Counterexample
If a lone stone has already served its tactical purpose (such as a probe or reduction), do not try to rescue it. Abandon it lightly rather than letting it drag you into a costly rescue mission.

Proverb Variants

“An isolated stone is an invitation to attack.”
“Give your stones friends to lean on.”
“Do not leave orphans on the board.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_let_your_group.title: Isolated Groups Are Easy To Attack And Hard To Save
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_let_your_group.content:
Core Meaning
Isolated groups are the primary cause of sudden losses in Go. When a group is completely severed from its allies, its options narrow drastically: it cannot connect, it cannot threaten counter-attacks, and it must dedicate all its energy to finding two eyes in a confined space.
Understanding that isolated groups are easy to attack teaches you both how to protect your own stones and how to target the opponent’s isolated formations.

Tactical Connection
Isolated groups suffer from:

Liberty starvation – surrounding walls steadily squeeze their breathing room
Lack of counter-threats – unable to coordinate with outside allies
Predictable defense – the attacker knows exactly where the defender must struggle to live


Classic Go Examples

























ScenarioDangerRemedySplitting attackOpponent drives a wedge between two friendly unitsReinforce the weaker unit and connect toward safetyFloating center groupOpponent caps from aboveUse light knight’s moves or jumps to slip through the netOverextended side stoneOpponent pincers tightlySlide into the corner for a base or counter-pincer

Why This Works

Attackers fight with numerical superiority – surrounding stones outnumber the defender in the local sphere.
Defense becomes expensive – every defensive move made to live inside gives the opponent outside influence.
Prevents double-attack traps – keeping groups healthy avoids facing simultaneous attacks on two fronts.


Counterexample
In sabaki operations deep inside an opponent’s massive framework, starting with an isolated stone is normal. The key is to remain light and be willing to reshape or sacrifice it.

Proverb Variants

“A severed group is half-dead already.”
“Connect first, fight second.”
“Isolate the enemy; unite your own.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_let_your_handi.title: Don't Let Your Handicap Stones Become Disconnected
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_let_your_handi.content:
Core Meaning
In a handicap game, Black starts with stones placed on the star points (hoshi), giving a tremendous initial advantage in whole-board influence. White’s only winning strategy is to cut Black’s stones apart, isolate them into small targets, and exploit complicated tactical fights.
The golden rule for Black in handicap Go is: keep your handicap stones connected. If Black’s stones coordinate and maintain lines of mutual support, White will never find the space or leverage to stage a comeback.

Strategic Connection
Preserving handicap advantage relies on:

Solid play – prefer simple, unbreakable shapes over fancy, thin overplays
Mutual defense – extend toward neighboring handicap stones
Denying cuts – fix cutting points immediately before White can complicate the board


Classic Go Examples

























White’s TacticBlack’s Proper ResponseMistake to AvoidWhite attaches to a star pointExtend solidly (nobi) to increase libertiesPlaying a wild counter-cut that creates multiple weak pointsWhite attempts a wedgeConnect on the stronger side and push White toward friendly stonesPanicking and playing an empty triangleWhite invades between two handicap stonesJump calmly to connect toward the cornerChasing White aggressively and getting split

Why This Works

Connected handicap stones command the whole board – White cannot attack a group that stretches across three star points.
Eliminates White’s tactical traps – White relies on Black’s mistakes and overextensions to catch up.
Victory through simplicity – maintaining connections allows Black to cruise to a comfortable territorial win.


Counterexample
Do not connect handicap stones so tightly that you form an overconcentrated mass of stones. Keep connections flexible (one-space jumps, knight’s moves, and solid extensions).

Proverb Variants

“In handicap games, connection is victory.”
“Do not let White split your stars.”
“Simplicity and solid shape preserve the handicap lead.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_make_20_points.title: Don't Make 20 Points In Your Moyo, Threaten 50
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_make_20_points.content:
Core Meaning
A grand framework (moyo) is often misunderstood by beginners who rush to enclose it into modest, secure territory. If you spend multiple moves sealing a moyo to take 20 points, you give the opponent free turns to claim the rest of the board.
Instead, the proverb advises: expand the moyo to threaten 50 or 60 points! By making the framework look gigantic, you compel the opponent to invade out of fear. When they invade deep into your sphere of influence, you attack the invader for massive profit across the entire board.

Strategic Connection
Moyo psychology and strategy:

Bait the invasion – a terrifying moyo forces the opponent to make a desperate, deep entry
Attack for profit – do not aim to kill the invader; use the attack to build surrounding territory
Stone efficiency – threatening vast territory accomplishes more than sealing small boundaries


Classic Go Examples

























StagePassive Strategy (Bad)Ambitious Strategy (Good)Developing frameworkPlaying low, flat moves to secure 15 pointsJumping high into the center to threaten a 50-point domainOpponent hesitatesSealing the side in goteExpanding the wings of the framework to force their handOpponent invades deeplyTrying desperately to kill the invaderCapping the invader, letting them live small while you take the outside

Why This Works

Moyos are hunting grounds, not banks – the power of a moyo is realized through attacking invaders.
Defenders live small – an invader surviving on 2 points gives you outside thickness worth 20 points.
Forces psychological pressure – an expanding moyo forces the opponent to take uncomfortable risks.


Counterexample
If your moyo is already so large that sealing it with one move guarantees an unassailable 40-point lead, sealing it calmly to lock in the win is completely sound.

Proverb Variants

“A moyo is not territory until the enemy invades.”
“Do not close the barn door when you can expand the pasture.”
“Threaten fifty to easily win thirty.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_play_good_ston.title: Don't Play Good Stones To Save Dead Stones
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_play_good_ston.content:
Core Meaning
Throwing good money after bad is a classic human mistake, and in Go it takes the form of playing good stones to rescue doomed stones. When a group has been caught in a ladder, surrounded with zero eye prospects, or reduced to a hopeless capturing race, adding more stones to try to save it only increases your loss.
Accept the loss calmly. Dead stones can often be utilized as kikashi (forcing plays), sacrifice stones, or ko threats—do not make them heavier by adding fresh stones to the grave.

Tactical Connection
Rescuing dead stones leads to:

Compounded losses – each extra stone added gives the opponent another prisoner
Loss of sente – playing futile rescue moves surrenders the initiative
Heavy burden – saving a dead stone creates an even larger weak group to worry about


Classic Go Examples

























Hopeless SituationBlunder (Good Stones on Bad)Masterful Play (Sacrifice)Stone caught in a ladderContinuing to run out the ladderUsing the ladder stone as a devastating whole-board ko threatCorner group dead in tsumegoAdding stones inside to struggleSqueezing from the outside to build an impenetrable wallCutting stone enclosed with 1 libertyExtending to 2 liberties into a netLeaving it as a forcing atari to settle the outside

Why This Works

Sacrifice is power – giving up dead stones gracefully yields immense outside compensation.
Limits the damage – stopping a loss early keeps you in the game.
Preserves light shape – unburdened by heavy dead stones, your remaining forces stay fast and active.


Counterexample
Always read carefully before declaring a group dead. If a tactical tesuji or counter-atari exists that can rescue the stones or turn the capturing race, fight to save them.

Proverb Variants

“Do not throw good stones after bad.”
“Dead stones make the best manure.”
“Abandon the small to seize the great.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_respond_to_eve.title: Don't Respond To Every Threat: Ask "Is This Really Dangerous?"
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_respond_to_eve.content:
Core Meaning
One of the biggest hurdles in advancing from beginner to intermediate Go is breaking the habit of answering every opponent move automatically. Opponents frequently play minor threats, small border pokes, or phantom attacks that do not threaten anything vital.
Before answering reflexively, stop and ask: “Is this really dangerous? What happens if I ignore it?” If the damage is small or nonexistent, playing elsewhere (tenuki) allows you to take control of the game.

Strategic Connection
Questioning threats unlocks:

Tenuki power – playing elsewhere is often the strongest move on the board
Tempo control – seizing sente forces the opponent to react to your plans
Accurate evaluation – distinguishes real threats from hollow bluffs


Classic Go Examples

























Opponent’s MoveAutomatic Reaction (Passive)Masterful Reading (Tenuki)Peep against a thick wallConnecting submissivelyIgnoring the peep to enclose a huge open cornerSecond-line poke in early fusekiAnswering locally on the first lineTaking a massive star-point extension along the sideThreatening to capture 1 small stoneSaving the stoneTreating the stone as light and attacking an enemy dragon

Why This Works

Sente is the soul of Go – whoever dictates the direction of play controls the match.
Small losses don’t decide games – losing 2 points locally to gain 15 points elsewhere is a winning trade.
Exposes bluffs – ignoring hollow moves proves that the opponent wasted a turn.


Counterexample
If the opponent’s move threatens the life of a major dragon, cuts two large living groups apart, or creates an unstoppable capturing race, you must respond with precision.

Proverb Variants

“When the opponent threatens, think of tenuki.”
“Is it urgent, or is it merely loud?”
“He who answers every move loses every game.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_rush_to_kill_y.title: Don't Rush To Kill Your Opponent's Groups
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_rush_to_kill_y.content:
Core Meaning
Rushing to kill an opponent’s group is a dangerous gamble. Go groups are resilient; when threatened with total annihilation, an opponent will unleash every desperate counter-cut, crosscut, and ko threat available. If the kill fails by a single liberty, your entire surrounding position often collapses in ruins.
Instead, the master attacks with calm patience: build territory and outside thickness while keeping the opponent under pressure. If the group happens to die naturally, that is a bonus—not the goal.

Strategic Connection
Patient attacking philosophy:

Attack for profit, not slaughter – convert pressure into guaranteed points
Keep your own shape solid – avoid leaving cutting defects in your attacking perimeter
Drive the enemy toward your strength – use your existing thickness as an anvil


Classic Go Examples

























Attacking AttitudeHigh-Risk MistakePatient Master PlayOpponent has 1 eyePlunging inside to kill and getting counter-cutSealing the outside to build center power; group lives tinyRunning enemy dragonChasing closely with contact atarisCapping from afar, taking 25 points along the sideComplex corner tsumegoPlaying a speculative killing moveSqueezing in sente to solidify outside boundaries

Why This Works

Living small is a loss for the defender – surviving with 2 points while surrendering outside walls is a strategic catastrophe for the opponent.
Eliminates risk – surrounding safely carries zero danger of sudden counter-collapse.
Maintains steady leads – banking real points wins more consistently than all-or-nothing gambling.


Counterexample
When a group is genuinely trapped, has zero outs, and a 100% verified killing sequence is read out cleanly, strike decisively to end the game.

Proverb Variants

“A good attack never aims for blood.”
“Let the enemy live in misery while you live in luxury.”
“Greed for the kill gives birth to disaster.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_start_fights_t.title: Don't Start Fights Too Early
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_start_fights_t.content:
Core Meaning
In the early opening (fuseki), the entire board is wide open. Starting an aggressive, messy tactical fight on move 10 before establishing a stable base or claiming corner frameworks is premature and reckless.
Early fighting creates multiple weak stones that wander through empty space without bases to support them. Build a secure foundation in the corners and sides first; when your positions are thick and stable, you can fight with confidence.

Strategic Connection
Opening pacing and discipline:

Foundation before warfare – secure corner enclosures (shimari) and side bases first
Avoid early complications – premature brawls turn the game into a volatile lottery
Develop whole-board harmony – position your stones where they will support future battles


Classic Go Examples

























StagePremature BrawlingSound Opening StrategyMove 6Invading deeply between opposing stonesSecuring an open corner or playing an enclosureMove 12Launching an overzealous crosscut in open centerExtending along the side from a settled cornerOpponent approachesStarting a wild counter-attack with no baseAnswering with a standard, solid joseki

Why This Works

Base-less stones are liabilities – fighting without bases turns every stone into a potential target.
