Open points are worth more – staking out 15 points in an open corner beats fighting for 2 points in the center.
Thickness wins middle-game fights – establishing early strength guarantees superiority when battles inevitably ignite later.


Counterexample
If the opponent commits a severe, unprovoked overplay that can be punished immediately without compromising your own opening balance, punish it soundly.

Proverb Variants

“Build your camp before you march to war.”
“The opening is for planting; the middle game is for harvesting.”
“Calm in the opening, fierce in the middle.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_try_to_win_in_.title: Don't Try To Win In The Opening
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_try_to_win_in_.content:
Core Meaning
Go cannot be won on move 15, but it can easily be lost. Players often spot a slight inaccuracy in an opponent’s opening and overextend violently in an attempt to deliver an immediate knockout blow.
The opening is about balanced distribution of power, stability, and broad frameworks. Trying to force a premature win leads to overextended, fragile shapes that collapse as soon as the opponent resists calmly.

Strategic Connection
Healthy opening mindset:

Cumulative advantage – win by accumulating small, solid advantages across the board
Avoid overextension – don’t stretch your stones past their breaking point
Respect the game’s length – maintain stamina and stability for the middle game and endgame


Classic Go Examples

























Opponent’s MoveOverextended Overplay (Bad)Balanced Response (Good)Slightly unusual corner approachLaunching an all-out, wild counter-attackAnswering solidly, taking free corner territoryOpponent makes a slow extensionDiving deep to kill their stonesTaking the biggest open side point to claim a whole-board leadOpponent tenukis from a josekiForcing an unread killing fightPunishing calmly in sente to build massive thickness

Why This Works

A game has over 200 moves – early advantages should be nurtured, not gambled away.
Solid play preserves the lead – taking guaranteed profit punishes enemy mistakes naturally.
Avoids self-inflicted crises – most opening disasters are caused by overzealous greed.


Counterexample
If the opponent plays a catastrophic blunder (such as walking into an obvious ladder or self-atari), capture the stones immediately.

Proverb Variants

“Go is a marathon, not a sprint.”
“Do not swing for a knockout on the first stone.”
“Balance in the opening leads to victory in the end.”

proverbs/Strategies/don_t_use_influence_.title: Don't Use Influence To Make Territory
proverbs/Strategies/don_t_use_influence_.content:
Core Meaning
One of the most famous and profound proverbs in all of Go: “Do not use influence to make territory.” When you build a magnificent wall or possess commanding center influence, your natural instinct might be to surround a box of center territory with it.
This is a grave waste of power. The center is vast and porous; surrounding 15 points with a massive wall requires too many moves. Influence is designed to attack enemy weak groups, reduce opposing frameworks, and project cross-board menace.

Strategic Connection
Proper utilization of influence:

Attack for profit – drive enemy groups toward your wall to crush them or harvest points along their escape path
Project dominance – use influence to invade or reduce the opponent’s spheres with total safety
Support friends – your thickness ensures your own nearby groups will never come under pressure


Classic Go Examples

























PositionMisuse of InfluenceProper Use of InfluencePossessing a 4-stone wallPlaying flat moves to fence off 10 center pointsInvading the opponent’s side, using the wall as a safe harborCenter influence facing opponentTrying to close the center in gotePincering an opponent’s approach stone and driving it toward the wallOpponent invades near your thicknessTrying desperately to seal territoryForcing the invader against your wall to extract huge outside gains

Why This Works

Walls are weapons, not fences – an anvil is meant to hammer things against, not to be admired.
Center territory is inefficient – enclosing points in the center takes twice as many stones as the side.
Indirect profit is larger – an active attack powered by influence yields territory on both flanks.


Counterexample
When an opponent’s massive blunder allows your influence to convert naturally into an unassailable 50-point central territory with a single effortless move, take it.

Proverb Variants

“Influence is for attacking, not for counting.”
“Do not build a golden cage with iron walls.”
“Drive the enemy against your thickness.”

proverbs/Strategies/ensure_all_your_grou.title: Ensure All Your Groups Have Potential For Two Eyes
proverbs/Strategies/ensure_all_your_grou.content:
Core Meaning
The ultimate rule of survival in Go is the formation of two eyes (me). A group with two independent eyes can never be captured, because the opponent cannot legally occupy both eyes simultaneously without committing suicide.
Constantly monitoring your groups to ensure they either have two eyes or a clear escape path into the open center is the primary duty of every player. A group without eye potential is an accident waiting to happen.

Tactical Connection
Eye potential requires:

Corner and edge efficiency – corners require the fewest stones to form two eyes
Recognizing dead shapes – avoid collapsing into square four or bulky five
Living before roaming – settle your base before embarking on aggressive excursions


Classic Go Examples

























Group StateDangerous HabitCorrect Survival PlayEnclosed on the sideWandering off to take tenukiPlaying the vital point to secure two eyesHeavy dragon in centerAssuming it can run foreverShaping a table shape or tiger’s mouth for eyesCorner under attackTrying to fight outside while eyelessSliding into the corner to carve out an eye base

Why This Works

Two eyes provide absolute immunity – living groups can never be captured.
Living groups support attacks – you cannot attack freely if your own base might die.
Prevents catastrophic game-enders – an eyeless dragon dying ruins 50 moves of great play.


Counterexample
Light reduction stones or temporary sacrifice probes do not need two eyes because they are meant to be discarded after performing their tactical duty.

Proverb Variants

“Two eyes make life; one eye invites death.”
“Live first, fight second.”
“The dragon without eyes is already a corpse.”

proverbs/Strategies/every_move_should_do.title: Every Move Should Do Something Useful
proverbs/Strategies/every_move_should_do.content:
Core Meaning
Beginners often place stones out of habit or vague instinct. This proverb is a direct reminder to evaluate the utility of every candidate move: does it expand territory, defend a weak group, attack an enemy defect, or secure sente?
If a candidate move does not accomplish any of these fundamental tasks, discard it immediately and search for a move that does.

Strategic Connection
Useful move criteria:

Territory – stakes out secure points along the 3rd or 4th line
Safety – adds liberties or makes eye shape for an endangered group
Attack – restricts an enemy group’s escape route or eye potential
Initiative – forces the opponent to answer, preserving your turn


Classic Go Examples

























Candidate MoveEvaluationDecisionConnecting an already safe groupZero utility (wasted move)Reject: play elsewhere (tenuki)Pushing on the 1st line in fuseki1-point value in goteReject: play an open corner insteadSplitting attack on 2 enemy groupsHigh utility (double attack)Play immediately

Why This Works

Go is a race of productivity – the player who accomplishes more per move wins.
Eliminates slack play – conscious evaluation filters out passive blunders.
Forces whole-board scanning – seeking utility directs attention to the highest-value areas.


Counterexample
A quiet, patient move that looks simple (like fixing a cutting defect in sente) is profoundly useful even if it doesn’t immediately capture stones.

Proverb Variants

“Never play a stone that does no work.”
“Ask your stone what it intends to achieve.”
“Idle stones lose games.”

proverbs/Strategies/fix_urgent_problems_.title: Fix Urgent Problems Before Making Big Moves
proverbs/Strategies/fix_urgent_problems_.content:
Core Meaning
The universal law of Go decision-making: “Urgent moves before big moves” (kyusho ga saki, daiba wa ato). A “big move” (daiba) is an open corner, large side extension, or moyo expander worth 15–20 points. An “urgent move” (kyusho) is a move that decides the life, death, connection, or safety of a fighting group.
No matter how large a big move is, an urgent move is always worth more: saving a weak group saves 30–50 points and prevents the opponent from gaining total board dominance.

Strategic Connection
Decision hierarchy:

Critical life-and-death & cuts (Urgent — Must play)
Stabilizing unsettled groups (Urgent — Must play)
Open corners & enclosures (Big — Play after urgent matters)
Side extensions & moyos (Big — Play in sequence)
Endgame boundaries (Yose — Play last)


Classic Go Examples

























DilemmaBig Move TemptationCorrect Urgent PlayGroup has 2 libertiesEnclosing an empty 20-point cornerExtending to safety or connecting the cutting pointOpponent threatens to sever dragonTaking a large side star pointConnecting via a bamboo jointInvader trapped in cornerPlaying an endgame slide elsewhereStriking the vital point to kill or seal the invader

Why This Works

Big moves can be taken later; dead groups are gone forever.
Fixing urgent defects removes enemy targets – once safe, you can attack freely.
Leaving urgent weaknesses invites disaster – the opponent will exploit the defect in sente and still get the big move.


Counterexample
If your “threatened” stones are just 1–2 throwaway stones whose capture does not affect the life of surrounding groups, ignore them and take the big move.

Proverb Variants

“Urgent moves before big moves.”
“Save your family before buying more land.”
“Safety first, glory second.”

proverbs/Strategies/force_exchanges_that.title: Force Exchanges That Benefit You
proverbs/Strategies/force_exchanges_that.content:
Core Meaning
In Go, you do not need to win everything. A masterful player constantly creates forcing exchanges (kikashi) where you give the opponent something small (like 2–4 points of low-line territory or a disposable stone) in exchange for something vastly more valuable: center thickness, absolute safety, or sente.
When you dictate the terms of an exchange, you steer the game into territory that favors your whole-board strategy.

Strategic Connection
Profitable exchange dynamics:

Kikashi plays – forcing moves that improve your shape while leaving the opponent heavy
Sacrifice for power – discarding minor stones to construct an unassailable outside wall
Trading territory for tempo – giving up small local points to seize initiative elsewhere


Classic Go Examples

























SituationSmall Concession GivenMajor Benefit ReceivedSqueezing an enemy cornerLetting White capture 2 stonesBuilding a massive outside wall facing your moyoCrosscut fightSacrificing 1 cutting stoneConnecting your main group and settling in senteApproach sequenceGiving opponent 3rd-line pointsGaining outward influence to attack a neighboring group

Why This Works

Relative value matters more than absolute capture – 10 points of thickness beats 4 points of capture.
Forcing moves preserve initiative – the opponent is locked into answering your lead.
Simplifies complex positions – trading away complications locks in clear strategic advantages.


Counterexample
Never force an exchange that damages your own lingering aji or eliminates a cutting weakness in the opponent’s position for no real compensation.

Proverb Variants

“Give a stone to take a wall.”
“Trade iron for gold.”
“Control the trade; control the game.”

proverbs/Strategies/force_the_enemy_towa.title: Force The Enemy Towards Your Thickness
proverbs/Strategies/force_the_enemy_towa.content:
Core Meaning
One of the supreme principles of Go direction of play: “Drive the enemy toward your thickness” (Atsumi ni chikadzukeru). When attacking an unsettled opposing group, you should never push it toward open space or friendly territory.
Instead, attack from the open side and herd the enemy group directly into the waiting wall of your existing thickness. Against an immovable wall with infinite liberties, the enemy group will find no eyes, no escape, and no counter-play.

Strategic Connection
Directional attacking mechanics:

Attacking direction – play from the weak side to drive the opponent toward the strong side
The Anvil concept – your thickness is the anvil; your attacking stones are the hammer
Maximizing thickness – turns passive walls into lethal attacking bastions


Classic Go Examples

























PositionWrong Direction (Bad)Correct Direction (Good)Friendly wall on the left, open rightAttacking from the left, pushing enemy rightAttacking from the right, pushing enemy left into the wallEnemy invades near thicknessTrying to block them from the wallForcing them against the wall where they will suffocatePincer attackPincering from the wall sidePincering from the open side to squeeze them against the wall

Why This Works

Thickness cannot be breached – an enemy crashing into your thick wall will die or live tiny in agony.
Attacking stones gain territory – your attacking moves from the open side naturally harvest free territory.
Avoids damaging your own frameworks – pushing enemies into open areas ruins your own development.


Counterexample
If your “thickness” actually has hidden cutting points or low liberties, driving an enemy into it might cause your own wall to collapse. Ensure your thickness is genuine before herding enemies into it.

Proverb Variants

“Drive the sheep toward the iron wall.”
“The hammer strikes toward the anvil.”
“Attack from your weak side toward your strong side.”

proverbs/Strategies/four_die_but_six_liv.title: Four Die, Six Live (Confined Eye Spaces)
proverbs/Strategies/four_die_but_six_liv.content:
Core Meaning
The proverb “Four die, six live” (Shi-shi roku-sei) is a cornerstone of second-line and confined space life-and-death. When a group is trapped along the edge of the board in a rectangular or linear formation:

A group with four stones in a row along the edge dies unconditionally if attacked properly.
A group with six stones along the edge possesses enough internal space to live unconditionally (or fight a favorable ko).

This numerical benchmark allows players to instantly assess the life-and-death status of edge groups without lengthy calculation.

Tactical Connection
Edge space survival thresholds:

4 stones (Dead) – insufficient internal space to make two eyes against a proper inside placement
5 stones (Unsettled) – whoever plays first decides the life or death of the group
6 stones (Alive) – ample space to guarantee two separate eyes


Classic Go Examples

























Stone Count on EdgeStatusAction Required4 stones surroundedDeadDefender must sacrifice; Attacker can tenuki (already dead)5 stones surroundedUnsettledSente decides: defender plays to live, attacker strikes to kill6 stones surroundedAliveDefender lives cleanly without needing extra defensive stones

Why This Works

Eye space geometry – four stones on the edge only yield 2 internal points, which is a dead square four.
Six stones yield multiple eye pockets – can divide the space into two separate 1-point eyes.
Instant reading shortcut – eliminates guesswork in tight corner and side tsumego.


Counterexample
Outside liberties and corner bends can alter these numbers. In the extreme corner, special rules apply (e.g. the “L-group” is dead, while “comb formation” lives). Always check for corner peculiarities.

Proverb Variants

“Four die, six live; five is contested.”
“Six stones on the second line sleep in peace.”
“Know your numbers before you crawl the edge.”

proverbs/Strategies/give_your_opponent_w.title: Give Your Opponent What They Want
proverbs/Strategies/give_your_opponent_w.content:
Core Meaning
When an opponent launches an aggressive threat or makes an ambitious demand, your instinctive reaction might be to resist with all your might. However, master players often “give the opponent what they want”.
If the opponent’s threat only takes a few points of local territory or captures a minor stone, resisting stubbornly may force you into awkward, heavy shape. Let them take their small prize while you claim a vastly superior whole-board reward elsewhere.

Strategic Connection
Flexibility over stubbornness:

Avoid emotional fighting – don’t fight just because the opponent challenged you
Calculate the trade – compare the value of their capture against the value of your tenuki
Let them become heavy – an opponent who spends 3 moves capturing 2 stones is falling far behind


Classic Go Examples

























Opponent’s DemandStubborn Resistance (Bad)Flexible Master PlayThreatening to cut off 2 small stonesStruggling to save them, creating a weak dragonGiving up the 2 stones; taking a 20-point corner enclosureCrawling along 2nd line for territoryBlocking painfully and getting cutLetting them crawl while you build massive center influenceInvading a small corner pocketTrying desperately to kill at high riskLetting them live small with 2 points while sealing the outside

Why This Works

Small desires lead to small rewards – letting the opponent satisfy a small greed keeps them focused on trivialities.
Preserves tempo – giving in locally often lets you keep sente for whole-board triumphs.
Prevents overplay disasters – avoiding unnecessary friction eliminates catastrophic tactical collapses.


Counterexample
Never give the opponent what they want if their demand is the capture of a key cutting group, the death of a major dragon, or a game-deciding territorial zone.

Proverb Variants

“Give small to take large.”
“Feed the tiger a scrap to save the kingdom.”
“Yield where it is small; prevail where it is great.”

proverbs/Strategies/good_moves_do_two_th.title: Good Moves Do Two Things At Once
proverbs/Strategies/good_moves_do_two_th.content:
Core Meaning
The hallmark of a high-dan move in Go is multitasking: playing a single stone that achieves two or more strategic objectives simultaneously. A move that only defends is slow; a move that only attacks is risky. But a move that defends your weak group while simultaneously attacking the opponent’s stones is the gold standard of Go efficiency.
When every stone you place performs dual duties, you double your board efficiency compared to an opponent who plays single-purpose moves.

Strategic Connection
Dual-purpose moves excel because:

Stone economy – accomplishes in one turn what normally takes two
Miai leverage – creates two strong continuations, ensuring at least one succeeds
Tempo acceleration – forces the opponent into difficult, split-focus defense


Classic Go Examples






























Dual-Purpose MovePrimary FunctionSecondary FunctionPincer extensionAttacks the opponent’s approach stoneExtends from your own corner enclosureCenter capping movePressures an opponent’s running groupExpands your own central moyoCorner slide (suberi)Secures your group’s living eye baseUndercuts the opponent’s corner territorySecond-line hane-connectSecures solid endgame boundary pointsThreatens a back-rank cutting tesuji in sente

Why This Works

Efficiency wins races – doing two things at once outpaces single-purpose play.
Creates dilemmas for the opponent – defending against one threat leaves the other open.
Harmonizes attack and defense – ensures attacking operations never leave you vulnerable behind.


Counterexample
Do not try to force a dual-purpose move when a single, urgent defensive move is required to prevent immediate tactical death. Absolute survival comes before multitasking.

Proverb Variants

“One stone, two birds.”
“Defend while attacking; expand while defending.”
“The best sword is also a shield.”

proverbs/Strategies/if_you_don_t_know_wh.title: When In Doubt, Play In The Biggest Open Area
proverbs/Strategies/if_you_don_t_know_wh.content:
Core Meaning
Go can sometimes feel overwhelming, with hundreds of empty intersections and no obvious local fight. When you find yourself completely unsure of what move to play, apply the timeless guiding rule: “Play in the biggest open area.”
Look across the board and identify the widest span of unoccupied lines—typically along an open side between two distant corner stones. Playing in the widest open expanse is almost guaranteed to be a high-value move that stakes out territory and expands your framework.

Strategic Connection
Macro-board navigation:

Simplicity in complexity – eliminates decision paralysis during the opening and middle game
Maximizes potential – empty areas offer the highest room for territorial growth
Balances whole-board influence – prevents the opponent from claiming uncontested side domains


Classic Go Examples

























Board ConditionDilemmaHighest Value DecisionCorners settled, sides openTop side has 5 empty spaces, Bottom has 9Play a star-point extension along the wide bottom sideLocal fight resolves in senteWondering where to poke locallyZoom out and play an approach move in the widest open quadrantOpponent builds a side frameworkChoosing between small reductionsExtending along the opposite open side to balance the race

Why This Works

Area equals points – the largest space holds the greatest number of potential points.
Deters massive opponent frameworks – claiming the open space stops the enemy from taking it.
Statistically robust – computer AI and human masters alike prioritize the largest open flank in fuseki.


Counterexample
Never play in the biggest open area if an urgent life-and-death crisis, unresolved cutting point, or dead group emergency exists on the board. Urgent moves always supersede big areas.

Proverb Variants

“When lost, follow the wide road.”
“The largest open field yields the richest harvest.”
“Big points live in open spaces.”

proverbs/Strategies/if_your_opponent_has.title: Attack The Enemy's Unsettled Group Before Defending
proverbs/Strategies/if_your_opponent_has.content:
Core Meaning
When both players possess unsettled, floating groups on the board, the player who attacks first seizes the momentum. The proverb advises: “Attack the enemy’s weak group before defending your own.”
By launching an active attack first, you force the opponent into a defensive, reactive posture. As you press their weak stones, your attacking moves naturally strengthen your own unsettled group from the outside, achieving defense through offense in sente.

Strategic Connection
Aggressive initiative dynamics:

Defense through offense – attacking moves can fortify your own position while applying pressure
Tempo dominance – keeps the opponent scrambling rather than allowing them to attack you
Double weak group rule – in a fight between two weak groups, the first to move gains the upper hand


Classic Go Examples

























SituationPassive Defense (Bad)Active Attack (Good)Both players have running dragonsPlaying slow, heavy eye-making movesCapping the enemy dragon to steer it toward your thicknessOpponent invades near your weak flankConnecting flatly in gotePincering the invader to build outside liberties in senteSemeai capturing raceDefending internal liberties passivelyThreatening an outside cut to disrupt enemy liberties

Why This Works

Psychological momentum – forcing the opponent to defend prevents them from discovering your own defects.
Synergistic defense – attacking stones naturally link up with your own weak units.
Avoids gote collapse – passive defense leaves the enemy free to attack you on their next turn.


Counterexample
If your own weak group is in immediate atari, has only 2 liberties, or faces unconditional death on the next move, you must fix it immediately. You cannot attack from beyond the grave.

Proverb Variants

“The best defense is a vigorous offense.”
“Strike first when both groups wander.”
“He who hesitates to attack will soon be defending.”

proverbs/Strategies/index.title: Go Strategies
proverbs/Strategies/index.content:

proverbs/Strategies/keep_an_eye_on_your_.title: Keep An Eye On Your Own Weak Points
proverbs/Strategies/keep_an_eye_on_your_.content:
Core Meaning
It is easy to become intoxicated by an aggressive attack and forget that your own rear lines are riddled with cutting points, shortage of liberties, or thin shapes. An attack that ignores its own defects is a house built on sand: one sharp counter-punch from the opponent will cause your entire position to collapse.
Constant self-awareness—evaluating your own liberties, cutting defects, and eye security before launching an attack—is the hallmark of a disciplined player.

Strategic Connection
Defensive vigilance principles:

Fix defects in sente – use forcing moves to patch your weaknesses while maintaining tempo
Read opponent counter-attacks – always ask what your opponent can cut after you move
Strengthen before striking – make a solid base so your attack cannot be reversed


Classic Go Examples

























Aggressive ActionHidden DangerPrudent Preventive PlayChasing an enemy dragonLeaving a double-cut behind your wallReinforcing the cut with a bamboo joint firstInvading deep into enemy moyoForgetting your own entry stone has only 2 libertiesExtending to 4 liberties before plunging deeperPlaying a fierce haneExposing a back-rank atariConnecting solidly or playing a hanging connection

Why This Works

Prevents sudden counter-reversals – eliminates the opponent’s sharpest tactical traps.
Gives attacks unshakeable backing – an attack backed by thick, defect-free shape cannot fail.
Reduces reading anxiety – a clean position allows you to focus 100% on the enemy.


Counterexample
Do not become so paranoid about minor, non-existent defects that you play passive gote moves when no real threat exists. Verify the threat through reading.

Proverb Variants

“Look to your own back before you strike the front.”
“A fortress with an open gate is no fortress at all.”
“Guard your cuts; then attack with joy.”

proverbs/Strategies/keep_extending_from_.title: Extend From Handicap Stones To Build Influence
proverbs/Strategies/keep_extending_from_.content:
Core Meaning
In handicap Go, Black’s stones on the star points are powerful seeds of whole-board dominance. However, their power remains dormant if Black allows White to surround them or plays passively in the corner.
To convert handicap stones into commanding victory, Black must actively extend from them along the sides and into the center. Extensions project broad corridors of influence, link the handicap stones together, and deny White room to breathe.

Strategic Connection
Handicap extension strategy:

Broad spacing – use two- and three-space extensions to control entire side flanks
Third and fourth line harmony – balance third-line stability with fourth-line height
Enclose while extending – turn corner star points into formidable enclosures


Classic Go Examples

























Handicap SetupPassive ErrorActive Extension StrategyStar points at top and bottomClumping stones tightly in one cornerExtending along the side star point to bridge the two stonesWhite approaches a handicap cornerBacking away into the cornerPlaying a knight’s move extension or high pincer to coordinate with alliesOpen centerPlaying low 2nd-line movesJumping with a one-space jump toward the center

Why This Works

Coordinates initial advantages – connects isolated star points into an unbroken whole-board net.
Crushes White’s space – White needs open room to stage complications; extensions suffocate White.
Creates natural territory – large territories form effortlessly between coordinated handicap extensions.


Counterexample
Do not extend so recklessly into enemy strength that your extension stone is cut off and captured. Always ensure extensions have lines of retreat toward friendly star points.

Proverb Variants

“Let your handicap stones breathe across the board.”
“Extend the stars to build the galaxy.”
“Spread your wings from every star.”

proverbs/Strategies/keep_forcing_moves_t.title: Keep Forcing Moves To Extend Your Lead
proverbs/Strategies/keep_forcing_moves_t.content:
Core Meaning
When you establish a lead in a match, the most reliable way to preserve and expand that lead is by maintaining the initiative through forcing moves (kikashi). Forcing moves demand an immediate, specific response from the opponent, ensuring you dictate the tempo and direction of the game while retaining sente.
By chaining forcing moves together, you systematically close down the board, eliminate complicated variations, and steadily convert your advantage into guaranteed points.

Strategic Connection
Forcing move mechanics:

Sente preservation – keeping the turn prevents the opponent from launching counter-invasions
Simplification – forces exchanges that settle boundaries cleanly
Threat accumulation – sets up latent cutting aji and future ko threats


Classic Go Examples

























Board PhasePassive Move (Losing Lead)Forcing Move (Extending Lead)Middle game boundaryPlaying a slow territorial gote movePeeping at an enemy cutting point in sente before settlingCorner reductionInvading deeply and getting into a messy fightPlaying a forcing shoulder hit to build center thickness in senteEndgameTaking a 2-point gote pointPlaying all available 1-point sente ataris and hane-connects first

Why This Works

Zero-cost advantage – forcing moves extract concessions while keeping your turn.
Restricts opponent counter-play – an opponent constantly answering moves cannot start fights.
Smooths the path to victory – narrows the complexity of the board until the win is guaranteed.


Counterexample
Do not play “forcing moves” that actually damage your own position (e.g. playing ataris that eliminate your own cutting aji or help the opponent fix their bad shape). Only play forcing moves that leave you better off.

Proverb Variants

“Keep the whip in your hand.”
“He who holds sente holds the outcome.”
“Force with purpose; simplify to win.”

proverbs/Strategies/keep_track_of_how_ma.title: Always Know The Liberty Count Of Every Group
proverbs/Strategies/keep_track_of_how_ma.content:
Core Meaning
Go at its absolute physical core is a game of liberties (dame). Every tactical decision—from living and dying to capturing races (semeai), cutting, and connecting—hinges entirely on the exact liberty count of the interacting groups.
The disciplined player maintains constant awareness of how many liberties their own groups have (to avoid sudden atari traps) and how many liberties the opponent’s groups possess (to spot instant capturing opportunities).

Tactical Connection
Liberty awareness governs:

Semeai calculations – knowing whether to fill outside liberties, approach liberties, or eye liberties
Cut viability – cuts only succeed when the cutting stones have more liberties than the target
Disaster prevention – spotting shortage of liberties (damezumari) before committing to a fight


Classic Go Examples

























Tactical SituationIgnorant Play (Disaster)Calculated Play (Victory)4-liberty vs 3-liberty racePlaying an outside endgame moveFilling the opponent’s outside liberty to win the raceApproaching a cut with 2 libertiesCutting blindly and getting capturedExtending to 3 liberties first, then cuttingOpponent group down to 2 libertiesIgnoring itPlaying atari or clamping to capture

Why This Works

Zero liberties equals death – stone removal is the ultimate consequence in Go.
Liberty count dictates tactics – shapes with 4+ liberties are flexible; shapes with 2 liberties are in peril.
Enables precise tesujis – under-the-stones, snapbacks, and squeeze plays rely on exact counts.


Counterexample
Do not spend moves adding liberties to groups that already have 8+ liberties and are unconditionally alive, unless doing so creates vital outside thickness.

Proverb Variants

“Count the breaths; know the victor.”
“In a capturing race, one liberty is the difference between heaven and earth.”
“Knowledge of liberties is the key to life.”

proverbs/Strategies/let_tewari_be_your_m.title: Let Tewari Be Your Mirror
proverbs/Strategies/let_tewari_be_your_m.content:
Core Meaning
Tewari is the advanced Go analysis technique of deconstructing a finished local sequence by analyzing the stones as if they were placed in a different order, or by removing equal numbers of friendly and opposing stones to evaluate efficiency.
The proverb “Let tewari be your mirror” advises players to judge whether a sequence was truly successful by looking at the final position: if your stones ended up in redundant, overconcentrated, or awkward locations while the opponent’s stones are active and efficient, the exchange was a failure—even if you captured a few stones.

Strategic Connection
Tewari analysis teaches:

True efficiency – reveals whether your stones are doing active work or sitting idle
Joseki evaluation – determines whether an opening sequence was balanced or biased
Objective self-review – strips away psychological attachment to reveal structural reality


Classic Go Examples

























Resulting PositionSurface IllusionTewari TruthCaptured 2 stones with 6 stones”I made a capture!”Tewari reveals 6 stones making 4 points is heavily overconcentratedSurrendered 2 stones for outside wall”I lost 2 stones!”Tewari reveals an impenetrable wall dominating the whole boardSolidly connected inside living eye”My group is safe!”Tewari reveals a wasted move inside already living territory

Why This Works

Exposes wasted moves – comparing the result to ideal shapes highlights inefficiency.
Eliminates capture bias – captures feel good emotionally, but tewari reveals their true point value.
Deepens positional judgment – trains your intuition to seek high-efficiency shapes from move 1.


Counterexample
In desperate middle-game survival, evaluating whether the final shape is “elegant” via tewari is secondary to the immediate physical reality of living.

Proverb Variants

“Tewari is the mirror of stone efficiency.”
“Look at the stones left behind, not the stones taken off.”
“Deconstruct the exchange to find the truth.”

proverbs/Strategies/leverage_your_walls_.title: Leverage Your Walls For Easy Territory
proverbs/Strategies/leverage_your_walls_.content:
Core Meaning
Building a massive, impenetrable wall in Go requires significant investment of moves. Once your wall is established, you must leverage its power to extract easy territory.
Do not try to surround territory directly touching the wall; instead, use the wall as a looming threat. Extend widely away from the wall along the side—because your wall is unassailable, any enemy stones that try to invade between the wall and your extension will be crushed against the ramparts.

Strategic Connection
Wall leverage dynamics:

N+1 Extension Rule – extend 3 spaces from 2 stones, 4 spaces from 3 stones, 5 spaces from 4 stones
Territory by intimidation – the sheer presence of the wall secures the adjacent side
Attacking platform – launch pincer and splitting attacks with zero fear of counter-attack


Classic Go Examples

























Wall AssetFlawed PlayMasterful Leverage3-stone vertical wallAdding extra stones right next to the wallMaking a wide 4-space extension along the sideOpponent approaches near wallBacking away into defensePincering tightly and driving the opponent toward the wallCentral wall facing open sideClosing the wall in goteInvading enemy territory with complete confidence

Why This Works

Walls project long-range force – a thick wall controls up to 5 spaces of open board around it.
Invasions become traps – opponents cannot easily make eye shape against a wall with infinite liberties.
Stone efficiency multiplication – 1 wall plus 1 extension stone encloses 30 points of territory.


Counterexample
Never assume a wall is a weapon if it contains cutting defects or low liberties. A wall with defects is a fragile target, not a stronghold.

Proverb Variants

“Extend widely from a thick wall.”
“The shadow of a great wall claims the land.”
“A wall without an extension is power asleep.”

proverbs/Strategies/make_a_fist_before_y.title: Make A Fist Before You Strike
proverbs/Strategies/make_a_fist_before_y.content:
Core Meaning
The martial proverb “Make a fist before you strike” (Kobushi wo nigitte kara nagure) teaches the fundamental prerequisite of every successful attack: solidify your own position before attacking the enemy.
If you punch with an open, loose hand with disjointed fingers, you will break your own hand upon impact. Similarly, if you launch an attack while your own surrounding stones are loose, thin, and full of cutting points, the opponent’s counter-attack will shatter your position. Clench your stones into a solid fist first; then strike with crushing power.

Tactical Connection
Pre-attack preparation steps:

Fix cutting defects – connect loose knight’s moves and peep points before attacking
Increase liberties – ensure your attacking base has ample breathing room
Seal escape routes – ensure your surrounding net has no gaps


Classic Go Examples

























Attack PlanLoose Hand (Blunder)Clenched Fist (Mastery)Attacking an enemy dragonDiving in to cut while your own base has 2 libertiesConnecting your own cutting point firmly in sente, then strikingCapping a running groupCapping from loose, disconnected stonesReinforcing your side group, then capping with absolute thicknessInvading enemy moyoInvading recklessly with no baseBuilding a solid staging base on the edge before launching the invasion

Why This Works

Eliminates counter-blows – an opponent under attack will search desperately for your weak points; a fist leaves none.
Maximizes attacking force – attacking from absolute thickness allows you to play the most severe, uncompromising moves.
Guarantees safety – even if the enemy manages to survive, your solid fist remains as permanent territory and power.


Counterexample
If the opponent’s group is on the verge of escaping or making two eyes on their very next move, you may need to strike immediately before they can settle, accepting temporary tactical complications.

Proverb Variants

“Clench the fist before delivering the blow.”
“Strengthen yourself before you destroy the enemy.”
“A solid base makes a deadly strike.”

proverbs/Strategies/make_forcing_moves_b.title: Make Forcing Moves Before Major Decisions
proverbs/Strategies/make_forcing_moves_b.content:
Core Meaning
Before committing to an irreversible strategic path—such as launching an invasion, settling a major boundary, or playing tenuki—you should always check if you have beneficial forcing moves (kikashi) available.
Forcing moves demand an immediate, predictable reply from your opponent. Playing them first ensures you extract maximum local concessions, solidify your outside shape, and test the opponent’s intentions before making your permanent commitment.

Strategic Connection
Pre-commitment forcing dynamics:

Retains sente – allows you to accomplish vital preliminary work without losing your turn
Clarifies intentions – the opponent’s response reveals which direction they prioritize
Avoids wasted aji – once the board changes, those forcing opportunities may vanish forever


Classic Go Examples

























Strategic CrossroadsPremature DecisionMasterful Forcing Play FirstPreparing a center invasionInvading immediately and getting counter-attackedPlaying a probe/forcing peep on the flank to establish an escape routeChoosing corner josekiCommitting to territory blindlyPlaying a forcing atari to see how the opponent connectsSacrificing stonesDiscarding stones silentlySqueezing the stones with forcing ataris before abandoning them

Why This Works

Forcing moves are free investments – when the opponent must respond, your move costs zero tempo.
Shapes the future battleground – forces the opponent into slightly heavier shape before the main fight.
Information advantage – observing their response informs your subsequent whole-board choices.


Counterexample
Do not play “forcing moves” that actually damage your own position by eliminating valuable future cutting aji or helping the opponent fix their weaknesses.

Proverb Variants

“Force first; decide second.”
“Ask the opponent’s opinion before choosing your path.”
“A timely kikashi clears the fog of war.”

proverbs/Strategies/make_forcing_moves_b.title: Test Your Opponent With Forcing Moves
proverbs/Strategies/make_forcing_moves_b.content:
Core Meaning
Probing and testing your opponent with light forcing moves (yousumi) is one of the most refined skills in Go. Before finalizing your own formation or launching a major operation, playing a forcing move tests how the opponent intends to defend.
Depending on whether the opponent connects solidly, resists with a counter-attack, or yields territory, you gain critical information that dictates which branch of your strategy to execute.

Tactical Connection
Testing the opponent yields:

Tactical flexibility – lets you adjust your follow-up based on their defensive choice
Tempo control – keeps the opponent on the defensive while you conduct experiments
Psychological pressure – tests whether the opponent reads accurately under pressure


Classic Go Examples

























Probe / Forcing MoveOpponent’s Choice AOpponent’s Choice BHigh peep against a knight’s moveOpponent connects solidly (Heavy)Opponent resists (Leaves a dangerous cutting point)Corner attachment probeOpponent defends the corner (Surrenders outside influence)Opponent blocks the outside (Surrenders corner territory)Second-line slide probeOpponent blocks (Gives you outside sente)Opponent tenukis (Allows you to scoop their base)

Why This Works

Eliminates guesswork – lets the opponent’s move determine your optimal plan.
Maintains initiative – forcing moves preserve sente throughout the inquiry.
Exploits opponent indecision – opponents often respond awkwardly to unexpected probes.


Counterexample
Never play a probe that you cannot afford to have cut off or ignored. If the opponent can boldly ignore your “forcing” move and counter-attack with fatal severity, the move is an overplay.

Proverb Variants

“Probe the corner before choosing the side.”
“Test the water before diving in.”
“A wise question reveals the opponent’s secret plan.”

proverbs/Strategies/make_sure_your_group.title: Make Sure Your Groups Can Form Two Eyes
proverbs/Strategies/make_sure_your_group.content:
Core Meaning
In Go, no matter how many stones you possess or how large your framework appears, an enclosed group without two true eyes (me) is completely dead.
Corners are the most natural place to make eyes because the board edges provide built-in protection. When groups move into the center or along the side, you must actively craft eye shape using structures like the tiger’s mouth, table shape, or two-space extensions.

Tactical Connection
Eye security fundamentals:

Corner priority – secure corner eye space early before moving outward
Distinguish true vs false eyes – ensure diagonal points are protected from false eye collapses
Eye-space division – internal space must be capable of dividing into two separate compartments


Classic Go Examples

























FormationVulnerabilityCorrection for Life3-stone straight eye spaceOpponent strikes the center vital pointPlay the center intersection yourself to make two eyesDiagonal corner unprotectedOpponent squeezes into a false eyeConnect the diagonal support stone firmlyCenter dragon running blindEyeless and vulnerable to a fatal capMake eye shape with a knight’s move or tiger’s mouth

Why This Works

Two eyes provide eternal life – rules forbid simultaneous capture of two independent eyes.
Secures territorial bases – a group with two eyes can safely support outward fighting.
Removes opponent attacking targets – living groups render enemy thickness powerless.


Counterexample
Temporary sacrifice stones or light reduction stones do not need two eyes. Only groups that carry vital territorial or strategic value must ensure two eyes.

Proverb Variants

“Two eyes are life; one eye is death.”
“Seek eyes before you seek glory.”
“The corner is the cradle of living eyes.”

proverbs/Strategies/never_play_the_first.title: Never Play The First Line Without Good Reason
proverbs/Strategies/never_play_the_first.content:
Core Meaning
The proverb “Never play on the first line without a good reason” reminds players that the first line (the edge line of the board) produces zero territory on its own. Playing on the first line during the opening or middle game is almost always a slow, wasted move that surrenders the initiative.
The first line is known as the “line of death”. Stones belong on the first line only for life-and-death survival, connecting under the stones, or executing high-value endgame plays like the monkey jump.

Strategic Connection
Line hierarchy in Go:

4th Line (Line of Influence / Power) – builds frameworks and center power
3rd Line (Line of Territory) – establishes secure, profitable bases
2nd Line (Line of Defeat / Base) – used for sliding bases and endgame connections
1st Line (Line of Death) – zero territory; strictly for tactical tesujis and endgame


Classic Go Examples






























Stage of GameFirst Line PlayVerdictOpening (Fuseki)Descending to the 1st line to protect 1 pointTerrible blunder: play an open corner insteadMiddle gameCrawling along the 1st line to save 1 stoneFatal mistake: abandon the stone and take the outsideEndgame (Yose)First-line hane-and-connect in senteExcellent: captures points and maintains initiativeTsumegoFirst-line placement to kill or liveEssential: vital point for life and death

Why This Works

Zero territorial expansion – 1st-line stones cannot expand downward.
Extremely low liberties – edge stones naturally possess fewer liberties and get squeezed easily.
Surrenders whole-board tempo – playing on the edge hands the opponent center dominance.


Counterexample
In the endgame, first-line hane-connects and monkey jumps are among the largest moves on the board. In tsumego, first-line placements (sagari / hane) are often the only moves that kill or live.

Proverb Variants

“The first line is the line of death.”
“Do not walk the edge while the center is open.”
“Only the endgame walks the first line.”

proverbs/Strategies/never_start_a_ko_fig.title: Never Start A Ko Fight You Can't Win
proverbs/Strategies/never_start_a_ko_fig.content:
Core Meaning
A ko fight is an all-out tactical gamble where players trade moves on the local ko against moves elsewhere on the board. The universal proverb warns: “Never start a ko you cannot win.”
Entering a ko fight when you have fewer ko threats than your opponent is an invitation to disaster. The opponent will ignore your weak threat, resolve the ko in their favor, and leave you with catastrophic losses on both fronts.

Tactical Connection
Ko prerequisites before igniting the battle:

Threat inventory – count both your ko threats and the opponent’s ko threats before starting
Evaluate the stakes – determine whether losing the ko results in game over
Prepare local threats – create forcing moves before capturing the ko


Classic Go Examples

























Ko SituationReckless ActionDisciplined ActionOpponent has 5 massive ko threats; you have 1Starting the ko fight immediatelySettling the position solidly in gote or avoiding the koLosing the ko loses 40 pointsFighting without reading threatsConnecting the ko to eliminate all riskOpponent has no ko threatsAvoiding the ko out of fearIgniting the ko immediately to force a total collapse

Why This Works

Ko fights are won by threats, not bravery – the player with more threats always wins the ko.
Double losses are fatal – losing a ko after playing an ignored threat loses both the ko and outside compensation.
Calculation prevents regret – counting threats takes 30 seconds and prevents losing the game.


Counterexample
If your group is already 100% dead and the only possible chance of survival is a “free” picnic ko or two-step ko, start the ko immediately—you have nothing to lose and everything to gain.

Proverb Variants

“Count your threats before opening the ko.”
“A ko without threats is a leap into the abyss.”
“Do not light a fire you cannot extinguish.”

proverbs/Strategies/never_start_a_ko_you.title: Entering A Ko Fight Without Enough Threats Is Disastrous
proverbs/Strategies/never_start_a_ko_you.content:
Core Meaning
A ko fight cannot be won by sheer will; it is governed strictly by the currency of ko threats. If you start a ko without having enough threats in the bank, your opponent will simply ignore your first small threat, capture the ko, and resolve the game.
Before initiating any ko, conduct a strict audit of the whole board. Identify every valid threat for both sides. If the balance of threats is against you, reinforce your position or seek alternative ways to settle.

Tactical Connection
Ko threat mechanics:

Absolute threats – threats that the opponent cannot afford to ignore under any circumstance
Local threats – threats generated by the stones directly involved in the ko fight
Aji-keshi threats – avoid using threats that destroy your own future profit


Classic Go Examples

























Ko BalanceResult of Starting KoProper AlternativeOpponent has 6 threats, you have 2Opponent ignores your threat; you lose everythingConnect or trade calmly without fighting the koEqual threats, but your ko loss is largerHigh-risk gambleEliminate the ko defect in sente before the fight startsOpponent has zero whole-board threatsOpponent cannot answer your koStart the ko immediately and demand concessions

Why This Works

Ko threats are finite currency – running out of currency forces immediate bankruptcy.
Opponent takes double profit – resolving the ko gives the opponent unconditional local safety.
Strategic clarity – knowing you cannot win the ko frees you to find creative, solid alternatives.


Counterexample
If the ko is a “flower-viewing ko” (hanami-ko)—where winning yields massive gains for you, but losing costs you virtually nothing—you can fight the ko casually to extract free concessions.

Proverb Variants

“A ko without threats is suicide.”
“Count the threats before you capture.”
“He who lacks threats must make peace.”

proverbs/Strategies/never_trust_your_opp.title: Never Trust Your Opponent
proverbs/Strategies/never_trust_your_opp.content:
Core Meaning
The proverb “Never trust your opponent” is an essential warning against wishful thinking and psychological complacency in Go. When an opponent plays an unexpected, bizarre, or seemingly bad move, beginners often assume: “They made a mistake, so I can ignore it or capture easily.”
Never assume an opponent’s move is harmless! Strong players constantly set traps, test your reading, or play clever tesujis. Always verify their moves through cold, objective calculation before responding.

Strategic Connection
Objective verification habits:

Check for hidden tesujis – look for snaps, throw-ins, double ataris, or ladders
Verify before tenuki – never play elsewhere without reading out the local consequences
Do not play on hope – assume the opponent will always play the strongest possible reply


Classic Go Examples

























Opponent’s MoveDangerous AssumptionDisciplined VerificationSacrificing a stone inside your territory”A free gift! I’ll take it.”Read if it’s a throw-in to squeeze liberties or falsify an eyePlaying a bizarre move in an open area”They don’t know what they’re doing.”Read whether it sets up a long-range ladder breaker (shicho-atari)Sudden tenuki from a local fight”They gave up; I’ll play elsewhere too.”Check if your local stones can now kill their group in sente

Why This Works

Assumptions cause blunders – the vast majority of catastrophic losses stem from unverified assumptions.
Respect keeps you sharp – treating every enemy move as potentially dangerous sharpens your reading.
Filters out bluffs – accurate reading easily disarms fake threats while respecting real ones.


Counterexample
Do not let healthy skepticism degenerate into paralyzing paranoia. If careful reading reveals that the opponent’s move is genuinely an overplay with zero tactical backing, punish it decisively.

Proverb Variants

“Trust your reading, not your opponent’s intentions.”
“Beware the Greek bearing gifts on the board.”
“Always read the opponent’s best move first.”

proverbs/Strategies/people_in_glass_hous.title: People In Glass Houses Shouldn't Throw Stones
proverbs/Strategies/people_in_glass_hous.content:
Core Meaning
This colorful proverb teaches a vital lesson in combat readiness: do not start fights if your own groups are weak and eyeless. Throwing stones (launching aggressive attacks or deep cuts) while living in a glass house (possessing fragile, low-liberty groups of your own) guarantees that the shockwaves of the battle will shatter your own position.
Before you attack the opponent, ensure your own house is built of stone, not glass. Fix your weaknesses first; then you can fight with impunity.

Strategic Connection
Fighting readiness principles:

Assess group stability – check the health of all nearby friendly units before launching attacks
Avoid multi-front wars – fighting with two weak groups simultaneously is the easiest way to lose
Fortify then strike – turn your glass house into a fortress before engaging the enemy


Classic Go Examples

























Your PositionTempting AttackResult & CorrectionYour corner group has 2 libertiesCutting the opponent’s center stonesDisaster: Opponent counter-attacks and kills your corner; fix corner firstYour side group has no baseInvading enemy moyo deeplyDisaster: You now have two dying groups; settle side base firstAll your groups are solid and aliveAttacking an enemy floating dragonTriumph: Opponent has nowhere to counter-attack; strike hard!

Why This Works

Weak groups cannot project power – attacking requires a secure rear base.
Opponents counter-attack weaknesses – an attacked opponent will immediately probe your fragile groups.
Solid positions enable bold play – when your own house is unbreakable, you can throw all the stones you want.


Counterexample
If your “glass house” is already doomed unless you create chaos, launching a desperate, all-out attack may be your only lottery ticket to survival.

Proverb Variants

“Make your own camp safe before assaulting the castle.”
“Do not fight with fire while sitting on gunpowder.”
“A weak group cannot lead a strong attack.”

proverbs/Strategies/play_away_from_stren.title: Play Away From Strength
proverbs/Strategies/play_away_from_stren.content:
Core Meaning
The proverb “Play away from strength” (Tsuyomi ni chikadzuku na) directs whole-board strategy: do not play stones close to areas where either you or your opponent already have solid strength.
Playing near enemy strength invites an immediate, disadvantageous battle against overwhelming odds. Playing near your own strength is equally inefficient, as it clumps your stones into overconcentrated clusters. Direct your stones toward the open, contested areas of the board where influence is undecided.

Strategic Connection
Direction of play near strength:

Near enemy thickness – keep a respectful distance; reduce from afar rather than invading deeply
Near friendly thickness – extend far away to maximize territorial scope; do not play tight moves
Contested open spaces – invest your stones where the balance of power is still up for grabs


Classic Go Examples

























Strength LocationMistakeCorrect DirectionOpponent has a massive 4-stone wallInvading 2 spaces away from the wallPlaying on the opposite side of the board; reducing lightly from high linesYou have an impenetrable corner fortressAdding another stone 2 spaces awayMaking a wide 5-space extension down the sideHeavy center fighting resolvedAdding moves to settled, alive groupsZooming out to play in the biggest open quadrant

Why This Works

Avoids fighting uphill battles – attacking enemy thickness is fighting against superior liberties.
Maximizes stone economy – stones deployed in open areas yield 3x the territory of stones played near walls.
Denies opponent targets – playing away from enemy strength gives their thick walls nothing to attack.


Counterexample
When using a clamp or endgame slide to reduce an opponent’s boundary in sente, playing close to strength is acceptable provided the sequence is read out and keeps initiative.

Proverb Variants

“Keep clear of the tiger’s den.”
“Do not plant trees in the shadow of a mountain.”
“Play where the board is empty, not where it is full.”

proverbs/Strategies/play_away_from_thick.title: Play Away From Thickness
proverbs/Strategies/play_away_from_thick.content:
Core Meaning
Thickness (atsumi) represents unshakeable power, abundant liberties, and zero tactical defects. The universal rule of Go strategy commands: “Stay away from thickness—both yours and your opponent’s.”
Entering an area dominated by opposing thickness is like charging into fortified artillery fire: your stones will be starved of liberties, capped, and forced into desperate survival. Steer your stones toward the open flanks, starving the opponent’s thickness of any targets to attack.

Strategic Connection
Dealing with thickness:

Starve the wall – thickness that has nothing to attack becomes an expensive, idle monument
Light reductions – use high 4th- and 5th-line moves to limit thickness rather than deep 3rd-line invasions
Build opposite domains – counter enemy thickness by developing your own open frameworks


Classic Go Examples

























Opponent’s FormationBlunderCorrect Strategic ManeuverSolid Pon-nuki in centerInvading directly beneath the pon-nukiErasing its influence from a distance with shoulder hitsMassive 5-stone side wallPlaying a 3rd-line invasion into its shadowErasing the framework with high knight’s movesCorner thickness facing centerPlaying contact moves against the cornerDeveloping the opposite corners and sides

Why This Works

Thickness is an offensive weapon – if you do not offer targets, the opponent cannot profit from their wall.
Prevents overconcentration for you – staying away from your own thickness maximizes your reach.
Controls game balance – keeps battles focused on ground where you enjoy equal or superior strength.


Counterexample
If an opponent’s “thick” formation actually has a hidden shortage of liberties or cutting defect that can be exploited by an immediate tactical tesuji, strike at the defect.

Proverb Variants

“Give thickness a wide berth.”
“Do not feed the dragon.”
“A wall with no enemies to fight is a wall that achieved nothing.”

proverbs/Strategies/play_away_from_your_.title: Play Away From Opponent's Strong Areas
proverbs/Strategies/play_away_from_your_.content:
Core Meaning
Placing your stones directly next to an opponent’s thick walls or living corner enclosures is a classic mistake. An opponent’s strong area cannot be killed, cannot be easily reduced from up close, and possesses unlimited liberties to counter-attack any adjacent stone.
By playing away from their strong areas, you deny their thickness any targets, while claiming your own territory in the open, contested areas of the board.

Strategic Connection
Spatial positioning principles:

Starve enemy power – thickness with no enemy stones nearby produces zero profit
Claim open territory – deploy your forces where points can be won efficiently
Reduce from a distance – use light, high-line moves rather than heavy contact invasions


Classic Go Examples

























Opponent’s StrengthPoor Choice (Too Close)Master Choice (Away From Strength)Thick 4-stone wall on leftPlaying on the 3rd line directly facing the wallExtending along the open right side star pointLiving corner fortressAttaching to the fortress stonesApproaching the opposite open cornerCenter influencePlunging deep insideErasing the center from the outside with shoulder hits

Why This Works

Avoids local numerical inferiority – fighting near enemy bastions is a battle against 10-to-1 odds.
Maximizes development speed – open spaces yield 3x the territory per move.
Maintains game balance – keeps the game focused on areas where you can establish an advantage.


Counterexample
If an opponent’s “strong area” has a vital shortage of liberties or a defect that can be exploited by an immediate endgame reduction in sente, play the reduction.

Proverb Variants

“Do not build in the shadow of the fortress.”
“Keep your distance from the dragon’s lair.”
“Play where you are strong, not where the enemy reigns.”

proverbs/Strategies/play_calmly_and_avoi.title: Play Calmly And Avoid Big Risks
proverbs/Strategies/play_calmly_and_avoi.content:
Core Meaning
When you hold a clear lead in a game (whether from a successful opening, an early capture, or a handicap setup), the burden of complication is entirely on your opponent. The trailing player must take desperate risks, launch wild invasions, and create chaotic fights to overturn the game.
The proverb “Play calmly and avoid big risks” instructs the leader to remain patient and serene: do not get dragged into dangerous, speculative brawls. Play solid, clean moves that steadily consolidate your lead and bring the game safely to victory.

Strategic Connection
Leading game management:

Simplify the board – trade complicated fights for solid, unshakeable territory
Solid connections – eliminate all cutting points and ko opportunities for the opponent
Avoid greed – you do not need to win by 100 points; winning by 5 points is complete victory


Classic Go Examples

























Trailing Opponent’s TacticGreedy / Risky Reaction (Bad)Calm Leader Play (Good)Deep, reckless invasionTrying desperately to kill the invader at high riskLetting them live with 2 points while sealing the outside to secure the winStarting a wild, chaotic koEngaging in a complex whole-board ko fightConnecting the ko cleanly to eliminate all volatilityComplex overplay in fusekiLaunching an all-or-nothing counter-attackAnswering solidly, taking guaranteed profit

Why This Works

Complexity favors the desperate – chaotic positions increase the probability of blunders.
Solid shape closes doors – giving the opponent no cutting targets extinguishes their hopes of a comeback.
A win is a win – minimizing variance guarantees consistent tournament success.


Counterexample
If you are trailing behind in points, playing “calmly and safely” is a slow path to defeat. When behind, you must take calculated risks and create complications to overturn the deficit.

Proverb Variants

“When ahead, seek simplicity; when behind, seek chaos.”
“The rich man does not pick fights in the street.”
“Calm waters carry the ship home.”

proverbs/Strategies/play_solid_moves_rat.title: Play Solid Moves Rather Than Complex Strategies
proverbs/Strategies/play_solid_moves_rat.content:
Core Meaning
In handicap games and beginner-to-intermediate study, players often believe they must execute brilliant, convoluted strategies to win. In reality, the most devastatingly effective way to play is using simple, rock-solid shapes (honte).
Solid connections, clean extensions, and sturdy eye shapes deny the opponent any tactical leverage. Against an opponent trying to trick you with complex overplays, playing solid, honest moves naturally causes their thin formations to collapse under their own weight.

Strategic Connection
The power of solid play (honte):

Zero defects – leaves no cutting points for the opponent to exploit
Unassailable thickness – solid stones provide infinite backup for future fights
Peace of mind – allows you to calculate with absolute confidence


Classic Go Examples

























PositionFancy Overplay (Fragile)Solid Shape (Unbeatable)Connecting two cutting pointsPlaying a thin, loose knight’s movePlaying a solid connection or bamboo jointResponding to an attachmentCounter-cutting wildly without readingExtending solidly (nobi) to increase libertiesSettling a cornerStarting an unnecessary ko fightSecuring two eyes cleanly

Why This Works

Overplays punish themselves – an opponent playing thin tricks will eventually overextend and die.
Honest moves never fail – solid shape (honte) is approved by both classical masters and modern AI.
Reduces mental fatigue – solid positions eliminate anxiety over hidden back-rank traps.


Counterexample
When you are far behind in the endgame and standard play guarantees a loss, you must abandon safety and attempt sharp, complex tactical complications.

Proverb Variants

“The honest move (honte) is the master’s move.”
“Simplicity is the highest sophistication.”
“Solid stones weather every storm.”

proverbs/Strategies/play_the_shape_move_.title: Play The Shape Move
proverbs/Strategies/play_the_shape_move_.content:
Core Meaning
Go masters often find the correct move in a split second by identifying the shape move (katachi). Good shape is the geometric arrangement of stones that maximizes liberties, facilitates eye formation, maintains flexible connections, and works with the highest possible efficiency.
When faced with multiple candidate moves, choosing the natural shape move (such as a bamboo joint, one-space jump, tiger’s mouth, or ponnuki) almost always produces the most resilient, active result.

Strategic Connection
Benefits of good shape:

Natural efficiency – stones perform multiple duties without straining
Inherent eye space – good shape naturally contains the seeds of two eyes
Resilience under pressure – good shape bends rather than breaks when attacked


Classic Go Examples

























ProblemBad Shape (Awkward)Proper Shape MoveConnecting two pairsClumping into an empty triangleConnecting via a bamboo jointEscaping from pressureCrawling heavily on line 2Jumping forward with a one-space jumpDefending a cut in senteConnecting solidly in goteForming a tiger’s mouth to threaten counter-atari

Why This Works

Shape embodies accumulated Go wisdom – proven formations refined over 4,000 years.
Saves reading time – trusting good shape guides you to candidate moves instantly.
Prevents overconcentration – good shape enforces optimal spacing between stones.


Counterexample
Do not play a shape move on blind autopilot if precise reading reveals an emergency tactical exception (such as an empty triangle that captures the key cutting stones).

Proverb Variants

“Good shape is half the battle.”
“Play the shape point; let the opponent worry.”
“Beauty in shape is strength in battle.”

proverbs/Strategies/play_to_maximize_you.title: Play To Maximize Your Future Possibilities
proverbs/Strategies/play_to_maximize_you.content:
Core Meaning
A common mistake is playing rigid, definitive moves too early, locking your stones into a single purpose and destroying all latent possibilities (aji). The master plays with an open mind, choosing moves that keep their position flexible and rich with future branching options.
Preserving aji means keeping multiple tactical paths open: depending on how the opponent responds later in the game, your stones can choose to cut, connect, sacrifice, or transform into center influence.

Strategic Connection
Preserving future potential:

Avoid Aji-keshi – do not play forcing ataris that destroy your own latent cutting options
Light structures – deploy stones that can easily adapt if the board changes
Dual-aim maneuvers – position stones so they threaten two distinct future continuations


Classic Go Examples

























SituationRigid Play (Aji-Keshi)Flexible Play (Preserving Aji)Peeping at enemy cutPeeping immediately and forcing solid connectionLeaving the cut open to exploit during a future fightAttacking enemy basePlaying contact atari from the wrong sidePincering from afar, leaving both inside cuts aliveRunning groupCommitting to heavy solid connectionsUsing light knight’s moves that can sacrifice if pinched

Why This Works

Uncertainty restrains the opponent – unplayed aji forces the opponent to play cautiously.
Adapts to whole-board changes – flexibility allows your stones to pivot as new battles ignite.
Multiplies ko threats – preserved defects provide an endless supply of ko threats.


Counterexample
When a specific sequence is completely forced, clearly wins the game on the spot, or resolves an urgent life-and-death crisis, execute it immediately.

Proverb Variants

“Preserve the aji; do not lock the door.”
“Flexibility is life; rigidity is death.”
“Leave multiple paths for tomorrow’s stones.”

proverbs/Strategies/play_urgent_moves_be.title: Play Urgent Moves Before Big Moves (Sente Strategy)
proverbs/Strategies/play_urgent_moves_be.content:
Core Meaning
The strategic hierarchy of Go begins and ends with the classic maxim: “Urgent moves before big moves.” An urgent move (kyusho) resolves the safety of a weak group, severs an enemy connection, or seizes the vital initiative in sente. A big move (daiba) stakes out broad territory in open space.
If you prioritize a big move over an urgent move, the opponent will exploit the urgent weakness, devastate your position in sente, and then still take the big move anyway.

Strategic Connection
Urgent prioritization principles:

Group survival trumps expansion – a dying group costs 30+ points and hands the opponent immense thickness
Seize sente – playing urgent moves forces the opponent to react, keeping the initiative with you
Defend before expanding – an unassailable position allows unrestricted future expansion


Classic Go Examples

























Choice A (Big Move)Choice B (Urgent Move)Strategic MandateEnclosing a 15-point side areaConnecting your 2-liberty cutting groupPlay B immediately — survival comes firstApproaching an open cornerStriking the vital point of an enemy dragonPlay B immediately — attack while the target is weakSliding on the 2nd line for pointsReinforcing a thin wall before it gets cutPlay B immediately — eliminate fatal defects

Why This Works

Urgency compounds – unresolved weaknesses grow more dangerous with every move.
Sente controls the board – urgent moves keep the opponent dancing to your tune.
Territory without safety is an illusion – territory built on top of weak groups collapses instantly.


Counterexample
If an endangered stone is small, disposable, and its capture carries zero whole-board consequence, you can sacrifice it to take a massive whole-board big move.

Proverb Variants

“Urgent moves before big moves.”
“Put out the fire before building the fence.”
“The vital point (kyusho) commands the game.”

proverbs/Strategies/protect_your_early_g.title: Protect Your Early Gains
proverbs/Strategies/protect_your_early_g.content:
Core Meaning
When you secure a favorable opening exchange, capture key stones, or establish a strong corner enclosure, your primary duty is to protect and consolidate your early gains.
Beginners often get reckless after an early success, wandering off to start risky new fights while leaving their newly won territory thin and open to counter-invasions. Consolidating your gains into unassailable bastions locks in your lead and prevents the opponent from staging an easy comeback.

Strategic Connection
Consolidation strategy:

Solidify borders – turn loose frameworks into secure points with timely extensions
Eliminate counter-aji – resolve cutting defects before the opponent can use them
Maintain patience – steady accumulation of secure points leads directly to victory


Classic Go Examples

























Early GainReckless Follow-Up (Bad)Consolidating Master Play (Good)Captured 3 cutting stones in cornerDiving into a wild center fightAdding a solid extension down the side to lock in 25 pointsBuilt a massive 3-stone wallTrying to invade deep enemy territoryExtending 4 spaces from the wall to bank side territorySettled a corner enclosure in sentePlaying random pokesExtending along the side star point to complete the framework

Why This Works

Guarantees the lead – turning potential territory into actual territory prevents reversals.
Deprives opponent of counter-play – gives the trailing opponent no weak targets to attack.
Builds a launching pad – secure gains provide infinite support for future middle-game battles.


Counterexample
Do not over-protect your gains by adding redundant stones inside territory that is already 100% safe. Protect via active extensions and outward-facing moves.

Proverb Variants

“Bank your gold before seeking more treasure.”
“A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.”
“Consolidate strength; then expand.”

proverbs/Strategies/review_your_opponent.title: Review Opponent's Framework Before Expanding
proverbs/Strategies/review_your_opponent.content:
Core Meaning
It is dangerously easy to develop tunnel vision, focusing solely on growing your own territory while completely ignoring the opponent’s growing framework across the board. If both players build frameworks unchallenged, the player with the larger, faster-growing moyo will win effortlessly.
Before expanding your own position, always pause and review the opponent’s framework. If their framework is outpacing yours, you must pivot immediately to reduce or invade before their perimeter becomes impenetrable.

Strategic Connection
Framework evaluation principles:

Speed comparison – measure whose moyo is developing faster
Boundary lines – identify the shared boundary where both frameworks collide
Timing reductions – reduce at the sector line before the moyo turns into solid territory


Classic Go Examples

























Board BalancePassive MistakeProactive StrategyOpponent builds grand SanrenseiGrowing your small side territoryPlaying a light shoulder hit or reduction along the sector lineBoth players have expanding moyosIgnoring the shared center borderPlaying the grand turn (big bend) at the junctionOpponent’s framework is wide openWaiting until it becomes thickInvading early at the 3-3 or side star point

Why This Works

Prevents monstrous moyos – erasing frameworks early is 10x easier than invading later.
Controls whole-board balance – ensures you never fall fatally behind in global territory.
Forces opponent to defend – timely reductions disrupt the opponent’s grand opening designs.


Counterexample
If your own framework is already significantly larger and faster than the opponent’s, you can safely continue expanding your own position and dare the opponent to reduce first.

Proverb Variants

“Look at the whole board before you extend.”
“Do not let the enemy’s shadow engulf your light.”
“Reduce the giant before it grows iron armor.”

proverbs/Strategies/sacrificing_a_few_st.title: Sacrificing Stones Can Lead To Bigger Gains
proverbs/Strategies/sacrificing_a_few_st.content:
Core Meaning
The willingness to sacrifice stones (sute-ishi) is the dividing line between amateur and master Go. Beginners treat every stone as precious and struggle desperately to save every single piece, often creating heavy, dying dragons in the process.
The master understands that stones are currency: giving up 2 or 3 small stones allows you to force the opponent into cramped, heavy shapes, build an impenetrable outside wall, or seize sente for a 30-point triumph elsewhere.

Strategic Connection
Sacrifice mechanics:

Squeeze tesuji (shibori) – sacrificing stones in atari to wrap around the opponent in a solid clump
Lightness (sabaki) – discarding contact stones to settle an invading group with ease
Tempo acceleration – letting the opponent capture in gote while you seize the whole board


Classic Go Examples

























SituationClinging to Stones (Disaster)Master Sacrifice (Triumph)Stone caught in a clampStruggling to escape, getting squeezedSacrificing the stone to seal the outside in senteCutting stone with 2 libertiesRunning it into a netPlaying forcing ataris around it to build an outside wallInvading enemy cornerTrying to live at all costsDiscarding the corner stones to claim dominant center power

Why This Works

Capturing takes time – an opponent spending 2 moves to capture 4 points falls behind in whole-board speed.
Squeeze creates thickness – forced captures leave the capturer overconcentrated and heavy.
Freedom of movement – unburdened by heavy stones, your forces stay fast and versatile.


Counterexample
Never sacrifice vital cutting stones that hold two weak enemy groups split apart. Only sacrifice disposable, non-essential stones.

Proverb Variants

“Give up the tail to save the head.”
“Discard a stone to take a country.”
“Sacrifice is the mother of thickness.”

proverbs/Strategies/separate_your_oppone.title: Separate Opponent's Stones And Keep Yours Connected
proverbs/Strategies/separate_your_oppone.content:
Core Meaning
If Go had to be summarized in a single tactical sentence, it would be: “Keep your own stones connected, and separate the opponent’s stones.”
Connected stones share liberties, defend each other mutually, and form unshakeable living groups. Separated stones are split into multiple struggling factions that must find eyes independently. When you divide an opponent into two weak groups, you can attack both simultaneously—ensuring that at least one will die or surrender massive profit.

Tactical Connection
Splitting and connection fundamentals:

Split to conquer – drive wedges and cuts between enemy formations
Connect for peace – use bamboo joints, solid connections, and kosumi
Double attack power – two weak groups cannot both be defended at once


Classic Go Examples

























StrategyAction On Your StonesAction On Opponent’s StonesFuseki developmentExtending toward allies to maintain connectionPincering to prevent enemy stones from linking upMiddle-game fightingPatching cutting defects with solid connectionsWedging across loose knight’s moves to split their forcesCenter combatKeeping an unbroken escape line to the baseCapping the enemy’s front stone to isolate it from allies

Why This Works

Unity is strength – 1 united group with 8 liberties easily overpowers two groups with 3 liberties each.
Splitting creates double targets – an opponent cannot save two weak groups at the same time.
Fundamental rule of warfare – divide and conquer has governed Go strategy for millennia.


Counterexample
Do not cut through enemy formations if your own cutting stone will immediately be caught in a ladder, net, or shortage of liberties. Cut only when you have the strength to fight.

Proverb Variants

“Connect your own; divide the enemy.”
“A split enemy is a defeated enemy.”
“Unity is life; separation is death.”

proverbs/Strategies/separate_your_oppone.title: Connect With Kosumi And Sever Enemy Stones
proverbs/Strategies/separate_your_oppone.content:
Core Meaning
Preserving your group’s unity while cutting the opponent is the fundamental core of Go tactics. One of the most elegant and dependable techniques for maintaining unbroken connection is the diagonal move (kosumi).
A well-timed kosumi provides a solid, un-cuttable link that avoids creating cutting defects. At the same time, looking for opportunities to wedge or cut across the opponent’s loose knight’s moves divides their army into vulnerable factions.

Tactical Connection
Kosumi connection advantages:

Immune to direct cuts – a kosumi cannot be cut with a single move
Increases liberties – avoids the liberty shortages common in contact crosscuts
Maintains eye potential – diagonal formations naturally curve into living eye pockets


Classic Go Examples
