Tactical ProblemRisky PlayKosumi / Connection Master PlayConnecting two stones under attackPlaying a flat extension that gets wedgedPlaying a kosumi diagonal connectionOpponent peeping at a cutting pointCounter-attacking wildlyConnecting solidly or playing a diagonal connectionSplitting two enemy stonesDiving in with an unsupported crosscutPeeping to weaken the connection, then cutting

Why This Works

Kosumi is un-cuttable – the diagonal link requires two moves for the opponent to break, guaranteeing a connection.
Divided enemies struggle for eyes – splitting an enemy group doubles their need for eye space.
Preserves whole-board initiative – solid connections allow you to attack without worrying about your own safety.


Counterexample
If speed across open terrain is required and no enemy cuts are threatened, a faster one-space jump or knight’s move is superior to a slower kosumi.

Proverb Variants

“The kosumi never fails to connect.”
“Cut the enemy; unite your own.”
“A diagonal step is a step on solid rock.”

proverbs/Strategies/six_die_but_eight_li.title: Six Die, Eight Live (Second Line Life and Death)
proverbs/Strategies/six_die_but_eight_li.content:
Core Meaning
The famous life-and-death proverb “Six die, eight live” (Roku-shi hachi-sei) establishes the definitive survival threshold for a group of stones crawling along the second line of the board:

A straight group of six stones along the second line dies if the opponent attacks the vital points first.
A straight group of seven stones is unsettled (sente decides: whoever plays first lives or kills).
A straight group of eight stones is unconditionally alive; even if the opponent strikes, the group has enough space to make two eyes.


Tactical Connection
Second line survival thresholds:

6 stones (Dead) – insufficient eye space; vulnerable to hane-and-placement kills
7 stones (Unsettled) – urgent! Playing first guarantees life; allowing opponent to strike kills
8 stones (Alive) – safe; no additional defensive moves required


Classic Go Examples

























Stone Count on Line 2StatusStrategic Action6 stones enclosedDeadDefender treats as dead/sacrifice; Attacker can tenuki7 stones enclosedUnsettledUrgent! Play the hane or vital point immediately to settle8 stones enclosedAlive100% safe; play elsewhere in sente

Why This Works

Eye space math – six stones only generate enough internal space for a dead four or bent three under attack.
Eight stones guarantee two compartments – ample internal space to divide into two true eyes.
Instant calculation shortcut – avoids spending precious tournament time calculating basic edge tsumego.


Counterexample
If the group has turns or bends around the corner, or if outside liberties provide emergency squeeze combinations, the basic numerical threshold may change.

Proverb Variants

“Six die, eight live; seven is the battlefield.”
“Eight stones on the second line sleep without fear.”
“Know the numbers of the second line.”

proverbs/Strategies/stay_ahead_on_libert.title: Stay Ahead On Liberties In Local Fights
proverbs/Strategies/stay_ahead_on_libert.content:
Core Meaning
In any local tactical confrontation or capturing race (semeai), liberty superiority is the ultimate decider of life and death. The player with more liberties can play forcing moves, ignore minor threats, and capture the opponent’s stones before their own group is endangered.
In handicap games especially, Black should use initial stones to maintain wide, open shapes with ample liberties, never allowing White to squeeze them into cramped, low-liberty traps.

Tactical Connection
Maintaining liberty superiority:

Extend before turning – an extension (nobi) adds 2 direct liberties
Avoid empty triangles – bad shape reduces your own liberties
Fill outside liberties first – in a semeai, reduce the opponent’s outside liberties before touching shared dame


Classic Go Examples

























Local ConfrontationLow-Liberty Mistake (Loss)High-Liberty Master Play (Win)Contact crosscut fightClumping into a heavy shape with 2 libertiesExtending into open space to reach 4+ libertiesSemeai capturing racePlaying a small endgame pointFilling the opponent’s vital external libertyOpponent attempts a squeezeSubmissively capturing a throw-in stoneExtending outward to maintain breathing room

Why This Works

More liberties = tactical safety – a group with 4+ liberties cannot be captured by sudden ataris.
Forces opponent concessions – the player trailing in liberties must play defensive moves.
Guarantees capturing race victories – winning a semeai by 1 liberty captures the entire enemy group.


Counterexample
Do not waste moves adding unnecessary liberties to a group that is already completely alive with two eyes and no capturing race nearby.

Proverb Variants

“He who holds the liberties holds the life.”
“Breathe deeply before you fight.”
“One more liberty is total victory.”

proverbs/Strategies/the_best_defense_is_.title: The Best Defense Is An Attack
proverbs/Strategies/the_best_defense_is_.content:
Core Meaning
Passive defense—making slow, heavy moves solely to survive—surrenders sente, hands the opponent immense thickness, and leaves you permanently on the back foot. The master understands that “the best defense is an active attack.”
When your group feels uncomfortable, look for a nearby enemy weakness to pressure. By attacking the opponent’s unsettled stones with forcing moves, you fortify your own position from the outside while keeping the opponent scrambling to react.

Strategic Connection
Active defense principles:

Defense in sente – forcing moves strengthen your shape while keeping the initiative
Leaning attacks – attack group A to build the strength needed to defend or attack group B
Psychological dominance – forcing the opponent to defend prevents them from exploiting your own defects


Classic Go Examples

























Defensive NeedPassive Error (Gote)Active Attack (Sente)Your side group feels weakAdding a slow solid connection insidePincering an adjacent enemy stone to build an outside baseRunning center dragonMaking a slow, heavy eyeCapping an enemy stone, building a wall to link up your dragonOpponent threatens to invadeSealing your border in goteInvading the opponent’s weaker flank to dictate the battleground

Why This Works

Keeps the initiative – forcing moves allow you to improve your shape without losing your turn.
Creates outward thickness – attacking stones naturally link up with your defending units.
Denies opponent attacking targets – an opponent busy saving their own stones cannot attack yours.


Counterexample
If your defending group has only 1 liberty or faces an immediate fatal atari, you must play direct defense immediately. You cannot launch an attack from a dead group.

Proverb Variants

“Attack to defend; move forward to survive.”
“Lean on the left to strike the right.”
“He who only defends is already conquered.”

proverbs/Strategies/the_enemy_s_key_poin.title: The Enemy's Key Point Is Your Key Point
proverbs/Strategies/the_enemy_s_key_poin.content:
Core Meaning
One of the most profound observations in Go: “The enemy’s key point is your key point” (Teki no kyusho wa waga kyusho). Whenever an intersection on the board represents a vital junction for your opponent—whether to complete a magnificent shape, connect two dragons, or make eye space—that exact same intersection is equally vital for you.
If you occupy that intersection first, you simultaneously destroy the opponent’s optimal plan while advancing your own strategic goals.

Strategic Connection
Key point dynamics:

Symmetrical importance – points that grant life to the defender grant a lethal attack to the attacker
Miai balance – seizing the single point that dictates the flow of the entire sector
Double value – worth double because it gives you a plus while handing the opponent a minus


Classic Go Examples

























Tactical SituationOpponent’s Dream MoveYour Master StrikeOpponent has a straight three eye spacePlaying the center to liveStrike the center vital point to killOpponent aims to bend at head of 2 stonesBending at the head to dominatePlay the hane at the head firstCenter moyo junctionOpponent jumping to expand their moyoPlay the capping reduction at that exact spot

Why This Works

Neutralizes enemy plans instantly – occupying their best move renders their preparation useless.
Maximum swing value – the swing between you playing the point vs opponent playing it is 20–40 points.
Simplifies candidate moves – reading the opponent’s best reply points directly to your own best move.


Counterexample
If occupying the enemy’s key point results in your stone being immediately captured in a ladder or net with no compensation, find an alternative way to neutralize the point.

Proverb Variants

“The enemy’s vital point is your vital point.”
“Take what the opponent desires.”
“Stand where the enemy wishes to build.”

proverbs/Strategies/the_enemy_s_vital_po.title: The Enemy's Vital Point Is Your Vital Point
proverbs/Strategies/the_enemy_s_vital_po.content:
Core Meaning
In tactical fighting and life and death, the intersection that solves the opponent’s problems is almost always the exact move that solves yours. The proverb “The enemy’s vital point is your vital point” (Teki no kyusho wa waga kyusho) is the master key for solving tsumego and discovering brilliant tesujis.
When searching for the killing move or the critical shape defense, ask: “If it were my opponent’s turn, where would they desperately want to play?” That intersection is your answer.

Tactical Connection
Vital point (kyusho) applications:

Life and death – the point that divides internal space into two eyes is the point that kills
Connection battles – the point that completes an unbreakable bamboo joint is the point to wedge
Shape destruction – the eye point of a tiger’s mouth is the point for a throw-in


Classic Go Examples

























Tactical PuzzleOpponent’s Defensive PointAttacker’s Vital StrikeBent three eye shapeCorner vertex (bend) makes 2 eyesStrike the corner vertex to killBulky five eye spaceCenter intersection livesPlunge into the center to execute nakadeKnight’s move waistOpponent connects the diagonalCut through the waist of the keima

Why This Works

Geometry is universal – vital intersections have physical shape properties that benefit both colors.
Reveals hidden tesujis – shifts perspective to look through the opponent’s eyes.
Eliminates tactical doubt – striking the vital point forces an immediate resolution.


Counterexample
Verify whole-board liberties. If striking the vital point puts your own stone in self-atari because of low outside liberties, reinforce first.

Proverb Variants

“The spot they need is the spot you take.”
“The vital point (kyusho) belongs to whoever claims it first.”
“Look through the enemy’s eyes to find the strike.”

proverbs/Strategies/the_first_move_in_th.title: Master Common Joseki In The Corner
proverbs/Strategies/the_first_move_in_th.content:
Core Meaning
Corner sequences in Go have been studied and refined for centuries into established patterns known as Joseki. The first moves in the corner set the entire trajectory for the match: they establish local territory, determine which player takes outside influence, and dictate the balance of sente and gote.
Learning standard, reliable joseki sequences ensures you maximize the efficiency of your early stones and avoid falling into devastating opening traps.

Strategic Connection
Joseki mastery benefits:

Opening efficiency – guarantees an equitable distribution of points and power
Direction of play harmony – choose josekis whose resulting walls face your friendly stones
Avoid opening disasters – protects against trick plays (hamete) and overplays


Classic Go Examples

























Opening ChoiceJoseki ObjectiveKey Whole-Board Consideration4-4 Point (Hoshi)Flexible, influence-oriented developmentChoose variations that project power toward your side extensions3-4 Point (Komoku)Balance of solid territory and side growthEnclose with a shimari or settle with a low approach3-3 Point (Sansan)Immediate, rock-solid corner cashAccept that opponent gets outside center thickness

Why This Works

Joseki represents proven balance – each player receives fair compensation when played correctly.
Corner efficiency is paramount – mistakes in the corner cost 15–20 points immediately.
Sets up whole-board synergy – proper joseki selection harmonizes with the rest of your board.


Counterexample
Do not play joseki on blind autopilot! A joseki that is locally balanced can be a catastrophic whole-board blunder if its resulting wall faces directly into an opponent’s impenetrable thickness. Always choose joseki based on the whole board.

Proverb Variants

“Learn joseki; then forget joseki.”
“The corner sets the board.”
“A good joseki serves the whole board.”

proverbs/Strategies/the_first_move_in_th.title: The First Move In The Corner Is Most Valuable
proverbs/Strategies/the_first_move_in_th.content:
Core Meaning
The four corners of the board are the most valuable real estate in Go. Because the board edges provide two natural protective boundaries, securing territory in the corner requires half the stones needed on the side and a quarter of the stones needed in the center.
The very first stone played in a corner claims a powerful anchor. Securing or approaching corners early establishes a foundation of points and life that supports your entire game.

Strategic Connection
Corner value hierarchy:

Corner points (Maximum value) – stake out 4-4, 3-4, 3-3, or 3-5 points immediately
Corner enclosures (shimari) – a two-stone corner enclosure is worth 15–20 solid points
Corner approaches (kakari) – prevents the opponent from making an uncontested enclosure


Classic Go Examples






























Move PriorityBoard ActionValuePriority 1Claiming an empty corner15–20 points of potentialPriority 2Enclosing your corner or approaching opponent’s12–15 pointsPriority 3Extending along the side star point8–10 pointsPriority 4Wandering into the center in early fusekiLow value in early opening

Why This Works

Corner physics – the corner requires only 2 walls of stones to enclose safe territory.
Easy eye formation – corner groups make two eyes effortlessly.
Anchors the board – secure corners grant you the tactical freedom to fight boldly elsewhere.


Counterexample
Once the corners are settled, do not linger in the corner playing small 2-point endgame plays. Transition immediately to side extensions and framework development.

Proverb Variants

“Corners are gold, sides silver, center grass.”
“The first stone in the corner reigns supreme.”
“Secure the corner to rule the board.”

proverbs/Strategies/two_stones_die_but_t.title: Two Stones Die, Three Live
proverbs/Strategies/two_stones_die_but_t.content:
Core Meaning
The proverb “Two stones die, but three live” (Ni-shi shi, san-sei) highlights the physical stability required to create a living base along the edge of the board.
A formation of only two connected stones on the second line is fragile and easily surrounded, squeezed, and killed. But adding a third stone creates the necessary span of internal breathing room and liberties to ensure unconditional life or a successful escape into the center.

Tactical Connection
Stone stability thresholds:

2 stones on edge – highly vulnerable to hane at the head, clamp, and liberty starvation
3 stones on edge – sturdy foundation that can divide into eyes or push forward safely
Liberty jump – the third stone increases liberties from 3 to 5+, preventing instant atari traps


Classic Go Examples

























Edge FormationVulnerabilityProper Shape Adjustment2 stones crawled on line 2Opponent hanes at the head and killsExtend to 3 stones (nobi) to secure stability2-stone cutting unit surroundedShort of liberties; dead in a netExtend to 3 stones to break the net and escape2 stones in corner pocketDead to a single vital point strikeAdd a stone to form a tiger’s mouth or 3-stone base

Why This Works

Structural threshold – three stones in line or bend provide enough anchor points for eye shape.
Liberty safety margin – 3 stones resist crosscuts and double ataris that easily crush 2 stones.
Directional power – three stones project forward momentum that cannot be stopped by a single block.


Counterexample
If your two stones already have an open escape route into the center or link to friendly living thickness, you do not need to add a third stone on the edge.

Proverb Variants

“Two stones wobble; three stones stand firm.”
“Three stones on the edge make a living base.”
“Add the third stone to see the light.”

proverbs/Strategies/two_weak_groups_are_.title: Two Weak Groups Are Dangerous; Strengthen Or Connect
proverbs/Strategies/two_weak_groups_are_.content:
Core Meaning
The proverb “Two weak groups are dangerous; strengthen one or connect them” is an urgent warning against spreading your defensive forces too thin. Defending one weak group is manageable; defending two weak groups simultaneously is nearly impossible.
When you have two weak groups, the opponent can launch a splitting attack (ryo-garami), attacking both in alternation. Defending group A leaves group B exposed, and defending group B lets group A collapse. You must immediately unite them or sacrifice one to ensure the other’s survival.

Strategic Connection
Managing two weak groups:

Connect them – link the two groups into a single, unified army with combined liberties
Settle one immediately – make one group completely alive so you only have one problem to manage
Sacrifice if necessary – abandon the smaller group lightly rather than trying to rescue both


Classic Go Examples

























DilemmaFatal Error (Trying to Save Both)Masterful SolutionTwo floating center groupsJumping both forward separatelyPlaying a connecting move (bamboo joint) to join themCorner group weak, side group weakPlaying tenuki to take pointsPlaying a solid base move to make the corner 100% aliveOpponent drives a wedge between two unitsStruggling on both sidesDiscarding the smaller unit as a sacrifice to save the larger

Why This Works

Eliminates double attacks – one strong group gives the opponent zero splitting leverage.
Halves defensive turns – you no longer have to spend two moves for every one move the opponent plays.
Restores whole-board initiative – once your position is consolidated, you can resume attacking.


Counterexample
If both groups have ample liberties and multiple clear paths to connect to friendly outside thickness, they are not genuinely weak.

Proverb Variants

“Never have two weak groups on the board.”
“Two weak groups cannot both cross the river.”
“Connect your weak stones or mourn them.”

proverbs/Strategies/two_weak_groups_will.title: Two Weak Groups Will Get You Into Trouble
proverbs/Strategies/two_weak_groups_will.content:
Core Meaning
Having two unsettled groups on the board is a guaranteed recipe for defeat. When an opponent spots two weak targets, they do not need to kill both to win: they can simply lean on one group to build the strength needed to annihilate the other.
This proverb instructs players facing this crisis to focus their efforts: do not split your attention. Choose the more valuable group, fortify it with solid shape, or connect the two groups directly so that your stones can breathe as one.

Tactical Connection
Double weak group dynamics:

Splitting attack danger – opponent plays moves that attack group 1 on the left and group 2 on the right
Concentrate resources – focus all moves on establishing an unassailable base for the primary group
Lightness – be willing to treat the secondary group as a light sacrifice


Classic Go Examples

























ScenarioDivided Attention (Defeat)Concentrated Play (Victory)Opponent pincers two separate stonesTrying to make small life for bothConnecting the two stones with a leaping jumpCorner under siege, center dragon eyelessSplitting moves between bothMaking the corner unconditionally alive in sente, then running centerOpponent attacks with a capCounter-attacking with the weaker unitPulling back to link up with friendly allies

Why This Works

One living group is better than two dead ones – concentrating ensures at least one survives.
Connection dissolves weakness – uniting two units pools their liberties and eye potential.
Frustrates the attacker – deprives the opponent of their favorite weapon: the double attack.


Counterexample
If your opponent also has two weak groups, the game becomes a complex four-way race where attacking their weaker unit first can save both of yours.

Proverb Variants

“Two weak groups bring certain ruin.”
“Save the child before you save the baggage.”
“United they stand; divided they fall.”

proverbs/Strategies/use_simple_joseki_th.title: Use Simple Joseki That Strengthen Your Position
proverbs/Strategies/use_simple_joseki_th.content:
Core Meaning
In handicap games and practical tournament play, complex, sharp joseki variations often create endless tactical complications that favor the stronger player. The proverb advises: “Use simple joseki that strengthen your position.”
Simple josekis (such as extending solidly, taking the corner, or jumping out cleanly) leave behind zero cutting points, give you solid territory, and preserve whole-board stability. When your corners are simple and strong, the opponent cannot find the chaos they need to stage a comeback.

Strategic Connection
Simple joseki benefits:

Zero tactical defects – eliminates double cuts, ladders, and tricky complications
Fast resolution – settles the local situation cleanly so you can focus on the whole board
Preserves handicap power – allows your natural stone advantage to shine


Classic Go Examples

























Opponent’s MoveComplicated Response (Risky)Simple Joseki (Safe & Strong)White attaches to 4-4 stonePlaying complex counter-hanes and crosscutsExtending solidly (nobi), taking guaranteed side powerWhite plays a 3-3 invasionTrying a sharp, complicated blocking variationStandard blocking and connecting, building a massive wallWhite plays a high pincerLaunching a double-counter-pincer brawlJumping to the center or sliding into the corner to settle

Why This Works

Eliminates trick plays (hamete) – simple shapes cannot be tricked.
Maintains whole-board harmony – solid corners support active play across all sides.
Reduces calculation errors – clean positions leave no room for reading blunders.


Counterexample
If you are far behind in the endgame or trailing heavily in points, playing “simple joseki” may be too passive; in that case, you must choose more aggressive, complex variations to fight for the lead.

Proverb Variants

“Simple joseki, solid victory.”
“Do not walk into the opponent’s labyrinth.”
“The simplest stone is often the strongest.”

proverbs/Strategies/use_your_handicap_st.title: Use Handicap Stones To Secure Corners Quickly
proverbs/Strategies/use_your_handicap_st.content:
Core Meaning
In handicap Go, Black begins with stones already occupying the star points (hoshi) in every corner. These stones give Black a massive head start, but a star-point stone by itself does not enclose corner territory—it can still be invaded at the 3-3 point.
To transform this starting advantage into permanent, unassailable territory, Black should use early moves to secure corner enclosures (shimari) quickly. Adding a single knight’s move or one-space jump to a star point turns the corner into a secure fortress of 15–20 points.

Strategic Connection
Handicap corner enclosure strategy:

Lock in points early – turn potential frameworks into guaranteed territory
Deny White easy invasions – prevent White from sliding under or invading at 3-3
Anchor the board – secure corners provide safe launching pads to attack White’s approaches


Classic Go Examples

























Board SetupPassive MistakeSound Handicap PlayStar point corner untouchedLetting White approach and take the corner baseEnclosing with a knight’s move enclosure (keima shimari)White approaches from one sideBacking away into defenseBacking off solidly or enclosing the other flank to secure the cornerMultiple handicap cornersChasing White in the centerEnclosing two or three corners to build a 50-point territorial bank

Why This Works

Corners are the fastest points – securing four corners builds an insurmountable point lead.
Removes White’s counter-targets – safe corners leave White with nowhere to attack.
Maximizes initial handicap investment – fully activates the star-point stones.


Counterexample
Do not spend three or four moves over-protecting a single corner. Once an enclosure is made, look outward to the sides and other corners.

Proverb Variants

“Enclose the corner; secure the star.”
“A corner enclosed is a battle won.”
“Turn handicap stars into golden fortresses.”

proverbs/Strategies/use_your_stones_to_s.title: Use Your Stones To Split The Opponent's Groups
proverbs/Strategies/use_your_stones_to_s.content:
Core Meaning
In both even and handicap games, the most effective way to turn your stone strength into victory is to drive wedges between the opponent’s groups. When an opponent attempts to connect two separate formations across open board space, placing a stone between them splits their army into two struggling units.
Dividing the enemy prevents them from sharing liberties or pooling their eye space. Once split, both groups must fight for survival simultaneously.

Tactical Connection
Splitting techniques:

Splitting attack (ryo-garami) – attack two separated groups in alternation
Cap between groups – play in the center corridor to block mutual escape routes
Wedge tesuji (warikomi) – push between two loose stones to sever their connection


Classic Go Examples

























Opponent’s PositionPassivity (Letting Connect)Splitting Master PlayOpponent has 2 units on top sideLetting them connect with a one-space jumpPlaying a splitting move right in the center to isolate bothOpponent’s corner tries to link to sideDefending your own boundaryWedging between the units to keep them permanently separatedTwo enemy dragons runningAttacking one from the outsideCapping between both dragons to attack them simultaneously

Why This Works

Doubles the opponent’s defensive burden – the defender must spend two moves to answer one of yours.
Guarantees profit – even if one group lives, the other group will be captured or yield massive outside points.
Dictates the board flow – keeps the opponent permanently on the defensive.


Counterexample
Do not attempt a splitting move if your own splitting stone will be surrounded and captured immediately without support. Ensure you have nearby thickness to back the split.

Proverb Variants

“Split the enemy army; conquer both halves.”
“Drive a wedge through their line.”
“Between two enemy camps lies the winning strike.”

proverbs/Strategies/watch_for_opportunit.title: Watch For Opportunities To Invade
proverbs/Strategies/watch_for_opportunit.content:
Core Meaning
While solid defense and steady development are fundamental, you cannot win Go by defending alone. As the game develops, you must actively watch for opportunities to invade the opponent’s frameworks before they solidify into permanent, impenetrable territory.
An invasion is not a reckless gamble; it is a timed tactical operation. The ideal moment to invade is when the opponent’s framework is wide and loose, your own groups are stable, and you have clear routes for sabaki or escape.

Strategic Connection
Invasion timing and principles:

Timing is everything – invade before the opponent plays a move that seals the boundary
Base requirements – ensure your own nearby groups are safe before launching an invasion
Light play (sabaki) – invading stones should remain light, flexible, and ready to sacrifice


Classic Go Examples

























Opponent’s FrameworkTimingTactical ChoiceWide 5-space side extensionBefore opponent reinforcesInvade on the 3rd line to steal the base and live4-4 corner stone un-enclosedEarly to mid fusekiInvade at the 3-3 point to take guaranteed corner cashLarge central moyoWhen boundary is loosePlay a shoulder hit or deep reduction along the sector line

Why This Works

Punctures enemy balloons – destroys 20–30 points of anticipated territory in one strike.
Forces opponent to fight on your terms – an invader playing lightly can easily find eyes or link up.
Maintains territorial parity – prevents the opponent from running away with an unassailable lead.


Counterexample
Never invade deeply if your own surrounding groups are weak or on fire. Fix your urgent problems first; otherwise, the opponent will counter-attack and kill both.

Proverb Variants

“Strike while the fence is still open.”
“Invade with light feet; do not leave heavy tracks.”
“A framework un-invaded is territory conceded.”

proverbs/Strategies/when_approaching_the.title: when_approaching_the_enemy_corner_choose_your_approach_height_wisely_explanation_low_appro
proverbs/Strategies/when_approaching_the.content:

title: “Choose Approach Height Wisely: Low vs High”
tags:

Strategy

Corner

Core Meaning
When approaching an opponent’s corner stone, the height of your stoneâ€”low (third line) or **high (fourth line)**â€”defines your strategic objective for the entire sector of the board:

A low approach (3rd line) is territorial and base-oriented: it dives under the corner to carve out a secure eye base along the edge and steal the opponent’s corner points.
A high approach (4th line) is influence- and center-oriented: it looks outward toward the center and adjacent sides, seeking thickness and attacking power rather than quick local cash.

Choosing your approach height based on the whole-board context ensures your stones harmonize with your overall plan.

Strategic Connection
Height selection criteria:

Choose Low (3rd line) â€“ when you need a secure, independent living base or when the side territory is large
Choose High (4th line) â€“ when you want outward thickness to support a center moyo or reduce enemy influence
Coordinate with allies â€“ match the height of your approach to the existing stones on the adjacent flank


Classic Go Examples






























Whole-Board ContextOptimal Approach HeightStrategic RationaleOpponent has a strong side wallLow Approach (3rd line)Slides underneath to establish a fast living baseYou have a grand center moyoHigh Approach (4th line)Builds center thickness to expand your grand frameworkOpponent has a 4-4 stoneLow Knight’s ApproachStandard balance between base and pressureOpponent has a 3-4 stoneHigh ApproachPrevents opponent from pressing you down on the lower line

Why This Works

Aligns tactics with strategy â€“ prevents playing high when you need eyes, or playing low when you need influence.
Third line equals cash; Fourth line equals power â€“ fundamental law of Go board lines.
Adapts to opponent thickness â€“ avoids getting sealed into low lines against thick enemy positions.


Counterexample
Do not play low approaches if the opponent can easily press your stone down onto the second line with devastating outward thickness.

Proverb Variants

“Low for base, high for space.”
“Third line takes the gold; fourth line commands the sky.”
“Approach with the height that fits the horizon.”

proverbs/Strategies/when_approaching_the.title: Low Approaches Secure Territory; High Build Influence
proverbs/Strategies/when_approaching_the.content:
Core Meaning
This proverb crystallizes the fundamental trade-off of corner approaches: “Low approaches secure territory; high approaches build influence.”
When you approach on the third line, your stone directly challenges the opponent’s corner base and can slide easily along the second line to live locally. When you approach on the fourth line, you willingly sacrifice immediate side territory to project power toward the center.
Deciding between cash territory and center power should never be arbitrary—let the whole board dictate your choice.

Strategic Connection
Strategic trade-offs:

Third line (Low) – guaranteed points, lower risk, faster eye formation, but flatter shape
Fourth line (High) – superior center mobility, combats enemy frameworks, but leaves the base open to undercutting
Balance – strong players alternate low and high moves to create a dynamic, balanced board posture


Classic Go Examples

























Strategy GoalApproach ChoiceFollow-Up ActionEstablishing a fast side baseLow knight’s approachSlide with suberi to secure two eyesFighting for center controlHigh approach (4th line)Jump into the center or build a wall facing your alliesReducing opponent’s side frameworkHigh approachKeep stones light and mobile to avoid getting trapped

Why This Works

Line physics – 3rd-line stones face the edge; 4th-line stones face the open center.
Determines joseki branch – your approach height steers the opponent into specific joseki responses.
Whole-board harmony – matching approach height to friendly stones creates unbeatable synergy.


Counterexample
If your opponent already has an impenetrable wall directly behind your intended low approach, playing low will trap you against the wall. Play high to stay mobile.

Proverb Variants

“The third line feeds the stomach; the fourth line feeds the soul.”
“Low makes life; high makes power.”
“Choose your line before you touch the corner.”

proverbs/Strategies/when_you_re_ahead_av.title: When You're Ahead, Avoid Needless Fighting
proverbs/Strategies/when_you_re_ahead_av.content:
Core Meaning
One of the most essential rules of tournament Go and game management: “When you are ahead, avoid needless fighting.”
When your territory count gives you a comfortable 10- or 15-point lead, you have already won the game—provided nothing dies. Starting complex, speculative fights, launching greedy deep invasions, or starting wild ko battles only introduces volatility and gives the opponent a chance to turn the game around.
Solidify your boundaries, connect your groups, play clean endgame moves, and cruise safely to victory.

Strategic Connection
Victory consolidation principles:

Reduce variance – the only thing that can defeat a winning player is a catastrophic tactical blunder
Honest moves (honte) – choose the solid connection over the fancy counter-cut
Let the opponent struggle – the trailing player must create complications; do not help them


Classic Go Examples

























SituationGreedy Mistake (Risking the Win)Masterful Play (Securing the Win)Leading by 15 points in endgameInvading deep enemy territory to “win by 30”Closing your borders in sente and banking the 15-point winOpponent starts a desperate koFighting the ko aggressivelyConnecting the ko cleanly to eliminate all counter-playOpponent overplays in centerEngaging in an all-or-nothing capture raceDefending your own living group, letting them live small

Why This Works

Winning by 0.5 points is complete victory – extra points do not count for extra wins in the tournament record.
Chaos is the trailing player’s ally – eliminating chaos extinguishes their only path to victory.
Calmness demoralizes the opponent – an opponent who realizes you will not give them tactical gifts will resign peacefully.


Counterexample
“Avoiding fighting” does not mean playing timidly submissive moves that surrender 20 points for free. Answer legitimate threats firmly while avoiding unprovoked brawls.

Proverb Variants

“The rich man does not quarrel.”
“When ahead, simplify; when behind, complicate.”
“A win by half a point is a masterpiece.”

terms/approach-move.title: Approach Move
terms/approach-move.content: A stone played near an opponent’s corner to reduce their territorial potential or establish your own footing.

terms/approaches.title: Approaches
terms/approaches.content:
Moves that challenge an opponent’s corner position by placing a stone nearby. Approaches can be high (4th line) for influence or low (3rd line) for secure territory.
Approaches in Go
Approach moves are opening plays aimed at challenging an opponent’s corner stone. The height of your approach usually reflects your goal: lower approaches are more territorial, while higher approaches emphasize influence and outside development.

terms/byoyomi.content: Overtime system where players have a limited number of periods (typically 30 seconds) to make moves after main time expires. Critical for time management in professional play.

terms/chinese-fuseki.content: An opening strategy placing a stone at the star point, then an approach, aiming to build a large framework quickly.

terms/dame.content: Neutral points on the board with no territorial value. They are filled in only during the endgame to complete the board.

terms/damezumari.content: Liberty shortage - critical in capturing races. Groups with damezumari often die unless they can create new liberties.

terms/dan.content: Advanced rank for expert players (1d-9d). Reaching 1d (shodan) marks the transition from amateur kyu ranks to mastery.
